# Wiz standard library reference

Generated from the elaborated modules: 95 modules, 5990 declarations, 7657 signatures, 56 operator notations. The table of contents links every section and declaration; a name in a doc comment links to its entry. Regenerate with `wiz doc --lib --reference docs/reference`.

## Contents

- [Notation and precedence](#notation)
- [BitBlast](#module-BitBlast) (167 declarations) — Bits of numbers and words, for bit-blasting (`import BitBlast`; stage 28d).
- [BitVec](#module-BitVec) (42 declarations) — Bit vectors of width `n` (`import BitVec`): a `Nat` below `2^n`. The bound is kept by construction (every operation reduces mod `2^n`), not by a proof (decision HD3; a proof-carrying subtype may come later). Arithmetic wraps around. Bit 0 is the least significant.
- [BitVecAdd](#module-BitVecAdd) (30 declarations) — The 34-bit carry/borrow adder in word form (`import BitVecAdd`).
- [BitVecShift](#module-BitVecShift) (49 declarations) — Shift lemmas for the hardware barrel shifter (`import BitVecShift`).
- [BvDecide](#module-BvDecide) (35 declarations) — `bv_decide` (stage 28d): an equation of words decided by SAT, with no new trust. `import BvDecide`.
- [Deriving](#module-Deriving) (68 declarations) — Deriving (HD8). `inductive T … deriving C` and `deriving instance C for T` run C's *deriver*: a Wiz function `Deriver := String → MacroM (List Syntax)`, registered with `attribute [deriver C] f`. It looks the type up (`MacroM.getInductive`) and returns the commands that make the instance. This module defines three classes, their derivers, and instances for the prelude's types.
- [Eff](#module-Eff) (70 declarations) — Algebraic effects as a library (stage 10).
- [EffHeap](#module-EffHeap) (19 declarations) — Heap cells as an effect (lib/Eff.wiz) interpreted into the heap programs of separation logic (lib/Hoare.wiz): the effect observation of plan S7 for state, and the reason `Commute` is not needed for state on different cells. docs/resources.md tells how this fits with Feral and the optics; wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md, M3.
- [Feral](#module-Feral) (341 declarations) — Feral (docs/stages/22-numbers.md, 22j) is a small Rust inside Wiz:
- [Functor](#module-Functor) (15 declarations) — Functors and applicative functors (stage 13d): `import Functor`.
- [Grail](#module-Grail) (71 declarations) — The vocabulary of grail's build files (stage 23d; docs/stages/23-grail.md). A package's `grail.wiz` defines `package : Package`, and the uncommitted `grail.local.wiz` defines `local : Settings` (this machine's settings: the toolchain, extra module roots). grail evaluates them and reads the result as an S-expression (`Package.render`, `Settings.render`), so a build file is an ordinary Wiz program built from the functions here.
- [HProp](#module-HProp) (82 declarations) — A shallow separation logic over a model heap (stage 24b), after Charguéraud's *Separation Logic Foundations* (Software Foundations vol. 6, "SLF"), chapters Hprop and Himpl. The program logic built on it is in `Hoare` (lib/Hoare.wiz).
- [Handle](#module-Handle) (18 declarations) — Owned handles (`import Handle`; cohesion step M6, wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md; docs/libraries.md).
- [Hdl.Apb](#module-Hdl.Apb) (17 declarations) — A thin AMBA APB bridge for `Hdl.Bus` (`import Hdl.Apb`). `Bus` is the internal single-outstanding, AXI4-Lite-shaped valid/ready bus (`Bus.ReqW` with byte strobes); this file does not add a fourth protocol, it maps that bus onto the APB signal set, in both directions:
- [Hdl.Arty](#module-Hdl.Arty) (11 declarations) — The Digilent Arty A7 (Artix-7 in a CSG324 package): its resources as an XDC pin table (`Hdl.Xdc`), and the two devices it comes with.
- [Hdl.Axi4](#module-Hdl.Axi4) (59 declarations) — The AXI4 burst subset of ARM IHI 0022, over `Hdl.Bus` (`import Hdl.Axi4`). `Hdl.AxiLite` gives the five AXI4-Lite channels the ARM names but stays at one beat per transfer; this module adds the burst fields and the burst adapters:
- [Hdl.Axi4Law](#module-Hdl.Axi4Law) (39 declarations) — The obligations of the AXI4 burst adapters in `Hdl.Axi4`, stated over value traces as in `Hdl.BusLaw` and `Hdl.ProtocolLaw`. `examples/hdl-axi4.wiz` (test group `bus-protocol`) evaluates the Boolean forms on INCR and WRAP bursts with a stalling bus slave, at the same time as it compares the value simulation, `Netlist.simulate` and `Circuit.simFast`. They are **tested, not proved**; only the small lemmas at the end are kernel-checked.
- [Hdl.AxiLite](#module-Hdl.AxiLite) (14 declarations) — AXI4-Lite channel bundles for `Hdl.Bus` (`import Hdl.AxiLite`). `Bus` is already the single-outstanding, AXI4-Lite-shaped core: `Bus.ReqW` is a write with `WSTRB` or a read, and `Bus.Resp` is the corresponding `B`/`R` answer. This file gives the ARM channel names a concrete shape so a design can expose them, rather than inventing another bus:
- [Hdl.Bits](#module-Hdl.Bits) (48 declarations) — Bit-level reasoning for circuits (`import Hdl.Bits`): the laws of one-bit signals at values, so that a proof does not dictate how control logic is written (finding C2 of the iCEstick toy CPU: `rfl` reduces a multiplexer on a known select, but not `Hw.and (Hw.lit 1 0) x` on a symbolic `x`). Design: wiz-notes/cohesion-hardware.md, 2.3.
- [Hdl.Bus](#module-Hdl.Bus) (61 declarations) — A small, board-independent valid/ready bus (`import Hdl.Bus`): a request/response record, a two-master round-robin arbiter, an address decode/route helper, and a behavioural RAM for simulation. It generalises the golem SoC's `GBus`/`Bus.wiz` (`wiz-rv/src/Rv/Golem/Bus.wiz`): the golem bus hard-codes a 32-bit address, 32-bit data, golem's DDR window and a 28-bit cache port; here the address and data widths are parameters and nothing knows a board or a memory map.
- [Hdl.BusLaw](#module-Hdl.BusLaw) (70 declarations) — The protocol laws of `Hdl.Bus` (`import Hdl.BusLaw`), stated as predicates over the value traces of a circuit, plus the small proofs the HDL model supports. The example `examples/hdl-bus-law.wiz` (test group `bus-law`) checks every predicate exhaustively or on long pseudo-random traces, and checks the value simulation, `Netlist.simulate` and `Circuit.simFast` against each other at the same time. A law checked that way is *tested, not proved*: the predicate is a `Prop`, the check is a Boolean function that was evaluated on its inputs, and only the lemmas marked as kernel-checked below are proved.
- [Hdl.Cdc](#module-Hdl.Cdc) (5 declarations) — Clock-domain crossings (`import Hdl.Cdc`).
- [Hdl.Core](#module-Hdl.Core) (622 declarations) — The HDL library (`import Hdl.Core`): describe digital circuits in Wiz, simulate them, prove things about them, and synthesise them to a netlist, Verilog, a test bench, a VCD waveform and pin constraints. docs/libraries.md ("H14 S0", "H14 S1") describes it; design notes are in drafts/hdl/Synth.wiz and wiz-notes/hdl-usability.md.
- [Hdl.Crc](#module-Hdl.Crc) (22 declarations) — CRC-8/SMBUS (polynomial `x^8 + x^2 + x + 1` = `0x07`, initial value 0, most significant bit first, no reflection, no final xor), twice: as hardware, one byte per clock cycle, and as a function on numbers, which is what a host computes. It is the CRC of the iCEstick project (`wiz-icestick-uart/src/Icestick/Crc.wiz`) with the board-specific vocabulary removed, so any design can use it.
- [Hdl.Ddr](#module-Hdl.Ddr) (14 declarations) — The native port of a DDR3 controller, as a thin interface (`import Hdl.Ddr`), and a fixed-latency model of it for simulation. The real controller lives in the wiz-ddr3 repository (`Ddr3.Ctrl`): importing it here would make this library depend on that repository's modules, so this module keeps only the part that is common to any controller -- the request/response handshake -- and documents the mapping.
- [Hdl.Display](#module-Hdl.Display) (69 declarations) — The command, data and address-window layer of the SSD1306 (128 × 64 or 128 × 32, monochrome) and SSD1331 (96 × 64, RGB 565) OLED controllers (`import Hdl.Display`). It is the reusable part of the OLED project (`wiz-icestick-uart`'s `Icestick.Oled`, `Icestick.OledRgb` and their Arty ports), with the panel models, the power switches, the effect generators and the frame timing left to the design.
- [Hdl.Mem](#module-Hdl.Mem) (60 declarations) — A small memory interface for hardware proofs (`import Hdl.Mem`), on the memory model of `Hdl.Core` (`HwTy.mem aw dw`, read with `Hw.memRead`, written with `Hw.memWrite`).
- [Hdl.Netlist](#module-Hdl.Netlist) (18 declarations) — A `Circuit` (`Hdl.Core`) has two simulations: the value simulation `Circuit.run` (the Mealy step at `HwTy.El` values) and the netlist simulation `Netlist.simulate` (the synthesised netlist's nodes). They are different programs, so their agreement is a theorem, not a definition. This file proves it for the *Mealy core* subset:
- [Hdl.Optic](#module-Hdl.Optic) (12 declarations) — Optics for HDL bundles (`import Hdl.Optic`). Design: wiz-notes/cohesion-hardware.md, 2.2; the optics are lib/Optic.wiz's.
- [Hdl.Pipe](#module-Hdl.Pipe) (52 declarations) — An *arrow* language for pipelines over `Circuit` (`import Hdl.Pipe`). A `Pipe i o` is a `Circuit i o` with its latency in cycles; the combinators compose circuits and add the latencies. It is additive: `Hdl.Core`'s `Circuit`/`Multi` semantics are unchanged, and a `Pipe` lowers to a `Circuit` (`Pipe.circuit`), so `Circuit.run`, `Circuit.netlist`, `Netlist.simulate`, `Hdl.Sim`'s `simFast`, `Verilog.emit` and all the `Circuit` lemmas apply unchanged.
- [Hdl.Prim](#module-Hdl.Prim) (41 declarations) — Primitive instances: vendor cells (an FPGA's I/O buffers, SERDES, PLLs, …) as black boxes in the HDL (`Hw.prim`; `Prim` and the netlist's `NetOp.inst` are in Hdl.Core, this module has the rest). A `Prim i o` declares one: its Verilog module name, parameters, a port name per leaf of its input and output codes, and optionally a behavioural model at values. At the wire instance a primitive is one netlist node (`NetOp.inst`) that `Verilog.emit` prints as a module instance; at values it is its model.
- [Hdl.ProtocolLaw](#module-Hdl.ProtocolLaw) (50 declarations) — The obligations of the protocol bridges in `Hdl.Apb` and `Hdl.Wishbone`, plus the `Bus.ReqW` (byte-strobe) form of the bus stability laws. Like `Hdl.BusLaw`, these are predicates over value traces and Boolean one-step forms; `examples/hdl-protocols.wiz` evaluates the Boolean forms on generated traces at the same time as it compares the value simulation, `Netlist.simulate` and `Circuit.simFast`. They are **tested, not proved** on those inputs.
- [Hdl.Sim](#module-Hdl.Sim) (41 declarations) — Fast netlist simulation for compiled programs (`import Hdl.Sim`).
- [Hdl.Spi](#module-Hdl.Spi) (30 declarations) — A mode 0 SPI master (`import Hdl.Spi`): CPOL = 0 (the clock idles low) and CPHA = 0 (data is sampled on the rising edge and shifted out on the falling edge), an 8-bit transfer, and a configurable divider. One bit takes `2 * div` clock cycles: `div` with the clock low, then `div` with it high. `div` is a meta-level `Nat` (1 … 65536) and only reaches the netlist as the constant the half-period counter is compared with.
- [Hdl.Temporal](#module-Hdl.Temporal) (60 declarations) — Temporal logic for circuits (`import Hdl.Temporal`): properties over unbounded time, in the style of LTL, SVA and TLA+, with the proof rules to establish them. Design notes: docs/libraries.md ("H14 T") and wiz-notes/hdl-temporal.md.
- [Hdl.Uart](#module-Hdl.Uart) (42 declarations) — A reusable 8N1 UART (`import Hdl.Uart`): a baud generator, a transmitter and a receiver with a configurable number of clock cycles per bit, and a loopback circuit that wires the transmitter's line into the receiver. It is the UART of the iCEstick project (`wiz-icestick-uart/src/Icestick/Uart.wiz`) with the board-specific parts removed, so that other designs can instantiate it: every part is a `Circuit` over bundles, polymorphic in the representation like the rest of the HDL, so the same definition simulates at values and synthesises to a netlist.
- [Hdl.Verified](#module-Hdl.Verified) (73 declarations) — the iCEstick demo's vocabulary (wiz-icestick-uart, src/Icestick/Gates.wiz, Oled.wiz)
- [Hdl.Wishbone](#module-Hdl.Wishbone) (15 declarations) — A thin classic Wishbone B4 bridge for `Hdl.Bus` (`import Hdl.Wishbone`), in both directions over the existing `Bus.ReqW` valid/ready model. It is deliberately the single-transfer, non-pipelined Wishbone subset (`CYC`/`STB`/`ACK`/`ERR`), not a new protocol:
- [Hdl.Xdc](#module-Hdl.Xdc) (23 declarations) — Pin constraints for Xilinx 7-series FPGAs (the XDC of Vivado, read also by nextpnr-xilinx): a package pin and an I/O standard for every port, by the port's name in the netlist, and the clock's period.
- [Hdl.Xilinx7](#module-Hdl.Xilinx7) (41 declarations) — Xilinx 7-series primitives (UG953, "7 Series FPGA Libraries Guide"), as `Prim` declarations and typed functions over them. These are the cells a DDR3 PHY on an Artix-7 needs (I/O buffers, ODDR, OSERDESE2, ISERDESE2, IDELAYE2, IDELAYCTRL, BUFG) and PLLE2_BASE as a `Clocking`. openXC7 (yosys synth_xilinx, nextpnr-xilinx, Project X-Ray) supports all of them.
- [HeapBorrow](#module-HeapBorrow) (14 declarations) — Feral's borrows on heap cells: the bridge between the functional model of owned data (lib/Region.wiz, lib/Optic.wiz: a `&mut A` is a value handed in and handed back) and the model heap of separation logic (lib/HProp.wiz, lib/Hoare.wiz: an owned cell is `l ↦ v`). docs/resources.md tells the whole story; wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md has the design.
- [Hoare](#module-Hoare) (82 declarations) — Stage 24c. Programs that read, write, allocate and free cells of a model heap, a weakest precondition for them, Hoare triples defined from it, and the structural rules (the frame rule among them), all proved by the kernel. The heap predicates come from `HProp` (lib/HProp.wiz); the tactics that make the proofs short are in `HoareTactics`, and the worked examples (swap, in-place list reversal, …) in `HoareExamples`.
- [HoareExamples](#module-HoareExamples) (29 declarations) — Stages 24c–24d. Small heap programs (`Prog`, lib/Hoare.wiz) with their specifications, proved with the `x`-tactics of `HoareTactics`: swapping two cells, a counter, and loops over mutable lists (`MList`): in-place reversal, length, incrementing every element, freeing. Every specification is a `Triple`, so `adequacy` applies to it: the program runs without a fault on any heap satisfying the precondition. `Prog.show` runs a program on a concrete heap.
- [HoareTactics](#module-HoareTactics) (159 declarations) — Stage 24d, after SLF's `xsimpl`, `xpull` and the `x`-tactics of chapter WPgen. With these, a triple of `Hoare` is usually proved by naming the steps rather than writing the proof term:
- [IO](#module-IO) (90 declarations) — Effects through a linear world token (stage 9), and the C foreign function interface.
- [Infoview](#module-Infoview) (104 declarations) — The infoview's model and its two renderers (stages 11m–n): goals as the language server sends them (`wiz/interactiveGoals`, `wiz/interactiveInfo`), laid out for a terminal (SGR colours, wrapped to a width, one selected subterm in reverse video) and for a browser (HTML with `data-ref` attributes). Pure functions; the terminal program (infoview/Tui.wiz) and the browser (web/) do the input and output. Tagged text itself (its JSON, flattening, navigation, HTML) is lib/Tagged.wiz, shared with the documentation's pages (11s).
- [Int](#module-Int) (38 declarations) — Integers (`import Int`): a natural number or the negative of a successor, as in Lean.
- [IntOrder](#module-IntOrder) (69 declarations) — The order of the integers (`import IntOrder`): `a ≤ b` when `b - a` is not negative, `a < b` when `a + 1 ≤ b`; the absolute value and the triangle inequality.
- [IntRing](#module-IntRing) (88 declarations) — Equations of commutative rings at `Int`, decided by reflection, and the ring laws of the integers (`import IntRing`):
- [Intern](#module-Intern) (18 declarations) — Interned strings (`import Intern`): an `InternTable` gives each distinct string a small id, a `U32`, so that strings compare and hash as words (equal ids, equal strings, within one table). Ids are stable: a string keeps its id as more are interned, and ids are handed out in order, 0, 1, 2, … A table is a functional value, updated in place when it is unique (as `StrMap`); keep one per program or per analysis, and key `U64Map`s (lib/WordMap.wiz) or index `U32Array`s by the ids.
- [Json](#module-Json) (69 declarations) — JSON (RFC 8259) in Wiz: values (`Json`), a parser (`Json.parse`) and a printer (`Json.render`). The infoview clients use it to speak the language server's protocol.
- [ListLemmas](#module-ListLemmas) (48 declarations) — Lemmas about the list functions of `lib/Text.wiz` (`import ListLemmas`): how `map`, `filter`, `any`, `all`, `append`, `reverse` and `length` interact, and membership.
- [Logic](#module-Logic) (86 declarations) — Propositional logic over the impredicative `Prop` (stage 24a).
- [MVar](#module-MVar) (16 declarations) — Shared state between threads: `import MVar` (stage 25d, docs/stages/25-concurrency.md).
- [Nat](#module-Nat) (83 declarations) — Natural numbers (`import Nat`): the commutative semiring laws, subtraction, and the order, proved by hand from `0` and `succ`.
- [Optic](#module-Optic) (64 declarations) — Optics for borrows (RD11): the target library of Feral's lowering of mutable borrows. See wiz-notes/borrows-as-optics.md.
- [OpticDerive](#module-OpticDerive) (7 declarations) — `deriving Lens` (`import OpticDerive`): a lens per field of a structure, its laws, and the independence of every two distinct fields. For `structure S Δ where f₁ : T₁ … fₙ : Tₙ` it defines, with the parameters Δ implicit,
- [Order](#module-Order) (3 declarations) — Notation for orders and equivalences (`import Order`): `a ≤ b`, `a < b` and `a ≈ b`, each a class with one instance per type. The relations are propositions.
- [PMap](#module-PMap) (49 declarations) — Persistent (immutable, structurally shared) maps and sets (`import PMap`): `PMap K V` and `PSet K`. Every update returns a new value and leaves the old one valid; the two share all the nodes the update did not touch, so an update allocates only the O(log n) nodes on the path from the root to the changed leaf (plus a constant number for rebalancing rotations).
- [Prelude](#module-Prelude) (250 declarations) — The Wiz prelude (`import Prelude`): the basic types, notation, classes and metaprogramming that every other library module builds on.
- [Rat](#module-Rat) (134 declarations) — Rational numbers as an ordered field, up to an equivalence (`import Rat`).
- [Ref](#module-Ref) (7 declarations) — Mutable cells owned by linear points-to tokens (`import Ref`; plan CS7b/S4, cohesion step M5, wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md; docs/resources.md).
- [Region](#module-Region) (54 declarations) — Regions (Rust lifetimes) and borrow handles for Feral's lowering (RD12). Plan: wiz-notes/rust-dsl-plan.md; rules: drafts/feral/LOWERING.md (L1, L3, L4, L12, L17, L20–L22); hand-lowered programs: drafts/feral/lowered/.
- [Result](#module-Result) (12 declarations) — The result monad of Feral's lowered code (RD7), shared by lib/Optic.wiz and lib/Region.wiz: a value (`ok a`) or a panic (`err e`).
- [Ring](#module-Ring) (49 declarations) — Equations of commutative semirings at `Nat`, decided by reflection (`import Ring`):
- [RingTactic](#module-RingTactic) (22 declarations) — `ring`: prove an equation of commutative (semi)rings by reading the goal (`import RingTactic`).
- [Sat](#module-Sat) (117 declarations) — Certified SAT (`import Sat`): an LRAT proof checker proved sound, Boolean formulas with a Tseitin translation proved sound, and the theorem that puts them together:
- [SatTactic](#module-SatTactic) (64 declarations) — `sat_decide` (stage 28b): decide a Boolean goal with a SAT solver, **without trusting it**. `import SatTactic`.
- [Scry.Ai](#module-Scry.Ai) (0 declarations) — The parser-free core of stage S5 (design `wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md` §4.6, §5.3): lattice/domain/transfer interfaces, unsigned machine intervals with constants and nullness, a widening worklist, narrowing, overflow/out-of-bounds/nullness alarms, and the post-fixpoint checker. See `wiz-notes/scry-ai.md`.
- [Scry.AiCfg](#module-Scry.AiCfg) (28 declarations) — The frontend-independent half of the abstract-interpretation core: a small language (`AExpr`/`ACond`/`AStmt`), a CFG (`ACfg`/`AEdge`), and the concrete-ish transfer functions for the `Value` domain of `Scry.AiDomain`. There is no parser and no Wil dependency: a Wil lowering will construct these values in stage S2/S5.
- [Scry.AiDomain](#module-Scry.AiDomain) (98 declarations) — The domain half of scry's abstract-interpretation core (design `wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md` §4.6, §5.3, stage S5). This module is independent of the Wil frontend: it defines the interfaces, the small numerical and nullness domains, and their *soundness obligations*. The obligations are `Prop`-valued statements, not proofs; §5.3's `check_sound` is conditional on them (the checker itself does not call them, which is the point of result checking).
- [Scry.AiExamples](#module-Scry.AiExamples) (17 declarations) — Hand-built CFGs, so that the engine and the checker can be exercised without a parser or a Wil frontend. `Tests/Scry.lean` evaluates the functions below; `wiz-notes/scry-ai.md` reproduces the same programs.
- [Scry.AiFixpoint](#module-Scry.AiFixpoint) (25 declarations) — Stage S5's untrusted fast path and its result checker.
- [Scry.Analysis](#module-Scry.Analysis) (55 declarations) — The **intraprocedural graph layer** over `Scry.Wil` (`import Scry.Analysis`): the CFG, dominators, reaching definitions, and the PDG's data-dependence (def-use) edges. There is no parser and no C lowering here; the input is a hand-built or lowered `Wil.Func`.
- [Scry.Cert](#module-Scry.Cert) (136 declarations) — **Derivation certificates** for scry's Datalog (`import Scry.Cert`): a finding is a fact plus a finite, acyclic derivation tree, and `Derivation.check` decides whether the tree is a valid rule instance by rule instance from the EDB.
- [Scry.Datalog](#module-Scry.Datalog) (34 declarations) — The **deep embedding** of scry's lattice-valued Datalog (`import Scry.Datalog`), with no surface syntax and no parser. A program is a value of `Program L`:
- [Scry.Egraph](#module-Scry.Egraph) (77 declarations) — A native e-graph engine for scry (`import Scry.Egraph`), with no egglog and no foreign dependency. It is the S12 slice of `wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md` §10: an equality-saturated term store with a union-find, congruence closure by rebuilding, a hash-consed e-node table, extraction, and a small pattern/rewrite loop with a fuel bound. A Datalog relation of equalities can feed it with `mergeFacts`/`mergeRows`.
- [Scry.Eval](#module-Scry.Eval) (59 declarations) — A semi-naive evaluator for `Scry.Datalog.Program` (`import Scry.Eval`), with a delta loop and provenance.
- [Scry.Store](#module-Scry.Store) (32 declarations) — The relation store for scry's Datalog engine (`import Scry.Store`): a **pure list model** of the relations a Datalog program derives.
- [Scry.Taint](#module-Scry.Taint) (37 declarations) — Intraprocedural **taint analysis as Datalog** (`import Scry.Taint`), over the def-use edges of `Scry.Analysis` and a small source/sink/sanitiser specification.
- [Scry.TaintExamples](#module-Scry.TaintExamples) (17 declarations) — The programs here are written with `Scry.Wil`'s builder, not lowered from C. They are the golden corpus for the `scry-taint` test group (`Tests/ScryTaint.lean`) and exercise one feature of the prototype each:
- [Scry.Wil](#module-Scry.Wil) (118 declarations) — Wil is the small three-address IR the `scry` analyser (design: `wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md`, §4.3) lowers C, C# and Python into. It is deliberately smaller than a compiler IR: enough to state a concrete semantics, so the abstract domains of stage S5 can be proved sound against it, and enough for the graph layers (CFG, dominators, CDG, def-use) of S2/S4.
- [Scry.WilExamples](#module-Scry.WilExamples) (15 declarations) — The programs below are the golden corpus of the Wil stage: they are written with `Scry.Wil`'s builder (`Wil.func`, `Wil.block`, `Wil.num`, `Wil.binop`, …) rather than lowered from C. Their expected results are in `Tests/Scry.lean`, and they exercise the features the concrete semantics claims:
- [Serial](#module-Serial) (43 declarations) — Serial ports and pseudo-terminals (sys-bytes): termios through `serial.c`.
- [Session](#module-Session) (19 declarations) — Session-typed linear channels: `import Session` (stage 25b–c, docs/stages/25-concurrency.md).
- [Std](#module-Std) (21 declarations) — The standard library for systems code (stage 12a): containers and text with native representations, updated in place when they are unique.
- [Sys](#module-Sys) (222 declarations) — System interfaces (stage 9h): the environment, files and directories, processes, clocks and file descriptors.
- [Tagged](#module-Tagged) (49 declarations) — Tagged text (stage 11m; a library of its own since 11s): a pretty-printed term whose subterms are tagged, as the language server sends it (`infoview-protocol.md` §2), and what both its browser front ends do with it: flatten it, number and navigate its tags, render it as HTML with hoverable subterms, and describe a subterm (`wiz/subtermInfo`).
- [Text](#module-Text) (57 declarations) — Text and lists (stage 9j): the string and list functions every program needs, in one module, pure (so `#eval` runs them) and linear in the length of their input.
- [Trace](#module-Trace) (41 declarations) — Traces and Mealy machines (`import Trace`): the common semantics of the HDL's circuits (lib/Hdl/Core.wiz, `Circuit.trace`), the temporal logic over them, and anything else that runs step by step. Design: wiz-notes/cohesion-hardware.md, 2.1.
- [Vec](#module-Vec) (53 declarations) — Bounded numbers and length-indexed vectors (`import Vec`).
- [Word](#module-Word) (155 declarations) — Machine integers (`import Word`).
- [WordArray](#module-WordArray) (107 declarations) — Unboxed arrays of machine words (`import WordArray`): `U8Array`, `U32Array` and `U64Array`, functional values updated in place when they are unique (as `Array`).
- [WordBytes](#module-WordBytes) (4 declarations) — `Bytes` as lists of `U8` (sys-bytes, stage 9k). A module of its own: IO and Sys count bytes as `Nat`s below 256 and don't import Word, so the conversions between the byte buffer and fixed-width words live here.
- [WordMap](#module-WordMap) (30 declarations) — Maps from 64-bit words (`import WordMap`): `U64Map V`, a functional finite map with `U64` keys, updated in place when it is unique (as `StrMap`). Keys of other word types, typed ids (`NodeId k`, 22e) and interned strings (lib/Intern.wiz) go through `U64` (`UIntN.resize`, or the id's bits).

## BitBlast

<a id="module-BitBlast"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>BitBlast</h4>
<p>Bits of numbers and words, for bit-blasting (<code>import BitBlast</code>; stage 28d).</p>
<p><code>Bits.bit n i</code> is bit <code>i</code> of <code>n</code> (structural: by halving), and each word operation&#39;s bits are given by a lemma (<a href="#Bits.land_bit"><code>Bits.land_bit</code></a>, …) that the <code>bv_decide</code> tactic uses as the proof of a circuit node (lib/SatTactic.wiz, 28c: a node&#39;s proof is anything that shows <code>σ v = op (σ a) (σ b)</code>).</p>
</div>

## BitVec

<a id="module-BitVec"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>BitVec</h4>
<p>Bit vectors of width <code>n</code> (<code>import BitVec</code>): a <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> below <code>2^n</code>. The bound is kept by construction (every operation reduces mod <code>2^n</code>), not by a proof (decision HD3; a proof-carrying subtype may come later). Arithmetic wraps around. Bit 0 is the least significant.</p>
<p>One type family (stage 22h): <code>BitVec n</code> <em>is</em> <code>UIntN n</code> (lib/Word.wiz), the machine-integer type, under the names hardware and proofs use. A bit vector and a word are interchangeable (no conversion); the kernel and proofs see the definitions below, each of which unfolds to Word&#39;s model (<code>BitVec.add a b</code> is <code>UIntN.ofNat n (a.toNat + b.toNat)</code>); compiled code gets Word&#39;s native representation (a word is its bits: no allocation below 2^63) and Word&#39;s natives, through the operation each one calls.</p>
<p>Operations that compute <code>2^n</code> take the width at runtime (<code>{ω n : Nat}</code>), as do <a href="#BitVec.toVec"><code>BitVec.toVec</code></a> and <a href="#BitVec.ofVec"><code>BitVec.ofVec</code></a> (they build or read the <code>n</code> bits); the others (<code>toNat</code>, comparisons) take it erased.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#BitVec"><code>BitVec</code></a>, <a href="#BitVec.ofNat"><code>BitVec.ofNat</code></a>, arithmetic (<a href="#BitVec.add"><code>BitVec.add</code></a>, <a href="#BitVec.mul"><code>BitVec.mul</code></a>, <a href="#BitVec.udiv"><code>BitVec.udiv</code></a>, …), bitwise operations and shifts, signed comparisons, the width operations of hardware (<a href="#BitVec.concat"><code>BitVec.concat</code></a>, <a href="#BitVec.extract"><code>BitVec.extract</code></a>, <a href="#BitVec.zeroExtend"><code>BitVec.zeroExtend</code></a>, <a href="#BitVec.signExtend"><code>BitVec.signExtend</code></a>) and conversions to and from <code>Vec Bool n</code>.</p>
<pre><code>import BitVec

#eval BitVec.toNat (BitVec.add (BitVec.ofNat 4 15) (BitVec.ofNat 4 1))   -- 0, it wraps
#eval BitVec.toNat (BitVec.extract 3 2 (BitVec.ofNat 8 12))              -- 3</code></pre>
</div>

## BitVecAdd

<a id="module-BitVecAdd"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>BitVecAdd</h4>
<p>The 34-bit carry/borrow adder in word form (<code>import BitVecAdd</code>).</p>
<p><code>Rv.Core</code>&#39;s ALU has one 34-bit addition for <code>add</code>, <code>sub</code>, the comparisons and address computation: the carry in is a low bit, the operands are <code>{a, 1}</code> and <code>{b&#39;, sub}</code> (<code>b&#39; = b</code>, or <code>~b</code> when subtracting), and the result is bits 1 … 32 of the sum (<code>slice 1 32</code>). At values this is not <a href="#BitVec.add"><code>BitVec.add</code></a>/<a href="#BitVec.sub"><code>BitVec.sub</code></a> for symbolic <code>a b</code>: the kernel sees a <code>concat</code>/<code>slice</code> over a 34-bit <a href="#UIntN"><code>UIntN</code></a> and two <a href="#Bits.low"><code>Bits.low</code></a>s. The bridge here is the <em>same</em> normal form as <code>lib/BitVecShift.wiz</code>: everything is a <a href="#Bits.low"><code>Bits.low</code></a> of a <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> expression, and the two steps that matter are</p>
<ul><li>the <code>low</code> of each <code>concat</code> operand is the operand&#39;s value (<a href="#Bits.low_of_lt"><code>Bits.low_of_lt</code></a> under the bound <code>a * 2 + 1 &lt; 2^33</code> that a 32-bit word gives), and</li><li>dividing the low <code>w+1</code> bits by 2 is dividing and taking the low <code>w</code> bits (<a href="#Bits.div_low_succ"><code>Bits.div_low_succ</code></a>), so the top (carry) bit falls off and the rest is <code>(2 q + 1) / 2 = q</code> (<a href="#Bits.div_two_add"><code>Bits.div_two_add</code></a>) or <code>(2 q) / 2 = q</code> (<a href="#Bits.div_two"><code>Bits.div_two</code></a>).</li></ul>
<p>The result: <code>BitVec.adc s a b</code> (the core&#39;s expression, with <code>s</code> the carry-in bit, which is the instruction&#39;s <code>sub</code> control signal) is <code>BitVec.sub a b</code> when <code>s</code> is 1 and <code>BitVec.add a b</code> when it is 0 (<a href="#BitVec.adc_eq"><code>BitVec.adc_eq</code></a>), so an ADD/ADDI/SUB proof is one <a href="#Eq.congrArg"><code>Eq.congrArg</code></a> on the register value.</p>
<p>Nothing here uses the native-refl escape hatch: every lemma is kernel-checked, and the <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> steps are explicit <a href="#Eq.trans"><code>Eq.trans</code></a> chains (a <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> identity that the kernel&#39;s normalizer closes would be <code>True</code>, and cannot be a rewrite step — see <code>wiz-notes/rv-shift-lemmas.md</code> §4/§7).</p>
</div>

<a id="BitVec.catToNat"></a>
### `BitVec.catToNat`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:62`

```text
{ω m : Nat} → {ω n : Nat} → (hi : BitVec m) → (lo : BitVec n) → UIntN.toNat (m + n) (BitVec.concat m n hi lo) = Bits.low (Nat.add m n) (Nat.add (Nat.mul (UIntN.toNat m hi) (Nat.pow 2 n)) (UIntN.toNat n lo))
```

<a id="Bits.dec32_lt"></a>
### `Bits.dec32_lt`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:75`

```text
Nat.Lt (Nat.add (Nat.mul (Bits.dec (Nat.pow 2 32)) 2) 1) (Nat.pow 2 33)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>2 · (2^32 - 1) + 1 &lt; 2^33</code> (closed numerals).</p>

<a id="Bits.cat_lt"></a>
### `Bits.cat_lt`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:79`

```text
(A : Nat) → Nat.Lt A (Nat.pow 2 32) → Nat.Lt (Nat.add (Nat.mul A 2) 1) (Nat.pow 2 33)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>A · 2 + 1 &lt; 2^33</code> for a 32-bit <code>A</code> (the bits of <code>{A, 1}</code> fit a 33-bit word).</p>

<a id="Bits.low33_cat"></a>
### `Bits.low33_cat`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:90`

```text
(A : Nat) → Nat.Lt A (Nat.pow 2 32) → Bits.low 33 (Nat.add (Nat.mul A 2) 1) = Nat.add (Nat.mul A 2) 1
```
<div class="doc"><p>The low 33 bits of <code>A · 2 + 1</code> are <code>A · 2 + 1</code> for a 32-bit <code>A</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.low33_cat0"></a>
### `Bits.low33_cat0`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:97`

```text
(A : Nat) → Nat.Lt A (Nat.pow 2 32) → Bits.low 33 (Nat.add (Nat.mul A 2) 0) = Nat.mul A 2
```
<div class="doc"><p>The low 33 bits of <code>A · 2 + 0</code> are <code>A · 2</code> for a 32-bit <code>A</code>. (The <code>+ 0</code> is kept: an equation between a stuck application and <code>x + 0</code> does not convert quickly, so the step that removes it is explicit.)</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.div_low_succ"></a>
### `Bits.div_low_succ`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:108`

```text
(w : Nat) → (n : Nat) → Nat.div (Bits.low (Nat.succ w) n) 2 = Bits.low w (Nat.div n 2)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>low (w+1) n / 2 = low w (n / 2)</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.div_two_add"></a>
### `Bits.div_two_add`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:113`

```text
(q : Nat) → Nat.div (Nat.add (Nat.mul 2 q) 1) 2 = q
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>(2 q + 1) / 2 = q</code>: an odd sum.</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.div_two"></a>
### `Bits.div_two`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:119`

```text
(q : Nat) → Nat.div (Nat.mul 2 q) 2 = q
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>(2 q) / 2 = q</code>: an even sum. (The <code>+ 0</code> of <a href="#Bits.div_mq"><code>Bits.div_mq</code></a> is removed explicitly: a stuck <code>q + 0</code> and <code>q</code> are not convertible.)</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.div_div"></a>
### `Bits.div_div`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:128`

```text
(k : Nat) → (j : Nat) → (n : Nat) → Nat.div (Nat.div n (Nat.pow 2 k)) (Nat.pow 2 j) = Nat.div n (Nat.pow 2 (Nat.add k j))
```
<div class="doc"><p>Dividing twice is dividing by the product: <code>(n / 2^k) / 2^j = n / 2^(k+j)</code> (<a href="#Bits.div_pow"><code>Bits.div_pow</code></a> and <a href="#Bits.high_high"><code>Bits.high_high</code></a>).</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.div_low_pow"></a>
### `Bits.div_low_pow`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:141`

```text
(w : Nat) → (n : Nat) → Nat.div (Bits.low (Nat.succ w) n) (Nat.pow 2 w) = Bits.low 1 (Nat.div n (Nat.pow 2 w))
```
<div class="doc"><p>The carry-out bit of a <code>low (w+1)</code> word: dividing it by <code>2^w</code> is its bit <code>w</code>, i.e. <code>low 1 (n / 2^w)</code>. The <code>2^w</code> analogue of <a href="#Bits.div_low_succ"><code>Bits.div_low_succ</code></a> (induction on <code>w</code>, with <a href="#Bits.div_div"><code>Bits.div_div</code></a> for the composition).</p>
</div>

### `Bits.mul2_add`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:160`

```text
(P : Nat) → Nat.mul 2 P = Nat.add P P
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>2 · P = P + P</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.div_one_of"></a>
### `Bits.div_one_of`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:165`

```text
(P : Nat) → (Z : Nat) → Nat.Lt 0 P → Nat.Le P Z → Nat.Lt Z (Nat.mul 2 P) → Nat.div Z P = 1
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>P ≤ Z &lt; 2P</code> gives <code>Z / P = 1</code> (<a href="#Bits.div_mq"><code>Bits.div_mq</code></a> at <code>m = P</code>, with <code>Z - P &lt; P</code>).</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.dec32_add_lt"></a>
### `Bits.dec32_add_lt`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:188`

```text
Nat.Lt (Nat.add (Bits.dec (Nat.pow 2 32)) (Nat.pow 2 32)) (Nat.mul 2 (Nat.pow 2 32))
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>(2^32 - 1) + 2^32 &lt; 2^33</code> (closed numerals).</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.borrow_le"></a>
### `Bits.borrow_le`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:192`

```text
(a : Nat) → (b : Nat) → Nat.Lt a (Nat.pow 2 32) → Nat.Lt b (Nat.pow 2 32) → Nat.le b a = Bool.true → Nat.div (Nat.add a (Nat.sub (Nat.pow 2 32) b)) (Nat.pow 2 32) = 1
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>b ≤ a</code> gives <code>(a + (2^32 - b)) / 2^32 = 1</code>: the sum is <code>2^32 + (a - b)</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="Bits.borrow_gt"></a>
### `Bits.borrow_gt`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:210`

```text
(a : Nat) → (b : Nat) → Nat.Lt a (Nat.pow 2 32) → Nat.Lt b (Nat.pow 2 32) → Nat.le b a = Bool.false → Nat.div (Nat.add a (Nat.sub (Nat.pow 2 32) b)) (Nat.pow 2 32) = 0
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>a &lt; b</code> gives <code>(a + (2^32 - b)) / 2^32 = 0</code>: the sum is below <code>2^32</code>.</p>
</div>


def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:237`


<a id="BitVec.adcW2_one"></a>
### `BitVec.adcW2_one`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:250`

```text
(b : BitVec 32) → UIntN.toNat 34 (BitVec.zext1 (32 + 1) (BitVec.concat 32 1 (BitVec.adcB (BitVec.ofNat 1 1) b) (BitVec.ofNat 1 1))) = Nat.add (Nat.mul (UIntN.toNat 32 (BitVec.not 32 b)) 2) 1
```

<a id="BitVec.adcFormToNat"></a>
### `BitVec.adcFormToNat`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:266`

```text
(s : BitVec 1) → (a : BitVec 32) → (b : BitVec 32) → UIntN.toNat 34 (BitVec.adcForm s a b) = Bits.low 34 (Nat.add (UIntN.toNat 34 (BitVec.zext1 (32 + 1) (BitVec.concat 32 1 a (BitVec.ofNat 1 1)))) (UIntN.toNat 34 (BitVec.zext1 (32 + 1) (BitVec.concat 32 1 (BitVec.adcB s b) s))))
```
<div class="doc"><p>The 34-bit sum is the low 34 bits of the two operands&#39; sum (a <a href="#BitVec.add"><code>BitVec.add</code></a> at 34 bits is <code>Bits.low 34</code>).</p>
</div>


<a id="BitVec.adc_zero_toNat"></a>
### `BitVec.adc_zero_toNat`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:279`

```text
(a : BitVec 32) → (b : BitVec 32) → UIntN.toNat 32 (BitVec.adc (BitVec.ofNat 1 0) a b) = Bits.low 32 (Nat.add (UIntN.toNat 32 a) (UIntN.toNat 32 b))
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>(adc 0 a b).toNat = low 32 (a + b)</code>: <code>(2 a + 1 + 2 b) / 2 = a + b</code>, and the slice&#39;s <code>low 32</code> stays.</p>
</div>


<a id="BitVec.adc_one_toNat"></a>
### `BitVec.adc_one_toNat`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:308`

```text
(a : BitVec 32) → (b : BitVec 32) → UIntN.toNat 32 (BitVec.adc (BitVec.ofNat 1 1) a b) = Bits.low 32 (Nat.add (UIntN.toNat 32 a) (Nat.sub (Nat.pow 2 32) (UIntN.toNat 32 b)))
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>(adc 1 a b).toNat = low 32 (a + (2^32 - b))</code>: <code>(2 a + 1 + 2 ~b + 1) / 2 = a + ~b + 1</code>, and <code>~b + 1 = 2^32 - b</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="BitVec.adc_zero"></a>
### `BitVec.adc_zero`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:347`

```text
(a : BitVec 32) → (b : BitVec 32) → BitVec.adc (BitVec.ofNat 1 0) a b = BitVec.add 32 a b
```
<div class="doc"><p>The 34-bit adder with carry-in 0 is <a href="#BitVec.add"><code>BitVec.add</code></a>.</p>
</div>


<a id="BitVec.adc_one"></a>
### `BitVec.adc_one`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:354`

```text
(a : BitVec 32) → (b : BitVec 32) → BitVec.adc (BitVec.ofNat 1 1) a b = BitVec.sub 32 a b
```
<div class="doc"><p>The 34-bit adder with carry-in 1 is <a href="#BitVec.sub"><code>BitVec.sub</code></a>.</p>
</div>


<a id="BitVec.adc_eq"></a>
### `BitVec.adc_eq`

def · `BitVecAdd.wiz:361`

```text
(s : BitVec 1) → (a : BitVec 32) → (b : BitVec 32) → BitVec.adc s a b = BitVec.muxBit 32 s (BitVec.sub 32 a b) (BitVec.add 32 a b)
```
<div class="doc"><p><strong>The bridge</strong>: the core&#39;s 34-bit add/sub is <code>add</code> (<code>s = 0</code>) or <code>sub</code> (<code>s = 1</code>).</p>
</div>


## BitVecShift

<a id="module-BitVecShift"></a>
<div class="doc"><p>Shift lemmas for the hardware barrel shifter (<code>import BitVecShift</code>).</p>
<p><code>lib/BitVec.wiz</code> defines <a href="#BitVec.shl"><code>BitVec.shl</code></a>/<code>lshr</code> through <code>Word</code>, but the barrel shifter in <code>Rv.Core</code> (and the Hdl examples) builds a shift from <code>concat</code>/<code>slice</code> stages, so the two are not convertible for symbolic data. These lemmas put both in the same normal form: the low <code>w</code> bits (<a href="#Bits.low"><code>Bits.low</code></a>, lib/BitBlast.wiz) of a product.</p>
<p>The one fact every stage needs: a left shift by <code>j</code> of a word below <code>2^(w+j)</code> is <code>2^j</code> times the shift of its low <code>w</code> bits (<a href="#Bits.low_shift"><code>Bits.low_shift</code></a>), and taking low bits twice is the second, smaller one (<a href="#Bits.low_low"><code>Bits.low_low</code></a>).</p>
</div>

## BvDecide

<a id="module-BvDecide"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>BvDecide</h4>
<p><code>bv_decide</code> (stage 28d): an equation of words decided by SAT, with no new trust. <code>import BvDecide</code>.</p>
<p>def t (x y : UIntN 8) : UIntN.land x (UIntN.lor x y) = x := by bv_decide</p>
<p>The goal <code>lhs = rhs</code> at <code>UIntN w</code> (or <code>BitVec w</code>), <code>w</code> a numeral, is bit-blasted into 28c&#39;s circuit: bit <code>i</code> of a word expression <code>e</code> is the node whose value is <code>Bits.bit (UIntN.toNat e) i</code>; an operation&#39;s bit is a gate over its operands&#39; bits, and the node&#39;s proof is the operation&#39;s lemma (<a href="#Bits.wland_bit"><code>Bits.wland_bit</code></a>, …), checked by the kernel like any other gate. Words the tactic does not look into are inputs (their bits are variables of the formula). The output is <code>Bits.eqUpTo (toNat lhs) (toNat rhs) w</code>, and <a href="#Bits.word_ext"><code>Bits.word_ext</code></a> turns it into <code>lhs = rhs</code>.</p>
<p>The fragment: <code>UIntN.land/lor/xor/not/add/sub/neg</code> and shifts by numerals (<code>shiftLeft</code>, <code>shiftRight</code>), the same under <a href="#BitVec"><code>BitVec</code></a>&#39;s names, and closed words (numerals, <code>UIntN.ofNat 8 13</code>: their bits are computed). Boolean goals may compare words (<code>UIntN.lt/le</code>, <code>BitVec.ult/ule</code>) under the connectives <code>sat_decide</code> reads.</p>
</div>

## Deriving

<a id="module-Deriving"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Deriving</h4>
<p>Deriving (HD8). <code>inductive T … deriving C</code> and <code>deriving instance C for T</code> run C&#39;s <em>deriver</em>: a Wiz function <code>Deriver := String → MacroM (List Syntax)</code>, registered with <code>attribute [deriver C] f</code>. It looks the type up (<a href="#MacroM.getInductive"><code>MacroM.getInductive</code></a>) and returns the commands that make the instance. This module defines three classes, their derivers, and instances for the prelude&#39;s types.</p>
<p>The classes are <a href="#Inhabited"><code>Inhabited</code></a> (a <code>default</code> value), <a href="#BEq"><code>BEq</code></a> (boolean equality) and <a href="#Repr"><code>Repr</code></a> (a value as Wiz source); their derivers are <a href="#deriveInhabited"><code>deriveInhabited</code></a>, <a href="#deriveBEq"><code>deriveBEq</code></a> and <a href="#deriveRepr"><code>deriveRepr</code></a>. The <code>Derive.*</code> functions are the toolkit for writing a deriver of your own (see docs/stages/07-type-classes.md, exercise 7.2).</p>
<pre><code>import Deriving

inductive Color where
  | red | green | blue
  deriving Inhabited, BEq, Repr

#eval Repr.repr (Inhabited.default : Color)   -- &quot;Color.red&quot;
#eval BEq.beq Color.red Color.blue            -- .false</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="DecidableEq"></a>
### `DecidableEq`

class · `Deriving.wiz:48`

```text
Type u → Type u
```
<div class="doc"><p>Equality as a <a href="#Bool"><code>Bool</code></a>: <code>DecidableEq.decide a b</code> is <code>.true</code> when <code>a</code> and <code>b</code> are equal, as <a href="#BEq.beq"><code>BEq.beq</code></a> is. It is the comparison Lean&#39;s <a href="#DecidableEq"><code>DecidableEq</code></a> provides for <code>=</code>, by the name the machine models use; Wiz has no <code>Decidable</code> proof object to return, so <code>decide</code> is the <a href="#Bool"><code>Bool</code></a> itself (what <code>if</code> and <code>&amp;&amp;</code> test). Derivable for an enumeration (every constructor is a constant) and for a single-constructor record (no recursive field); fields are compared with their own instances and proof fields are not compared, as in <a href="#BEq"><code>BEq</code></a>.</p>
</div>

**Constructors and fields**

- <a id="DecidableEq.mk"></a>`mk` : `{A : Type u} → (A → A → Bool) → DecidableEq A`
- <a id="DecidableEq.decide"></a>`decide` : `{A : Type u} → [self : DecidableEq A] → A → A → Bool`

## Eff

<a id="module-Eff"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Eff</h4>
<p>Algebraic effects as a library (stage 10).</p>
<p>An effect is a set of operations, each with the type of its answer. A computation <code>Eff r A</code> is a tree of operations from the row <code>r</code>, with continuations (a free monad). Handlers interpret the first effect of the row and leave the rest. Rows can be reordered only where the effects provably commute (<a href="#Commute"><code>Commute</code></a>).</p>
<p>The pieces:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#Effect"><code>Effect</code></a>, <a href="#Row"><code>Row</code></a>, <a href="#Eff"><code>Eff</code></a> (the free monad over a row), <a href="#send"><code>send</code></a> (perform an operation), <a href="#Member"><code>Member</code></a> (an effect is in a row), <a href="#Eff.run"><code>Eff.run</code></a> (no effects left).</li><li>Effects with their handlers: <a href="#State"><code>State</code></a> (<a href="#get"><code>get</code></a>, <a href="#put"><code>put</code></a>, <a href="#runState"><code>runState</code></a>), <a href="#Reader"><code>Reader</code></a> (<a href="#ask"><code>ask</code></a>, <a href="#runReader"><code>runReader</code></a>), <a href="#Exn"><code>Exn</code></a> (<a href="#throw"><code>throw</code></a>, <a href="#runExn"><code>runExn</code></a>), <a href="#Console"><code>Console</code></a> (<a href="#println"><code>println</code></a>, <a href="#runConsole"><code>runConsole</code></a>).</li><li>Lowering a whole row to one monad: <a href="#Handler"><code>Handler</code></a>, <a href="#Handlers"><code>Handlers</code></a>, <a href="#interpret"><code>interpret</code></a>; reordering a row: <a href="#Commute"><code>Commute</code></a>, <a href="#reorder"><code>reorder</code></a>.</li><li>Fusion (10b): <a href="#MonadState"><code>MonadState</code></a>, <a href="#MonadReader"><code>MonadReader</code></a>, <a href="#MonadConsole"><code>MonadConsole</code></a> let a program run either as a tree (<code>Eff r</code>) or directly in <a href="#StateT"><code>StateT</code></a>/<a href="#ReaderT"><code>ReaderT</code></a>/<a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a>, with no tree built.</li><li>One-shot effects (CS4–6): <a href="#Eff1"><code>Eff1</code></a>, whose handlers resume exactly once, so continuations may capture linear resources.</li></ul>
<pre><code>import Eff

def tick {r : Row} [Member (State Nat) r] : Eff r Unit := do
  n ← get;
  put (Nat.succ n)
def twice : Eff (Row.cons (State Nat) Row.nil) Nat := do
  tick;
  tick;
  get
#eval Eff.run (runState twice 0)   -- (2, 2)</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="Eff1"></a>
### `Eff1`

def · `Eff.wiz:272`

```text
Qty → Row → Type → Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>One-shot effects (CS4–6). The continuations of <a href="#Eff"><code>Eff</code></a> are ω fields, so a computation can&#39;t keep a linear resource (a channel endpoint, a token) in one: the resource would be used any number of times. <code>Eff1 q r R A</code> is the same computations, Church-encoded over an answer type <code>R</code>, whose handler gets each continuation at quantity 1: it must resume exactly once (one-shot, as in OCaml 5), and in exchange a continuation may capture linear resources. The result is used <code>q</code> times: <code>ω</code> for ordinary results, <code>1</code> for a computation that hands back a linear resource. Handlers that resume twice (backtracking) or never (exceptions) need <a href="#Eff"><code>Eff</code></a>. (Church-encoded rather than a tree: a linear field can&#39;t be matched back out of data yet, plan L2.) The effects, rows and <a href="#Member"><code>Member</code></a> are those of <a href="#Eff"><code>Eff</code></a>.</p>
</div>

**Instances for this type (2)**

- [`instMonadEff1RR`](#instMonadEff1RR) : `{r : Row} → {R : Type} → Monad (Eff1 ω r R)`
- [`instMonad1Eff1RR`](#instMonad1Eff1RR) : `{r : Row} → {R : Type} → Monad1 (Eff1 ω r R)`

## EffHeap

<a id="module-EffHeap"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>EffHeap</h4>
<p>Heap cells as an effect (lib/Eff.wiz) interpreted into the heap programs of separation logic (lib/Hoare.wiz): the effect observation of plan S7 for state, and the reason <a href="#Commute"><code>Commute</code></a> is not needed for state on different cells. docs/resources.md tells how this fits with Feral and the optics; wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md, M3.</p>
<ul><li><code>Cell V l</code> is a state effect on the cell at location <code>l</code> (<code>State V</code> with the location in its type, so a row can hold several cells and <a href="#Member"><code>Member</code></a> tells them apart).</li><li><a href="#Eff.toProg"><code>Eff.toProg</code></a> is <a href="#interpret"><code>interpret</code></a> (lib/Eff.wiz) with each cell handled by <a href="#get"><code>get</code></a>/<code>set</code> on its location: an <a href="#Eff"><code>Eff</code></a> program over cells <em>is</em> a heap program, so its specification is a <a href="#Triple"><code>Triple</code></a> of <code>Eff.toProg c</code>, and the <code>x</code>-tactics prove it.</li><li>Commutation. <code>Commute (Cell V p) (Cell V q) (Prog V)</code> does not hold: <a href="#Commute"><code>Commute</code></a> asks for an equation of computations, and <code>get p; get q</code> and <code>get q; get p</code> are different trees. What does hold is that both orders meet the same specification from <code>(p ↦ x) ⋆ (q ↦ y)</code> (<a href="#Cell.commute"><code>Cell.commute</code></a>): <code>⋆</code> says the cells are different, and that is all the reordering needs. So for state, the commutation proofs of 10a become a consequence of separation, proved once for every pair of operations.</li></ul>
</div>


## Feral

<a id="module-Feral"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Feral: a Rust-like language embedded in Wiz</h4>
<p>Feral (docs/stages/22-numbers.md, 22j) is a small Rust inside Wiz:</p>
<pre><code>import FeralCore                 -- the runtime of lowered code (drafts/feral/lib, for now)
import Feral
feral
  fn swap {&#39;a &#39;b} (x : &amp;&#39;a mut U64) (y : &amp;&#39;b mut U64) : Unit := { let t := *x; *x := *y; *y := t }
end</code></pre>
<p>The parts, in order: the grammar (<code>feral_ty</code>, <code>feral_expr</code>, …), the few utilities lib/Text.wiz lacks (<a href="#Fe.split"><code>Fe.split</code></a>, <a href="#Fe.nth"><code>Fe.nth</code></a>, …), syntax access (<a href="#Fe.kids"><code>Fe.kids</code></a>, <a href="#Fe.sub"><code>Fe.sub</code></a>), the front end&#39;s types (<a href="#Fe.Ty"><code>Fe.Ty</code></a>) with unification (<a href="#Fe.unify"><code>Fe.unify</code></a>), generated code (<a href="#Fe.Out"><code>Fe.Out</code></a>), the environment (<a href="#Fe.Var"><code>Fe.Var</code></a>) and monad (<a href="#Fe.M"><code>Fe.M</code></a>), outlives evidence (<a href="#Fe.evidence"><code>Fe.evidence</code></a>), borrow requests (<a href="#Fe.Req"><code>Fe.Req</code></a>), the lowering (<a href="#Fe.expr"><code>Fe.expr</code></a>, <a href="#Fe.scopeOne"><code>Fe.scopeOne</code></a>, …), items (<a href="#Fe.sigOf"><code>Fe.sigOf</code></a>, <a href="#Fe.fnText"><code>Fe.fnText</code></a>) and the macro (<a href="#Fe.macro"><code>Fe.macro</code></a>). Names are prefixed <code>Fe.</code>.</p>
<p><code>feral … end</code> is a command macro written in Wiz (this file): it type-checks the items with a checker whose types carry regions, and lowers each to Wiz source, which the elaborator and the kernel then check as usual. <code>#lower feral … end</code> also shows the generated Wiz. The lowering rules are drafts/feral/LOWERING.md (L1 … L22; the comments below cite them); the generated code uses lib/Region.wiz, lib/Optic.wiz and, for a <code>structure</code>&#39;s field lenses, lib/OpticDerive.wiz.</p>
<p>Borrow errors (E0499, E0502, E0515, E0597, a missing <code>&#39;a : &#39;b</code>) are reported at the Feral source by this front end. They are also type errors of the lowered program: <code>#unchecked feral … end</code> lowers without the front end&#39;s verdict, so that tests can see the kernel reject the same programs. Mutable borrows lower to linear handles (<a href="#Uniq"><code>Uniq</code></a>, <a href="#Mut"><code>Mut</code></a>, <a href="#MutOpt"><code>MutOpt</code></a> at quantity 1, cohesion M4b), so duplicating one (E0499) or keeping one past its scope is a type error of the lowering too. What is <em>not</em> is reading the lender under a renamed <a href="#Lent"><code>Lent</code></a> token in hand-written Wiz (LOWERING.md, L21; the lender is an ω value): that is ruled out by the shape of what this file emits.</p>
<p>Positions: runtime <a href="#Syntax"><code>Syntax</code></a> has none, so every function here carries the <em>path</em> of the node it works on (child indices from the block), and errors are <code>Syntax.errorAt path</code>. The generated text marks what comes from which node (<a href="#Fe.Out.at"><code>Fe.Out.at</code></a>), so that hovers, go to definition and errors of the generated Wiz land on the Feral source.</p>
</div>

def · `Feral.wiz:352`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p>Positions: <code>.at p o</code> renders <code>o</code> between markers (private-use characters) that name the input node at <code>p</code>: U+E000, the path in decimal with <code>.</code> between indices, U+E001, the text, U+E002. The command elaborator strips them from the generated source and gives the syntax parsed from the text between them the range of that node (Elab/ProcMacro.lean, <code>stripMarks</code>), so that hovers, go-to-definition and errors land on the Feral source.</p>
</div>

## Functor

<a id="module-Functor"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Functor</h4>
<p>Functors and applicative functors (stage 13d): <code>import Functor</code>.</p>
<p><code>f &lt;$&gt; a</code> maps <code>f</code> over <code>a</code>; <code>f &lt;$&gt; a &lt;*&gt; b</code> applies <code>f</code> to two results. Every <a href="#Monad"><code>Monad</code></a> is an <a href="#Applicative"><code>Applicative</code></a> and every <a href="#Applicative"><code>Applicative</code></a> a <a href="#Functor"><code>Functor</code></a> (the two generic instances below), so <code>&lt;$&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;*&gt;</code> work for <a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a>, <code>Eff r</code>, <a href="#StateT"><code>StateT</code></a>, <a href="#TacticM"><code>TacticM</code></a> and any other monad without more declarations. A type with a better <code>map</code> or <code>seq</code> (or one that is not a monad, such as a signal) declares its own instance: a later instance wins over the generic ones (stage 7b).</p>
<p><a href="#Monad"><code>Monad</code></a> (in the Prelude) doesn&#39;t extend <a href="#Applicative"><code>Applicative</code></a>: classes have no <code>extends</code> yet, so its <code>pure</code> is its own field and <code>do</code> notation is unchanged. This module is separate from the Prelude because the names <a href="#Functor"><code>Functor</code></a>, <a href="#List.map"><code>List.map</code></a> and the instances for <a href="#Option"><code>Option</code></a> are already used by programs that import only the Prelude.</p>
<p>Besides the classes, the module gives <a href="#Option"><code>Option</code></a>, <a href="#Except"><code>Except</code></a> and <a href="#List"><code>List</code></a> their <a href="#Monad"><code>Monad</code></a> and <a href="#Functor"><code>Functor</code></a> instances.</p>
<pre><code>Nat.succ &lt;$&gt; Option.some 1 = Option.some 2
(fun a b =&gt; a + b) &lt;$&gt; [1, 2] &lt;*&gt; [10, 20] = [11, 21, 12, 22]</code></pre>
</div>

</div>

## Grail

<a id="module-Grail"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Grail</h4>
<p>The vocabulary of grail&#39;s build files (stage 23d; docs/stages/23-grail.md). A package&#39;s <code>grail.wiz</code> defines <code>package : Package</code>, and the uncommitted <code>grail.local.wiz</code> defines <code>local : Settings</code> (this machine&#39;s settings: the toolchain, extra module roots). grail evaluates them and reads the result as an S-expression (<a href="#Package.render"><code>Package.render</code></a>, <a href="#Settings.render"><code>Settings.render</code></a>), so a build file is an ordinary Wiz program built from the functions here.</p>
<ul><li><a href="#Package.new"><code>Package.new</code></a> starts a package; <a href="#Package.lib"><code>Package.lib</code></a>, <a href="#Package.check"><code>Package.check</code></a>, <a href="#Package.exe"><code>Package.exe</code></a>, <a href="#Package.tests"><code>Package.tests</code></a>, <a href="#Package.selfhost"><code>Package.selfhost</code></a> and <a href="#Package.command"><code>Package.command</code></a> add <a href="#Target"><code>Target</code></a>s.</li><li><a href="#Package.dep"><code>Package.dep</code></a> depends on another package from git (<a href="#Dep"><code>Dep</code></a>).</li><li><a href="#Command.new"><code>Command.new</code></a> and its builders (<a href="#Command.input"><code>Command.input</code></a>, <a href="#Command.output"><code>Command.output</code></a>, …) describe an external step of the build graph (23i).</li><li><a href="#Settings.set"><code>Settings.set</code></a> and <a href="#Package.set"><code>Package.set</code></a> set <code>key value</code> pairs.</li></ul>
<pre><code>import Grail
def package : Package :=
  Package.new &quot;shapes&quot;
    |&gt; Package.lib &quot;shapes&quot; &quot;src&quot;
    |&gt; Package.tests &quot;golden&quot; &quot;tests&quot;</code></pre>
</div>

## HProp

<a id="module-HProp"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>HProp: heap predicates and separation logic</h4>
<p>A shallow separation logic over a model heap (stage 24b), after Charguéraud&#39;s <em>Separation Logic Foundations</em> (Software Foundations vol. 6, &quot;SLF&quot;), chapters Hprop and Himpl. The program logic built on it is in <code>Hoare</code> (lib/Hoare.wiz).</p>
<p>A heap is a total function from locations to optional values, <code>Heap V := Nat → Option V</code>, and a heap predicate is a predicate on heaps, <code>HProp V := Heap V → Prop</code>. The main definitions:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#emp"><code>emp</code></a> (the empty heap), <code>l ↦ v</code> (<a href="#pts"><code>pts</code></a>, exactly one cell), <code>hpure P</code> (a pure fact, SLF&#39;s <code>\[P]</code>), <a href="#htop"><code>htop</code></a>, <a href="#hexists"><code>hexists</code></a>, <a href="#hforall"><code>hforall</code></a>;</li><li>the separating conjunction <code>H₁ ⋆ H₂</code> (<a href="#star"><code>star</code></a>: the heap splits into two disjoint parts) and the magic wand <code>H₁ −∗ H₂</code> (<a href="#wand"><code>wand</code></a>);</li><li>entailment <code>H ⊢ H&#39;</code> (<a href="#Entails"><code>Entails</code></a>), a partial order;</li><li>the laws: <a href="#star.comm"><code>star.comm</code></a>, <a href="#star.assoc"><code>star.assoc</code></a>, <a href="#star.emp_l"><code>star.emp_l</code></a>, the frame property <a href="#star.mono"><code>star.mono</code></a>, <a href="#wand.adjoint"><code>wand.adjoint</code></a>, <a href="#pts.same_loc"><code>pts.same_loc</code></a>, ….</li></ul>
<p>Two things make this cheaper in Wiz than in Coq:</p>
<ul><li>Observational equality is extensional. An equation of heaps computes to pointwise equality (<code>h₁ = h₂</code> <em>is</em> <code>(0 l : Nat) → h₁ l = h₂ l</code>), and an equation of heap predicates computes to pointwise <code>↔</code>. SLF&#39;s <code>himpl_antisym</code> needs the propext and funext axioms in Coq; here it is a pair of lambdas (<a href="#Entails.antisym"><code>Entails.antisym</code></a>), and every law that is an equation of heap predicates is proved without an axiom.</li><li>Heaps are total functions (SLF uses finite maps). Nothing here needs finiteness; the program logic gets fresh locations from a bound kept with the heap instead.</li></ul>
<p>No law here needs an axiom. For example, <code>⋆</code> is commutative as an <em>equation</em>:</p>
<pre><code>def swapCells (l m : Nat) (v w : Nat) : (l ↦ v) ⋆ (m ↦ w) = (m ↦ w) ⋆ (l ↦ v) :=
  star.comm (l ↦ v) (m ↦ w)</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="HProp.ext"></a>
### `HProp.ext`

def · `HProp.wiz:251`

```text
{V : Type} → {H : HProp V} → {H' : HProp V} → ((h : Heap V) → H h = H' h) → H = H'
```
<div class="doc"><p>Extensionality for heap predicates: an equation of heap predicates is pointwise <code>↔</code> (it computes to <code>(0 h : Heap V) → (0 _ : (0 _ : H h) → H&#39; h) × ((0 _ : H&#39; h) → H h)</code>), so this needs no axiom.</p>

## Handle

<a id="module-Handle"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Handle</h4>
<p>Owned handles (<code>import Handle</code>; cohesion step M6, wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md; docs/libraries.md).</p>
<p>An OS handle (a <a href="#File"><code>File</code></a>, an <a href="#Fd"><code>Fd</code></a>, a <a href="#Child"><code>Child</code></a>) is an ordinary (ω) value in lib/Sys.wiz, closed by its finalizer when the last reference goes, or by an explicit close that the type system does not track. <code>Owned h</code> is the obligation to release <code>h</code>: a token at quantity 1, indexed by the handle (as <code>MVar.Hole m</code> and <code>Lock.Guard l</code> are, 25d), so</p>
<ul><li>it can&#39;t be dropped: every acquired handle is released exactly once, on every path;</li><li>it can&#39;t be copied: a handle is released once, not twice;</li><li>every operation through <a href="#Handle.use"><code>Handle.use</code></a> takes it and hands it back, so there is no use after release <em>through this API</em>, and the token can move to another thread with the closure that captured it (<a href="#Chan.fork"><code>Chan.fork</code></a>).</li></ul>
<p><strong>Which handles this covers.</strong> Only handles obtained through the owned constructors below (<a href="#File.withOwned"><code>File.withOwned</code></a>, <a href="#Fd.withOwned"><code>Fd.withOwned</code></a>, <a href="#Process.spawnOwned"><code>Process.spawnOwned</code></a>): each opens a fresh handle and mints its one token, and nothing else can mint one (<code>Handle.own</code> is private), so for those handles the release (<a href="#File.releaseOwned"><code>File.releaseOwned</code></a>, …: the real close, not an overridable instance) happens exactly once. A handle from lib/Sys.wiz&#39;s ω API (<a href="#File.open"><code>File.open</code></a>, …) has no token and nothing here says anything about it.</p>
<p>What it does not do: <code>h</code> itself stays an ω value, so code that calls lib/Sys.wiz&#39;s operations on <code>h</code> directly (<code>File.close h</code> inside <a href="#Handle.use"><code>Handle.use</code></a>&#39;s action, say) is not checked. Making the handles themselves linear (and the operations direct style, <code>(1 o : Owned f) → … → IO (Owned f)</code>) needs linear Σ fields (linear-case stage 2); then lib/Sys.wiz and lib/Serial.wiz move onto this module.</p>
<p>Trusted: the two natives <code>wiz_handle_own</code>/<code>wiz_handle_disown</code> (runtime/: an empty box, as an MVar hole) and their private <code>extern</code>s; nothing else reaches <a href="#Owned"><code>Owned</code></a>. Extern privacy is by name only: another module could bind <code>wiz_handle_own</code> with any type (it would show in <code>#print axioms</code>), the same gap as MVar.Hole, Lock.Guard and Chan.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Apb

<a id="module-Hdl.Apb"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Apb</h4>
<p>A thin AMBA APB bridge for <code>Hdl.Bus</code> (<code>import Hdl.Apb</code>). <code>Bus</code> is the internal single-outstanding, AXI4-Lite-shaped valid/ready bus (<a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> with byte strobes); this file does not add a fourth protocol, it maps that bus onto the APB signal set, in both directions:</p>
<ul><li><code>Apb.busToApbC aw dw</code>: a <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> master on an APB slave. The bridge runs APB&#39;s two phases (SETUP: <code>PSEL</code> high, <code>PENABLE</code> low; ACCESS: <code>PSEL</code> and <code>PENABLE</code> high until <code>PREADY</code>), captures the request when it starts SETUP so the APB fields are stable for the whole transfer, and answers the bus at the end of ACCESS. <code>PADDR</code>, <code>PWDATA</code>, <code>PWRITE</code> and <code>PSTRB</code> come from <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> (<code>PSTRB</code> is zero on reads, as APB requires); <code>PRDATA</code> and <code>PSLVERR</code> become <code>rdata</code>/<code>err</code>. One bus request is one APB transfer, so responses come back in request order. The bridge returns to IDLE for at least one cycle between transfers (APB&#39;s SETUP phase).</li><li><code>Apb.apbToBusC aw dw</code>: an APB master on a <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> slave. It is combinational: APB&#39;s ACCESS phase (<code>PSEL &amp;&amp; PENABLE</code>) is the bus <code>valid</code>, <code>PWRITE</code> is <code>we</code>, <code>PADDR</code>/<code>PWDATA</code>/<code>PSTRB</code> are the payload, and the bus&#39;s <code>ready</code>/<code>rvalid</code>/<code>rdata</code>/<code>err</code> drive <code>PREADY</code>/<code>PRDATA</code>/<code>PSLVERR</code>. SETUP is not a bus request; the APB master holds the fields through ACCESS until <code>PREADY</code>, which is exactly the bus source obligation.</li></ul>
<p>Both directions pass every byte strobe through unchanged and never generate a response without a request. <code>examples/hdl-protocols.wiz</code> (test group <code>bus-protocol</code>) checks the stability, response-order and strobe laws over generated traces, and compares the value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a> cycle for cycle.</p>
<p>APB is ARM IHI 0024; this is the APB4 subset (byte strobes, <code>PSLVERR</code>) with one outstanding transfer and no <code>PWAKEUP</code>/<code>PPROT</code>/<code>PSTRB</code>-less variants.</p>
</div>

<a id="Apb.step"></a>
### `Apb.step`

def · `Hdl/Apb.wiz:113`

```text
{r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → {ω aw : Nat} → {ω dw : Nat} → Apb.St aw dw r → Apb.In aw dw r → r (HwTy.prod (Apb.St.code aw dw) (Apb.Out.code aw dw))
```
<div class="doc"><p>One cycle of the bus-to-APB bridge. A request is captured on IDLE -&gt; SETUP; SETUP always becomes ACCESS; ACCESS ends on <code>PREADY</code> and answers the bus in that same cycle (<code>ready</code> for both kinds, <code>rvalid</code> only for a read). A bus master that drops <code>valid</code> in IDLE starts nothing; one that violates the bus obligation mid-transfer cannot shorten the APB transfer, which completes normally.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Arty

<a id="module-Hdl.Arty"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Arty</h4>
<p>The Digilent Arty A7 (Artix-7 in a CSG324 package): its resources as an XDC pin table (<code>Hdl.Xdc</code>), and the two devices it comes with.</p>
<p>Pins from Digilent&#39;s master XDC files (github.com/Digilent/digilent-xdc, Arty-A7-35-Master.xdc and Arty-A7-100-Master.xdc: the same pins on both boards), all LVCMOS33. Port names as there, with the RGB LEDs as one bus and the UART by direction as the FPGA sees it.</p>
<p>| port      | width | pins                                      | what                        | |-----------|-------|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------| | <code>clk</code>     | 1     | E3                                        | 100 MHz oscillator          | | <code>led</code>     | 4     | H5 J5 T9 T10                              | LD4 … LD7 (green), high: on | | <code>rgb</code>     | 12    | G6 F6 E1, G3 J4 G4, J3 J2 H4, K1 H6 K2    | LD0 … LD3: r g b each       | | <code>btn</code>     | 4     | D9 C9 B9 B8                               | BTN0 … BTN3, high: pressed  | | <code>sw</code>      | 4     | A8 C11 C10 A10                            | SW0 … SW3                   | | <code>uart_rx</code> | 1     | A9                                        | FT2232 channel B → FPGA     | | <code>uart_tx</code> | 1     | D10                                       | FPGA → FT2232 channel B     | | <code>ck_rst</code>  | 1     | C2                                        | RESET button, low: pressed  | | <code>ja</code>…<code>jd</code> | 8     | see below                                 | Pmod headers, pins 1-4, 7-10 |</p>
<p>(Digilent&#39;s names for the UART are from the host&#39;s side: <code>uart_txd_in</code> is A9, <code>uart_rxd_out</code> D10.) The RGB LEDs are bright: drive them at a low duty cycle.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Axi4

<a id="module-Hdl.Axi4"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Axi4</h4>
<p>The AXI4 burst subset of ARM IHI 0022, over <code>Hdl.Bus</code> (<code>import Hdl.Axi4</code>). <code>Hdl.AxiLite</code> gives the five AXI4-Lite channels the ARM names but stays at one beat per transfer; this module adds the burst fields and the burst adapters:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#Axi4.Aw"><code>Axi4.Aw</code></a>/<a href="#W"><code>W</code></a>/<code>B</code> and <a href="#Axi4.Ar"><code>Axi4.Ar</code></a>/<code>R</code> are the full AXI4 write and read channels: <code>AxLEN</code>, <code>AxSIZE</code>, <code>AxBURST</code> (FIXED/INCR/WRAP), <code>AxID</code>, <code>WLAST</code>/<code>RLAST</code> and the response <code>BRESP</code>/<code>RRESP</code> with the ID echoed back.</li><li><a href="#Axi4.SlaveIn"><code>Axi4.SlaveIn</code></a>/<code>SlaveOut</code>/<code>MasterOut</code>/<code>MasterIn</code> put the five channels and their <code>*READY</code> signals in the usual directions.</li><li><a href="#Axi4.beatAddr"><code>Axi4.beatAddr</code></a> is the address of beat <code>k</code> of a burst: INCR adds <code>2^SIZE</code> per beat, WRAP walks the aligned window of <code>(LEN + 1) * 2^SIZE</code> bytes and wraps at its end, FIXED holds the address. <a href="#Axi4.beatSeq"><code>Axi4.beatSeq</code></a> is the whole address list.</li><li><code>Axi4.wrC aw dw idw</code> is a write adapter: an AXI4 master&#39;s <code>AW</code>/<a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> burst becomes one <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> write per beat, and one <code>B</code> response at the end. <code>Axi4.rdC aw dw idw</code> is the read direction: an <code>AR</code> burst becomes one <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> read per beat, and <code>R</code> beats with <code>RLAST</code> on the last one. Both adapters hold the bus request (and the AXI beat) while the bus slave stalls, so no beat is lost or duplicated under backpressure.</li></ul>
<p>The subset is deliberately the one a single-beat bus can serve. Each adapter is single outstanding (the next <code>AW</code>/<code>AR</code> is accepted after the previous response has been handed back), <code>AW</code> and <a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> need not arrive together (<code>AWREADY</code> is high at rest), but the write adapter consumes one <a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> beat per completed bus beat, and <code>AxSIZE</code> must not exceed the bus data width (<code>2^SIZE</code> bytes per beat). The attributes (<code>AxPROT</code>, <code>AxCACHE</code>, <code>AxLOCK</code>, <code>AxQOS</code>, <code>AxREGION</code>, and the user signals) and the exclusive accesses are not part of this subset. <a href="#Axi4.Burst"><code>Axi4.Burst</code></a>/<a href="#Axi4.orderOf"><code>Axi4.orderOf</code></a> model multiple outstanding IDs at values: with several requests in flight the responses must be a permutation of the requests that preserves each ID&#39;s own order. The single-outstanding adapters are the special case where that order is the issue order.</p>
<p><code>examples/hdl-axi4.wiz</code> (test group <code>bus-protocol</code>) runs INCR and WRAP bursts in both directions, with a bus slave that stalls, and checks the <code>Hdl.Axi4Law</code> obligations (address progression, beat count, <code>WLAST</code>/<code>RLAST</code>, write strobes, response ID/order). The value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a> are compared cycle for cycle, and yosys <code>check -assert</code>/<code>synth_ice40</code> runs on the emitted Verilog when yosys is on PATH.</p>
</div>

<a id="Axi4.wrStep"></a>
### `Axi4.wrStep`

def · `Hdl/Axi4.wiz:306`

```text
{r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → {ω aw : Nat} → {ω dw : Nat} → {ω idw : Nat} → Axi4.WrSt aw dw idw r → Axi4.WriteIn aw dw idw r → r (HwTy.prod (Axi4.WrSt.code aw dw idw) (Axi4.WriteOut.code aw dw idw))
```
<div class="doc"><p>One cycle of the AXI4 write adapter. <code>AW</code> is accepted at rest (capturing the burst fields); each <a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> beat is consumed exactly when the bus answers that beat&#39;s <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> (the request address is the captured beat address), and the final beat moves to the <code>B</code> phase, where <code>BVALID</code> is held until <code>BREADY</code>. A bus error on any beat of the burst makes <code>BRESP</code> <code>SLVERR</code>. <code>WLAST</code> is not trusted to end the burst: <code>LEN</code> says how many beats there are (a mismatched <code>WLAST</code> is an input violation, checked by the laws).</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Axi4Law

<a id="module-Hdl.Axi4Law"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Axi4Law</h4>
<p>The obligations of the AXI4 burst adapters in <code>Hdl.Axi4</code>, stated over value traces as in <code>Hdl.BusLaw</code> and <code>Hdl.ProtocolLaw</code>. <code>examples/hdl-axi4.wiz</code> (test group <code>bus-protocol</code>) evaluates the Boolean forms on INCR and WRAP bursts with a stalling bus slave, at the same time as it compares the value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a>. They are <strong>tested, not proved</strong>; only the small lemmas at the end are kernel-checked.</p>
<p>The laws, by obligation:</p>
<ul><li><strong>Legal bursts.</strong> <a href="#Axi4.Law.legal"><code>Axi4.Law.legal</code></a>: <code>AxSIZE</code> fits the bus data width (<code>2^SIZE</code> bytes per beat) and a WRAP burst has 2, 4, 8 or 16 beats (<a href="#Axi4.legalWrap"><code>Axi4.legalWrap</code></a>, <a href="#Axi4.Law.legalLen"><code>Axi4.Law.legalLen</code></a>).</li><li><strong>Address progression.</strong> The <code>k</code>-th beat&#39;s address is <a href="#Axi4.beatAddr"><code>Axi4.beatAddr</code></a>: INCR adds <code>2^SIZE</code>, WRAP walks its aligned <code>(LEN + 1) * 2^SIZE</code> window and wraps at the end, FIXED holds the base. <a href="#Axi4.Law.AddressProgression"><code>Axi4.Law.AddressProgression</code></a> says the bus addresses of a burst are exactly <a href="#Axi4.beatSeq"><code>Axi4.beatSeq</code></a>, and <a href="#Axi4.Law.WrBeatOk"><code>Axi4.Law.WrBeatOk</code></a>/<code>RdBeatOk</code> check one beat at the adapter pins.</li><li><strong>Beat count.</strong> A burst has <code>LEN + 1</code> beats: <a href="#Axi4.Law.BeatCount"><code>Axi4.Law.BeatCount</code></a> on the number of bus beats, the number of <a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> beats and the number of <code>R</code> beats. <code>WLAST</code>/<code>RLAST</code> are high exactly on beat <code>LEN</code> (<a href="#Axi4.Law.WLastOk"><code>Axi4.Law.WLastOk</code></a>/<code>RLastOk</code>).</li><li><strong>Write strobes.</strong> Every <a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> beat&#39;s <code>WSTRB</code> arrives unchanged on the bus request (<a href="#Axi4.Law.WrBeatOk"><code>Axi4.Law.WrBeatOk</code></a>), one per beat, in order: no byte strobe is dropped or repeated under backpressure.</li><li><strong>Response ordering and IDs.</strong> <code>B</code> echoes the <code>AW</code> ID and <code>BRESP</code> is <code>SLVERR</code> exactly for a bus error; <code>R</code> echoes the <code>AR</code> ID, carries the bus data and <code>SLVERR</code>, and <code>RLAST</code> marks the last beat (<a href="#Axi4.Law.BRespOk"><code>Axi4.Law.BRespOk</code></a>/<code>RRespOk</code>). With several IDs in flight the adapters are single outstanding, so responses come back in issue order, the single-ID case of <a href="#Axi4.ResponseOrder"><code>Axi4.ResponseOrder</code></a> (different IDs may overtake each other in the general AXI4 rule, modelled at values by <a href="#Axi4.orderOf"><code>Axi4.orderOf</code></a>).</li></ul>
</div>
