## Hdl.AxiLite

<a id="module-Hdl.AxiLite"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.AxiLite</h4>
<p>AXI4-Lite channel bundles for <code>Hdl.Bus</code> (<code>import Hdl.AxiLite</code>). <code>Bus</code> is already the single-outstanding, AXI4-Lite-shaped core: <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> is a write with <code>WSTRB</code> or a read, and <a href="#Bus.Resp"><code>Bus.Resp</code></a> is the corresponding <code>B</code>/<code>R</code> answer. This file gives the ARM channel names a concrete shape so a design can expose them, rather than inventing another bus:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#AxiLite.Aw"><code>AxiLite.Aw</code></a>/<a href="#W"><code>W</code></a>/<code>B</code> are the write address, write data and write response channels; <a href="#AxiLite.Ar"><code>AxiLite.Ar</code></a>/<code>R</code> are the read address and read response channels.</li><li><a href="#AxiLite.MasterOut"><code>AxiLite.MasterOut</code></a>/<code>MasterIn</code> and <a href="#AxiLite.SlaveIn"><code>AxiLite.SlaveIn</code></a>/<code>SlaveOut</code> are the five channels with their <code>*READY</code> signals in the direction the name says.</li><li><a href="#AxiLite.writeOf"><code>AxiLite.writeOf</code></a>/<code>readOf</code> are the documented <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> view of a write/read in the subset <code>Bus</code> supports: one outstanding transfer, no bursts, no IDs, and <code>AW</code>/<a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> presented together (so <code>awvalid &amp;&amp; wvalid</code> is the bus <code>valid</code>). <a href="#AxiLite.errOf"><code>AxiLite.errOf</code></a> turns a non-<code>OKAY</code> <code>BRESP</code>/<code>RRESP</code> into the bus&#39;s <code>err</code>.</li></ul>
<p>The subset is deliberately the shape <code>Bus</code> already has: single outstanding, no bursts, no <code>AxLEN</code>/<code>AxSIZE</code>/<code>AxBURST</code>/<code>AxID</code>/<code>AxPROT</code>, no exclusive or cache attributes. For a full AXI4-Lite slave the <code>AW</code> and <a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> channels may arrive in different cycles; that needs a small queue and is not claimed here. The APB and Wishbone bridges (<code>Hdl.Apb</code>, <code>Hdl.Wishbone</code>) take <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> as their internal form.</p>
<p><code>examples/hdl-protocols.wiz</code> (test group <code>bus-protocol</code>) round-trips these bundles through <a href="#Bundle.toEl"><code>Bundle.toEl</code></a>/<a href="#Bundle.ofEl"><code>Bundle.ofEl</code></a> and checks a sample of the <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> views.</p>
<p>AXI4-Lite is ARM IHI 0022, chapter C.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Bits

<a id="module-Hdl.Bits"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Bits</h4>
<p>Bit-level reasoning for circuits (<code>import Hdl.Bits</code>): the laws of one-bit signals at values, so that a proof does not dictate how control logic is written (finding C2 of the iCEstick toy CPU: <code>rfl</code> reduces a multiplexer on a known select, but not <code>Hw.and (Hw.lit 1 0) x</code> on a symbolic <code>x</code>). Design: wiz-notes/cohesion-hardware.md, 2.3.</p>
<ul><li><code>Bit.ind</code>: a property of every bit is a property of 0 and of 1. With it, every law of one-bit logic is two (or four, eight) closed evaluations: <code>Bit.ind</code> and <code>rfl</code>. It rests on the words&#39; range (stage 22l: a <code>UIntN 1</code> is 0 or 1, <a href="#UIntN.cases1"><code>UIntN.cases1</code></a>).</li><li>The laws as named lemmas (<a href="#Bit.and_zero"><code>Bit.and_zero</code></a>, <a href="#Bit.or_one"><code>Bit.or_one</code></a>, <a href="#Bit.not_not"><code>Bit.not_not</code></a>, …), and the multiplexer normal form: <a href="#Bit.and_mux"><code>Bit.and_mux</code></a> (<code>a &amp; b = a ? b : 0</code>), <a href="#Bit.or_mux"><code>Bit.or_mux</code></a>, <a href="#Bit.not_mux"><code>Bit.not_mux</code></a>, so a proof can turn gate-level control logic into the multiplexers that <code>rfl</code> reduces, or the other way round; <a href="#HwTy.El.mux_same"><code>HwTy.El.mux_same</code></a> at any type.</li><li>The bridge to Booleans: <a href="#Bit.toBool"><code>Bit.toBool</code></a> is a homomorphism (<a href="#Bit.toBool_and"><code>Bit.toBool_and</code></a> …) and <a href="#Bit.eq_of_toBool"><code>Bit.eq_of_toBool</code></a> turns an equation of bits into one of Booleans, the goals that <code>sat_decide</code> (stage 28b) decides with a kernel-checked certificate.</li></ul>
</div>

<a id="Bit.eqv"></a>
### `Bit.eqv`

def · `Hdl/Bits.wiz:30`

```text
(x : BitVec 1) → (y : BitVec 1) → BitVec.toNat 1 x = BitVec.toNat 1 y → x = y
```
<div class="doc"><p>two bits are equal when their numbers are (a closed equation of bits: <code>Bit.eqv _ _ rfl</code>; plain <code>rfl</code> can fail where two equal words were built with different range proofs)</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Bus

<a id="module-Hdl.Bus"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Bus</h4>
<p>A small, board-independent valid/ready bus (<code>import Hdl.Bus</code>): a request/response record, a two-master round-robin arbiter, an address decode/route helper, and a behavioural RAM for simulation. It generalises the golem SoC&#39;s <code>GBus</code>/<code>Bus.wiz</code> (<code>wiz-rv/src/Rv/Golem/Bus.wiz</code>): the golem bus hard-codes a 32-bit address, 32-bit data, golem&#39;s DDR window and a 28-bit cache port; here the address and data widths are parameters and nothing knows a board or a memory map.</p>
<p>The handshake is the usual one: a master asserts <code>valid</code> and holds the request until the slave answers with <code>ready</code> (the request was taken) or, for a read, <code>rvalid</code> with the data. <code>err</code> marks a request the decoder did not map (it is answered at once, so a wild pointer cannot hang a machine). A request is one clock cycle at values and one netlist cycle in simulation; <a href="#Bus.ramC"><code>Bus.ramC</code></a> answers two cycles after the request, which is the simple model golem&#39;s cache stand-in used.</p>
<p>The parts:</p>
<ul><li><code>Bus.Req aw dw</code> / <code>Bus.Resp dw</code>: the request and response records (<code>deriving Bundle</code>);</li><li><code>Bus.ReqW aw dw</code>: a request with byte enables (<code>wstrb</code>, <code>dw / 8</code> bits), and <a href="#Bus.ReqW.ofReq"><code>Bus.ReqW.ofReq</code></a>/<code>toReq</code> to use it where a word-level <a href="#Bus.Req"><code>Bus.Req</code></a> is expected;</li><li><code>Bus.arbC aw dw</code>: two masters onto one slave, round-robin when both ask and neither owns the bus, holding the owner until its answer (so a master that holds <code>valid</code>, as a core does, is never starved mid-word); <a href="#Bus.arbStepAtBits"><code>Bus.arbStepAtBits</code></a>/<a href="#Bus.arbStepAt"><code>Bus.arbStepAt</code></a> is the same step with the grant (<code>g</code>) as an input, which is the form the proofs in <code>Hdl.BusLaw</code> use;</li><li><code>Bus.arbNStep n aw dw</code>: the N-master generalisation over value vectors (<a href="#Vec"><code>Vec</code></a>): a round-robin grant over a <code>last</code> index, the same hold-until-answered rule, and one response per master. <a href="#HwTy"><code>HwTy</code></a> has no vector code, so this is an executable reference model (value-level <a href="#Mealy"><code>Mealy</code></a>), not a circuit; <a href="#Bus.arbC"><code>Bus.arbC</code></a> remains the synthesisable two-master API;</li><li><code>Bus.routeC aw dw base size</code>: the address decode: requests inside <code>[base, base+size)</code> go to the slave, anything else is answered immediately with <code>err</code> high and zero data (golem&#39;s <code>GBus.route</code>, without golem&#39;s memory map);</li><li><code>Bus.ramC shift aw ab dw</code>: a behavioural RAM with <code>2^ab</code> words of <code>dw</code> bits, a <code>shift</code>-bit word offset inside <code>addr</code> (0 for a word-addressed bus, 2 for a 32-bit byte-addressed one) and a two-cycle answer;</li><li><code>Bus.ramWC shift aw ab dw</code>: the same RAM with byte enables (<a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a>), a read-modify-write on the addressed word.</li></ul>
<p>All parts are plain <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a>s or step functions over bundles, polymorphic in the representation, so the same definitions simulate at values, simulate as a netlist and synthesise. The example is <code>examples/hdl-bus.wiz</code>, checked by the <code>bus-crc</code> test group: the value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a> agree cycle for cycle.</p>
</div>

<a id="Bus.Req"></a>
### `Bus.Req`

structure · `Hdl/Bus.wiz:58`

```text
Nat → Nat → (HwTy → Type) → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A bus request: <code>valid</code> and the request fields. <code>addr</code> is a word address for a word-addressed bus (or a byte address when the slave&#39;s <code>shift</code> says so), <code>we</code> a write when high, and <code>wdata</code> the word to write. It has no byte strobes: a cache or a board port that needs them keeps them in its own request record (as golem&#39;s <code>CacheReq</code> does) and adapts.</p>
</div>

**Constructors and fields**

- <a id="Bus.Req.mk"></a>`mk` : `{aw : Nat} → {dw : Nat} → {r : HwTy → Type} → r Bus.Bit → r Bus.Bit → r (HwTy.bits aw) → r (HwTy.bits dw) → Bus.Req aw dw r`
- <a id="Bus.Req.valid"></a>`valid` : `{aw : Nat} → {dw : Nat} → {r : HwTy → Type} → Bus.Req aw dw r → r Bus.Bit`
- <a id="Bus.Req.we"></a>`we` : `{aw : Nat} → {dw : Nat} → {r : HwTy → Type} → Bus.Req aw dw r → r Bus.Bit`
- <a id="Bus.Req.addr"></a>`addr` : `{aw : Nat} → {dw : Nat} → {r : HwTy → Type} → Bus.Req aw dw r → r (HwTy.bits aw)`
- <a id="Bus.Req.wdata"></a>`wdata` : `{aw : Nat} → {dw : Nat} → {r : HwTy → Type} → Bus.Req aw dw r → r (HwTy.bits dw)`

<a id="Bus.ReqW"></a>
### `Bus.ReqW`

structure · `Hdl/Bus.wiz:80`

```text
Nat → Nat → (HwTy → Type) → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A bus request with byte enables: the same fields as <a href="#Bus.Req"><code>Bus.Req</code></a> plus <code>wstrb</code>, one bit per byte of <code>wdata</code> (<code>dw / 8</code> bits, low byte first). A write applies byte <code>k</code> only when bit <code>k</code> of <code>wstrb</code> is set; a read ignores it. For a data width that is not a multiple of 8 the strobe covers the low <code>8 * (dw / 8)</code> bits and the remaining high bits keep their old value; use a multiple of 8 for a byte-addressed bus. <a href="#Bus.ReqW.ofReq"><code>Bus.ReqW.ofReq</code></a> turns a plain request into one that writes every byte, so <a href="#Bus.Req"><code>Bus.Req</code></a> stays the simple word-level API.</p>
</div>

**Constructors and fields**

- <a id="Bus.ReqW.mk"></a>`mk` : `{aw : Nat} → {dw : Nat} → {r : HwTy → Type} → r Bus.Bit → r Bus.Bit → r (HwTy.bits aw) → r (HwTy.bits dw) → r (HwTy.bits (Nat.div dw 8)) → Bus.ReqW aw dw r`
- <a id="Bus.ReqW.valid"></a>`valid` : `{aw : Nat} → {dw : Nat} → {r : HwTy → Type} → Bus.ReqW aw dw r → r Bus.Bit`

<a id="Bus.arbStepAtBits"></a>
### `Bus.arbStepAtBits`

def · `Hdl/Bus.wiz:184`

```text
{r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → {ω aw : Nat} → {ω dw : Nat} → r Bus.Bit → r Bus.Bit → r Bus.Bit → r Bus.Bit → Bus.Req aw dw r → Bus.Req aw dw r → Bus.Resp dw r → r (HwTy.prod Bus.Arb.code (Bus.ArbOut.code aw dw))
```
<div class="doc"><p>One cycle of the arbiter with the grant already chosen: <code>g = 0</code> gives the bus to master <code>a</code>, <code>g = 1</code> to master <code>b</code>. This is the indexed form of <a href="#Bus.arbStep"><code>Bus.arbStep</code></a> (the arbiter&#39;s choice is an input to the step, not part of it), so a proof can fix <code>g</code> and case-split on the small control bits. <a href="#Bus.arbStep"><code>Bus.arbStep</code></a> is the definition with <code>g = Bus.pick s a.valid b.valid</code>.</p>
</div>

<a id="Bus.arbStep"></a>

def · `Hdl/Bus.wiz:213`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p>One cycle of the arbiter: choose the grant by the round-robin rule, then run the indexed step. Keeping the choice out of <a href="#Bus.arbStepAt"><code>Bus.arbStepAt</code></a> makes the properties of one grant a two-case proof (<code>g = 0</code> or <code>g = 1</code>).</p>

<a id="Bus.arbNCStep"></a>
### `Bus.arbNCStep`

def · `Hdl/Bus.wiz:418`

```text
{r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → {ω n : Nat} → {ω aw : Nat} → {ω dw : Nat} → r Bus.Bit → r (HwTy.bits n) → r (HwTy.bits n) → r (Bus.prodN n (Bus.Req.code aw dw)) → Bus.Resp dw r → r (HwTy.prod (Bus.ArbNS.code n) (Bus.ArbNOut.code n aw dw))
```
<div class="doc"><p>One cycle of the N-master circuit: the same rule as <a href="#Bus.arbNStep"><code>Bus.arbNStep</code></a>. The grant is the owner while busy, else <a href="#Bus.pickNHw"><code>Bus.pickNHw</code></a>; the owner keeps the bus until the slave answers or drops <code>valid</code>; the forwarded request is the granted one (quiet when there is none); only the granted master gets the response.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.BusLaw

<a id="module-Hdl.BusLaw"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.BusLaw</h4>
<p>The protocol laws of <code>Hdl.Bus</code> (<code>import Hdl.BusLaw</code>), stated as predicates over the value traces of a circuit, plus the small proofs the HDL model supports. The example <code>examples/hdl-bus-law.wiz</code> (test group <code>bus-law</code>) checks every predicate exhaustively or on long pseudo-random traces, and checks the value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a> against each other at the same time. A law checked that way is <em>tested, not proved</em>: the predicate is a <code>Prop</code>, the check is a Boolean function that was evaluated on its inputs, and only the lemmas marked as kernel-checked below are proved.</p>
<p>The usual handshake: a source asserts <code>valid</code> and holds the request until the sink answers (<code>ready</code>, or <code>rvalid</code> for a read). The laws are</p>
<ul><li><code>Stable</code>: while stalled (<code>valid</code> and not answered), <code>valid</code> and the whole request are held; <code>ValidStable</code>, <code>PayloadStable</code> and <code>AddressStable</code> split it up;</li><li><code>AnsweredAfter</code>: a response is only ever given to a request that was offered <code>d</code> cycles earlier (0 for the combinational router, 2 for <a href="#Bus.ramC"><code>Bus.ramC</code></a>/<a href="#Bus.ramWC"><code>Bus.ramWC</code></a>);</li><li><code>AtMostOneAck</code>: the arbiter answers at most one master per cycle (mutual exclusion); with <code>Stable</code> this is <code>SingleOwner</code>, the observable single-master ownership;</li><li><code>NoStarvation</code>: a master that keeps offering is eventually answered, under a fair sink (checked on traces where the sink answers often enough);</li><li><code>RouteCorrect</code>: a hit forwards the request unchanged and passes the sink&#39;s answer; a miss forwards no request and answers at once with <code>err</code>;</li><li><code>ReadAfterWrite</code>: the RAM reads back the word a write has just stored, with strobes applied byte by byte.</li></ul>
</div>

## Hdl.Cdc

<a id="module-Hdl.Cdc"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Cdc</h4>
<p>Clock-domain crossings (<code>import Hdl.Cdc</code>).</p>
<p>A <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> has one clock domain: all its registers tick together and <a href="#Circuit.run"><code>Circuit.run</code></a> is one step per input. A design with two clocks is a composition of such circuits, each clocked by its own domain, wired at the top: <a href="#ClockDomain"><code>ClockDomain</code></a> names the Verilog net, and <code>Circuit.netlistIn d name c</code> puts a circuit&#39;s registers on <code>d</code>.</p>
<p>Data that crosses from one domain into another must go through a synchroniser. <code>Cdc.sync2 dst d</code> is two flops in the destination domain (<code>dst</code>&#39;s), the first one sampling the asynchronous data <code>d</code>; it is a <a href="#Prim"><code>Prim</code></a> declared with <a href="#Prim.declSync"><code>Prim.declSync</code></a>, so <a href="#Netlist.domainErrors"><code>Netlist.domainErrors</code></a> lets its data come from exactly one other domain, puts its output in <code>dst</code>&#39;s domain, and rejects every other crossing (a register sampling another domain, a combinational path that mixes domains, a memory written from another domain, ...).</p>
<pre><code>def d2 : ClockDomain := ClockDomain.named &quot;clk2&quot;
-- in the clk2 circuit: `d` (from the clk circuit) two clk2 edges later
def synced {r : HwTy → Type} [Hw r] (d : r HwTy.bit) : r HwTy.bit :=
  Cdc.sync2 (Hw.clockOf d2) d</code></pre>
<p>The cell has no behavioural model (a model is one total function of its inputs, so a two-flop delay can only be written as the identity), and the checked runners refuse a multi-domain netlist anyway (<a href="#Netlist.domainRefusals"><code>Netlist.domainRefusals</code></a>): a two-clock design needs an event schedule, which <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> does not have. <a href="#Cdc.verilog"><code>Cdc.verilog</code></a> is the Verilog module the emitted instance refers to; append its text to the module&#39;s file (the <code>async_reg</code> attributes keep the two flops together in synthesis).</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Core

<a id="module-Hdl.Core"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Core: hardware description</h4>
<p>The HDL library (<code>import Hdl.Core</code>): describe digital circuits in Wiz, simulate them, prove things about them, and synthesise them to a netlist, Verilog, a test bench, a VCD waveform and pin constraints. docs/libraries.md (&quot;H14 S0&quot;, &quot;H14 S1&quot;) describes it; design notes are in drafts/hdl/Synth.wiz and wiz-notes/hdl-usability.md.</p>
<p>Combinational logic is <em>tagless-final</em> code, polymorphic in its representation <code>r : HwTy → Type</code> (the class <a href="#Hw"><code>Hw</code></a>), with two instances: values (<a href="#HwTy.El"><code>HwTy.El</code></a>, for simulation and proofs) and wires (<a href="#Wire"><code>Wire</code></a>, for netlist construction). The same definition is both the specification and the hardware. A sequential circuit is a <code>Circuit i o</code>, a Mealy machine whose step is such code; its state is the registers.</p>
<ul><li><strong>Types are codes</strong> (<a href="#HwTy"><code>HwTy</code></a>): bit vectors, products, and <code>named s t</code>, a type with a name (<a href="#HwTy.El"><code>HwTy.El</code></a>, <a href="#HwTy.width"><code>HwTy.width</code></a> and the bus encoding ignore the name; the netlist uses it for ports, registers and wires).</li><li><strong>Wires are structured</strong>: a value of a product type is a product of node ids, so pairs and projections cost nothing, and ports and registers are one per leaf, named by the path of <code>named</code> segments (<code>tx_cnt</code>).</li><li><strong>Memories</strong>: <code>HwTy.mem aw dw</code>, <code>2^aw</code> words of <code>dw</code> bits, a function at values; read with <a href="#Hw.memRead"><code>Hw.memRead</code></a> (combinational), written with <a href="#Hw.memWrite"><code>Hw.memWrite</code></a> (at the clock edge, when it is the state&#39;s next value). In Verilog an array, which yosys maps to block RAM.</li><li><strong>Primitives</strong>: <code>Prim i o</code> (lib/Hdl/Prim.wiz) is a vendor cell, a black box printed as its Verilog module; <a href="#Hw.prim"><code>Hw.prim</code></a> instantiates it. Their ports carry a kind (data, a clock net, a pad, a bidirectional pad, marked by a <code>named</code> segment beginning with <code>@</code>); only primitives&#39; ports connect clock and pad leaves, and <a href="#Netlist.kindErrors"><code>Netlist.kindErrors</code></a> checks it.</li><li><strong>Clock domains</strong>: a <a href="#ClockDomain"><code>ClockDomain</code></a> names the Verilog net of a clock and its period. A circuit&#39;s registers and memories are all on the one domain it is built for (<code>Circuit.netlistIn d</code>; <a href="#Circuit.netlist"><code>Circuit.netlist</code></a> is <a href="#ClockDomain.sys"><code>ClockDomain.sys</code></a>). A design with two clocks is a wiring of single-clock circuits; data crossing from one domain into another must pass a synchroniser (<a href="#Prim.declSync"><code>Prim.declSync</code></a>, <code>Hdl.Cdc</code>&#39;s <a href="#Cdc.sync2"><code>Cdc.sync2</code></a>), and <a href="#Netlist.domainErrors"><code>Netlist.domainErrors</code></a> rejects every other crossing.</li><li><strong>Bundles</strong>: structures of signals (<code>structure Tx (r : HwTy → Type) where line : r Bit …</code>) are <a href="#Bundle"><code>Bundle</code></a>s: <code>deriving Bundle</code> gives their code and the conversions, and field access is the ordinary <code>s.line</code>.</li><li><strong>Sharing.</strong> <code>Wire t</code> is a netlist-building computation, so a wire used twice would be built twice. The builder hash-conses (identical nodes are one node), and a meta-level <code>let</code> of an object value whose body is an object value is elaborated as <code>ShareLet.share v (fun x =&gt; body)</code> (auto-share), which at <a href="#Wire"><code>Wire</code></a> runs <code>v</code> once. Write <code>let ω x := …</code> to opt out, <a href="#Hw.share"><code>Hw.share</code></a> for explicit sharing and <code>Hw.label &quot;name&quot; x</code> to name a wire.</li></ul>
<p>The main definitions: <a href="#Hw"><code>Hw</code></a> (the operations), <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> and its combinators (<a href="#Circuit.seq"><code>Circuit.seq</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.par"><code>Circuit.par</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.loop"><code>Circuit.loop</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.delay"><code>Circuit.delay</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.withReset"><code>Circuit.withReset</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.withEnable"><code>Circuit.withEnable</code></a>) with lemmas about <a href="#Circuit.run"><code>Circuit.run</code></a>; <a href="#Circuit.netlist"><code>Circuit.netlist</code></a>, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a>, <a href="#Verilog.emit"><code>Verilog.emit</code></a>, <a href="#Testbench.verilog"><code>Testbench.verilog</code></a>, <a href="#Vcd.ofRun"><code>Vcd.ofRun</code></a> and <a href="#Pcf.emit"><code>Pcf.emit</code></a>.</p>
<pre><code>import IO
import Hdl.Core

-- an 8-bit counter with a clock enable: the output is the count
def counter : Circuit (HwTy.bits 0) (HwTy.bits 8) :=
  Circuit.mk (HwTy.bits 8) (BitVec.ofNat 8 0) (fun s _ =&gt; Hw.pair (Hw.add s (Hw.lit 8 1)) s)

def main : IO Unit := IO.println (Verilog.emit (Circuit.netlist &quot;counter&quot; (Circuit.withEnable counter)))</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="HwTy"></a>
### `HwTy`

inductive · `Hdl/Core.wiz:187`

```text
Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>Hardware types, as codes: what a signal carries.</p>
<ul><li><code>bits n</code>: a bit vector of width <code>n</code>;</li><li><code>prod a b</code>: a pair (a bundle of two signals);</li><li><code>named s t</code>: <code>t</code> with a name. The name changes nothing about the values (<a href="#HwTy.El"><code>HwTy.El</code></a>, <a href="#HwTy.width"><code>HwTy.width</code></a> and the bus encoding ignore it); the netlist uses it for ports, registers and wires (<a href="#HwTy.leafNames"><code>HwTy.leafNames</code></a>).</li></ul>
<p>A code rather than a type, so that circuits can compute with it: <code>HwTy.El t</code> is the type of its values, <code>HwTy.Ids t</code> that of its wires.</p>
</div>

<a id="Hw"></a>
### `Hw`

class · `Hdl/Core.wiz:396`

```text
(HwTy → Type) → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>The combinational operations, tagless final: code written against <code>[Hw r]</code> for an arbitrary representation <code>r : HwTy → Type</code> runs at every instance. <code>Hw HwTy.El</code> computes values (simulation, proofs); <code>Hw Wire</code> builds a netlist (synthesis).</p>
<pre><code>def incr {r : HwTy → Type} [Hw r] (x : r (HwTy.bits 8)) : r (HwTy.bits 8) :=
  Hw.add x (Hw.lit 8 1)</code></pre>
<p>The arithmetic wraps around at the width; <code>eq</code> and <code>ult</code> give one bit; <code>mux c x y</code> is <code>x</code> when <code>c</code> is 1. <code>share</code>, <code>tag</code>/<code>untag</code> and <code>label</code> cost no hardware.</p>
</div>

<a id="Netlist"></a>
### `Netlist`

structure · `Hdl/Core.wiz:777`

```text
Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A netlist: flat, widths concrete, one node per bit-vector operation (or primitive instance). Node <code>k</code> is the <code>k</code>-th of <code>nodes</code> and its arguments refer to earlier nodes; <code>hints</code> are wire names (from <a href="#Hw.label"><code>Hw.label</code></a>); <code>clocks</code> are its clock domains (one <code>always</code> block each; a single-clock design has just <a href="#ClockDomain.sys"><code>ClockDomain.sys</code></a>). <a href="#Circuit.netlist"><code>Circuit.netlist</code></a> makes one, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> runs it and <a href="#Verilog.emit"><code>Verilog.emit</code></a> prints it.</p>
</div>

<a id="HTrie"></a>
### `HTrie`

inductive · `Hdl/Core.wiz:848`

```text
Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A hash trie: <code>depth</code> levels of binary branching on the hash&#39;s bits, exact buckets at the leaves (a lookup compares whole keys, so a hash collision costs time, never correctness). The netlist builder&#39;s hash-consing table, and the maps and sets of this module.</p>
</div>

<a id="Circuit"></a>
### `Circuit`

structure · `Hdl/Core.wiz:1697`

```text
HwTy → HwTy → Type 1
```
<div class="doc"><p>A sequential circuit: a Mealy machine with state type <code>st</code>, initial state <code>init</code> and a step that is hardware code (at every representation): from the current state and the input, the next state and the output. The state is the registers; this is the only way to make feedback.</p>
<pre><code>-- a counter: the output is the count, which goes up every cycle
def counter : Circuit (HwTy.bits 0) (HwTy.bits 8) :=
  Circuit.mk (HwTy.bits 8) (BitVec.ofNat 8 0) (fun s _ =&gt; Hw.pair (Hw.add s (Hw.lit 8 1)) s)</code></pre>
</div>

**Constructors and fields**

- <a id="Circuit.mk"></a>`mk` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (st : HwTy) → HwTy.El st → ({r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r st → r i → r (HwTy.prod st o)) → Circuit i o`
- <a id="Circuit.st"></a>`st` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → Circuit i o → HwTy`
- <a id="Circuit.init"></a>`init` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (self : Circuit i o) → HwTy.El self.1`
- <a id="Circuit.step"></a>`step` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (self : Circuit i o) → {r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r self.1 → r i → r (HwTy.prod self.1 o)`

<a id="Mealy.runFrom_take"></a>
### `Mealy.runFrom_take`

def · `Hdl/Core.wiz:1758`

```text
{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (c : Circuit i o) → (n : Nat) → (s : HwTy.El c.1) → (xs : Trace (HwTy.El i)) → Circuit.runFrom i o c s (Trace.take (HwTy.El i) n xs) = Trace.take (ind (fun i' y => Type) (fun i' xs' ih => (ecase xs'.1 [fun rest h => BitVec rest.1, fun rest h => h.1 × h.2.1, fun rest h => h.1, fun rest h => BitVec rest.1 → BitVec rest.2.1]) xs'.2 ih) () o) n (Mealy.outAt (HwTy.El c.1) (HwTy.El i) (ind (fun i' y => Type) (fun i' xs' ih => (ecase xs'.1 [fun rest h => BitVec rest.1, fun rest h => h.1 × h.2.1, fun rest h => h.1, fun rest h => BitVec rest.1 → BitVec rest.2.1]) xs'.2 ih) () o) (Circuit.stepEl i o c) s xs)
```
<div class="doc"><p>(the statement lib/Hdl/Temporal.wiz uses)</p>
</div>

<a id="Circuit.withReset"></a>

def · `Hdl/Core.wiz:1836`

<div class="doc"><p>A synchronous reset: while <code>rst</code> (a new first input) is high the next state is <code>c.init</code> (the outputs in that cycle are <code>c</code>&#39;s, from the current state). In the netlist, every register gets <code>rst</code> as its reset (<code>if (rst) r &lt;= init;</code> in Verilog).</p>

<a id="Circuit.withEnable"></a>

def · `Hdl/Core.wiz:1844`

<div class="doc"><p>A clock enable: while <code>en</code> (a new first input) is low the state holds (the outputs are still <code>c</code>&#39;s, from the current state and input). In the netlist, every register gets <code>en</code> as its enable.</p>
</div>


<a id="Circuit.withResetEnable"></a>
### `Circuit.withResetEnable`

def · `Hdl/Core.wiz:1858`

```text
{ω i : HwTy} → {ω o : HwTy} → Circuit i o → Circuit (HwTy.prod (HwTy.named (String.mk [Char.mk 114, Char.mk 115, Char.mk 116]) HwTy.bit) (HwTy.prod (HwTy.named (String.mk [Char.mk 101, Char.mk 110]) HwTy.bit) i)) o
```
<div class="doc"><p>(H14 S4) The reset and enable convention. A design that has a reset or a clock enable takes them as its first inputs, named <code>rst</code> and <code>en</code>, reset first: <code>rst</code> wins over <code>en</code> (a held register is still reset), and both are synchronous and active high (as <code>if (rst) r &lt;= init; else if (en) r &lt;= next;</code>). For a whole circuit: <code>Circuit.withResetEnable c</code>; for one register: <a href="#Circuit.registerR"><code>Circuit.registerR</code></a>/<code>registerE</code>/ <code>registerRE</code>; for one field of a state inside a step function: <code>Hw.regNext rst en init cur next</code> (the next value of a register whose value is <code>cur</code>). Each of them becomes the register&#39;s reset and enable in the netlist, not a multiplexer. Every register still has its initial value (<code>initial</code> in Verilog: the iCE40 needs no reset).</p>
</div>

<a id="Bundle"></a>
### `Bundle`

structure · `Hdl/Core.wiz:3333`

```text
((HwTy → Type) → Type) → Type 1
```
<div class="doc"><p>A bundle: a structure of signals, parameterised by the representation (<code>structure Tx (r : HwTy → Type) where line : r Bit; …</code>), so that <code>s.line</code> is field access. <code>code</code> is its hardware type (a product of <code>named</code> fields), <code>pack</code> and <code>unpack</code> convert. <code>deriving Bundle</code> writes it as <code>Tx.bundle</code>; values are <code>Tx HwTy.El</code>.</p>
<p>A bundle is a plain value, not an instance: structures are structural types, so two structures with the same field types are one type and instance resolution could not tell their bundles apart.</p>
</div>

**Constructors and fields**

- <a id="Bundle.mk"></a>`mk` : `{F : (HwTy → Type) → Type} → (code : HwTy) → ({r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → F r → r code) → ({r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r code → F r) → Bundle F`
- <a id="Bundle.code"></a>`code` : `{F : (HwTy → Type) → Type} → Bundle F → HwTy`
- <a id="Bundle.pack"></a>`pack` : `{F : (HwTy → Type) → Type} → (self : Bundle F) → {r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → F r → r self.1`
- <a id="Bundle.unpack"></a>`unpack` : `{F : (HwTy → Type) → Type} → (self : Bundle F) → {r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r self.1 → F r`

<p><code>deriving Bundle</code> is made too if it is not there yet), the bundle as one bus: <code>S.width Δ</code>, <code>S.toBits Δ : S Δ r → r (HwTy.bits (S.width Δ))</code>, <code>S.ofBits Δ</code>, <code>S.unpack_pack Δ : S.unpack Δ (S.pack Δ s) = s</code> (at values), and <code>S.bitPack Δ : BitPack (S Δ HwTy.El)</code>.</p>

<div class="doc"><p>A test bench for the module <code>Verilog.emit n</code> makes: it replays the vector file <code>vec</code> (<code>cycles</code> lines, each one cycle in hexadecimal: the input ports then the expected output ports, in port order, the first in the high bits; ports of width 0 left out). ## Hdl.Crc

<a id="module-Hdl.Crc"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Crc</h4>
<p>CRC-8/SMBUS (polynomial <code>x^8 + x^2 + x + 1</code> = <code>0x07</code>, initial value 0, most significant bit first, no reflection, no final xor), twice: as hardware, one byte per clock cycle, and as a function on numbers, which is what a host computes. It is the CRC of the iCEstick project (<code>wiz-icestick-uart/src/Icestick/Crc.wiz</code>) with the board-specific vocabulary removed, so any design can use it.</p>
<p>The specification is <a href="#Crc.bit"><code>Crc.bit</code></a> (one bit), <a href="#Crc.iter"><code>Crc.iter</code></a> (n bits), <a href="#Crc.step"><code>Crc.step</code></a> (one byte), <a href="#Crc.ofList"><code>Crc.ofList</code></a> (a whole message), <a href="#Crc.hex"><code>Crc.hex</code></a> (a nibble as an ASCII hexadecimal digit) and <a href="#Crc.reply"><code>Crc.reply</code></a> (the iCEstick&#39;s two-hex-digit answer line). The hardware is <a href="#Crc.hwBit"><code>Crc.hwBit</code></a>, <a href="#Crc.hwIter"><code>Crc.hwIter</code></a> and <a href="#Crc.hwStep"><code>Crc.hwStep</code></a> (eight unrolled <code>hwBit</code> steps on <code>c XOR d</code>), and the streaming circuit <a href="#Crc.crcC"><code>Crc.crcC</code></a>: input <code>valid</code>/<code>data</code>, output <code>valid</code>/<code>crc</code>, one byte per cycle while <code>valid</code> is high.</p>
<p>The known-answer test is in the module (<a href="#Crc.checkDigits"><code>Crc.checkDigits</code></a>, <a href="#Crc.checkValue"><code>Crc.checkValue</code></a>, <a href="#Crc.check_ok"><code>Crc.check_ok</code></a>): CRC-8/SMBUS of the ASCII <code>&quot;123456789&quot;</code> is <code>0xF4</code> = 244. The test group <code>bus-crc</code> (<code>examples/hdl-crc.wiz</code>) also compares the hardware with the specification on every <code>(crc, byte)</code> pair (65536 inputs), checks <a href="#Crc.hexDigit"><code>Crc.hexDigit</code></a> against <a href="#Crc.hex"><code>Crc.hex</code></a> on all 16 nibbles, and runs <a href="#Crc.crcC"><code>Crc.crcC</code></a> through the value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a>.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Ddr

<a id="module-Hdl.Ddr"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Ddr</h4>
<p>The native port of a DDR3 controller, as a thin interface (<code>import Hdl.Ddr</code>), and a fixed-latency model of it for simulation. The real controller lives in the wiz-ddr3 repository (<code>Ddr3.Ctrl</code>): importing it here would make this library depend on that repository&#39;s modules, so this module keeps only the part that is common to any controller -- the request/response handshake -- and documents the mapping.</p>
<p>The interface (<a href="#Ddr.Req"><code>Ddr.Req</code></a>/<a href="#Ddr.Resp"><code>Ddr.Resp</code></a>) is exactly the handshake of <code>Ddr3.Ctrl</code>&#39;s <code>PortIn</code>/ <code>PortOut</code> (a closed-page DDR3 controller with a 128-bit native port):</p>
<p>| <a href="#Ddr.Req"><code>Ddr.Req</code></a> | <code>Ddr3.Ctrl.PortIn</code> | meaning                                      | |-----------|--------------------|----------------------------------------------| | <code>valid</code>   | <code>valid</code>            | a request is presented                       | | <code>we</code>      | <code>we</code>               | 1: write, 0: read                            | | <code>addr</code>    | <code>addr</code> (24 bits)   | byte address                                 | | <code>wdata</code>   | <code>wdata</code> (128 bits) | the burst to write (BL8: <code>b*16 + j</code> is beat <code>b</code>, DQ <code>j</code>) | | <code>wmask</code>   | <code>wmask</code> (16 bits)  | which bytes to write: bit <code>b*2 + l</code> is byte <code>b</code> of lane <code>l</code> |</p>
<p>| <a href="#Ddr.Resp"><code>Ddr.Resp</code></a> | <code>Ddr3.Ctrl.PortOut</code> | meaning                                    | |------------|---------------------|--------------------------------------------| | <code>ready</code>    | <code>ready</code>             | the controller can take a request this cycle | | <code>rvalid</code>   | <code>rvalid</code>            | a read burst is on <code>rdata</code> this cycle       | | <code>rdata</code>    | <code>rdata</code> (128 bits)  | the burst read                              |</p>
<p>A request is transferred when <code>valid &amp;&amp; ready</code>; a read&#39;s data comes back later with <code>rvalid</code> (the controller&#39;s own read latency, including the PHY). The controller&#39;s calibration outputs (<code>calDone</code>, <code>calFail</code>, the delay taps and slip maps) are board-level diagnostics and stay on the controller&#39;s port; the model here reports <code>ready</code> low until it has finished its one-cycle response instead.</p>
<p><a href="#Ddr.modelC"><code>Ddr.modelC</code></a>: a small single-ported model with the same handshake: <code>ready</code> is high unless a read response is in flight, a write is written at the clock edge with <code>wmask</code> applied byte by byte, and a read is accepted and answered in the next cycle from a 64K-word (1 MiB) memory. It is deliberately simple -- it is for simulating a system around the interface (a cache, a DMA engine, a memory test) and for checking the handshake, not for timing. Substitute the real controller&#39;s circuit when the repo is available; the rest of a design sees only <a href="#Ddr.Req"><code>Ddr.Req</code></a>/<a href="#Ddr.Resp"><code>Ddr.Resp</code></a>.</p>
<p>What remains (see <code>wiz-notes/rune.md</code>): the real controller&#39;s wrapper (hiding <code>PhyIn</code>/ <code>Dfi</code>), timing parameters (<code>Ddr3.Timing</code>), and a clock-domain-crossing variant of the port for a design on another clock.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Display

<a id="module-Hdl.Display"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Display</h4>
<p>The command, data and address-window layer of the SSD1306 (128 × 64 or 128 × 32, monochrome) and SSD1331 (96 × 64, RGB 565) OLED controllers (<code>import Hdl.Display</code>). It is the reusable part of the OLED project (<code>wiz-icestick-uart</code>&#39;s <code>Icestick.Oled</code>, <code>Icestick.OledRgb</code> and their Arty ports), with the panel models, the power switches, the effect generators and the frame timing left to the design.</p>
<p>The module has three layers:</p>
<ul><li><strong>Commands.</strong> <a href="#Display.Ssd"><code>Display.Ssd</code></a> and <a href="#Display.S1331"><code>Display.S1331</code></a> are the datasheet command sets the demos use; <a href="#Display.Ssd.bytes"><code>Display.Ssd.bytes</code></a> and <a href="#Display.S1331.bytes"><code>Display.S1331.bytes</code></a> turn one command into its bytes (arguments included). <a href="#Display.rgb565"><code>Display.rgb565</code></a> packs a colour, and the <code>Ssd</code>/<code>S1331</code> pixel helpers read and write pixels in a page-addressed frame or split a 16-bit colour.</li><li><strong>Init sequences and windows.</strong> <code>Display.Ssd.init rows</code> / <a href="#Display.S1331.init"><code>Display.S1331.init</code></a> are the controller configuration sequences of the OLED project (display off, clock, multiplex, addressing, remap, COM scan, contrast, charge pump, …). <code>Display.Ssd.window rows</code> (<code>columns</code> 0 … 127 and <code>pages</code> 0 … rows/8 - 1) and <a href="#Display.S1331.window"><code>Display.S1331.window</code></a> (<code>columns</code> 0 … 95 and <code>rows</code> 0 … 63) set the full-panel address window. <code>start</code> is init + window + display on.</li><li><strong>Writing.</strong> <a href="#Display.Byte"><code>Display.Byte</code></a> is one byte with its D/C level (<code>dc = false</code>: a command, <code>dc = true</code>: display data). <a href="#Display.serC"><code>Display.serC</code></a> writes bytes given one cycle at a time (<a href="#Display.WIn"><code>Display.WIn</code></a>: <code>valid</code>/<code>dc</code>/<code>data</code>), and <a href="#Display.seqC"><code>Display.seqC</code></a> walks a meta-level <code>List Display.Byte</code> by itself from a start pulse and then pulses <code>done</code>; both emit the four-wire SPI pins (<code>sclk</code>, <code>mosi</code>), chip select and D/C. The serialiser is the OLED project&#39;s: 16 cycles a byte, mode 0 (data changes on the falling edge and is sampled on the rising edge), most significant bit first, CS low for the whole sequence and high when idle (SCLK is low before the first byte and stays high while idle, as the OLED project&#39;s serialiser does). All pins are registers of the state, so they cannot glitch.</li></ul>
<p>There is one interface, four-wire SPI: neither the SSD1306 nor the SSD1331 source in the OLED project has a parallel (8080/6800) path, so none is parameterised here. A board with a parallel panel can drive <a href="#Display.Ssd.bytes"><code>Display.Ssd.bytes</code></a> / the command lists itself.</p>
<p>Simulation: every part is a <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> over bundles, polymorphic in the representation like the rest of the HDL, so the same definitions simulate at values, run as netlists (<a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a>, <code>Hdl.Sim</code>) and synthesise. The example <code>examples/hdl-display.wiz</code> decodes the emitted pins back into command/data bytes and checks that the sequence, its D/C levels, the address window and the pixel helpers are the datasheet&#39;s.</p>
<p>What remains: a frame streamer (the OLED project&#39;s pixel generator, which packs eight pixels a byte) and the PmodOLED/PmodOLEDrgb power-on sequencer (RES pulse, VBAT/VCC delays), both of which are board-specific; the SSD1331&#39;s gentle power ramp; scrolling commands.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Mem

<a id="module-Hdl.Mem"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Mem</h4>
<p>A small memory interface for hardware proofs (<code>import Hdl.Mem</code>), on the memory model of <code>Hdl.Core</code> (<code>HwTy.mem aw dw</code>, read with <a href="#Hw.memRead"><code>Hw.memRead</code></a>, written with <a href="#Hw.memWrite"><code>Hw.memWrite</code></a>).</p>
<p>The point of the module is to have one place for the facts a memory proof keeps needing, instead of re-deriving them per instruction or per RAM:</p>
<ul><li><strong>Word memory.</strong> <a href="#Mem.read"><code>Mem.read</code></a>/<a href="#Mem.write"><code>Mem.write</code></a> are the core operations with the type written down; <a href="#Mem.index"><code>Mem.index</code></a>/<a href="#Mem.lane"><code>Mem.lane</code></a> split a byte address into word index and lane, and <a href="#Mem.wordByte"><code>Mem.wordByte</code></a> is byte <code>i</code> of a word. <code>read_write_same</code>, <code>read_write_other</code> and <code>read_write_off</code> are the read-after-write/no-alias laws (<a href="#HwTy.El.memRead_write_hit"><code>HwTy.El.memRead_write_hit</code></a>/<code>_miss</code>/<code>_off</code>, restated for <a href="#Mem.read"><code>Mem.read</code></a>/<a href="#Mem.write"><code>Mem.write</code></a>).</li><li><strong>Byte memory.</strong> A byte-addressable memory is <code>HwTy.mem aw 8</code>; <a href="#Mem.byteRead"><code>Mem.byteRead</code></a>, <a href="#Mem.byteWrite"><code>Mem.byteWrite</code></a> and the same three laws are its interface. A byte write with the enable high is <a href="#Mem.byteEnabled"><code>Mem.byteEnabled</code></a>; with it low, <a href="#Mem.byteDisabled"><code>Mem.byteDisabled</code></a> (the byte-enable law at byte granularity).</li><li><strong>Byte enables in a word.</strong> <a href="#Mem.byteMask"><code>Mem.byteMask</code></a> builds the <code>dw</code>-bit mask of <code>dw / 8</code> strobes (the same construction as <a href="#Bus.byteMask"><code>Bus.byteMask</code></a>, but here it does not depend on <code>Hdl.Bus</code>), and <a href="#Mem.merge"><code>Mem.merge</code></a> is the read-modify-write value. <a href="#Mem.writeBytes"><code>Mem.writeBytes</code></a> writes a word with a strobe. <code>byteMask_full32</code>/<code>byteMask_zero32</code> are the two closed cases at the common 32-bit width; the example checks every strobe and every byte lane of 8-, 16- and 32-bit words.</li><li><strong>One-cycle and two-cycle RAMs.</strong> <a href="#Mem.Req"><code>Mem.Req</code></a>/<a href="#Mem.Resp"><code>Mem.Resp</code></a>/<a href="#Mem.Ram"><code>Mem.Ram</code></a> are the request, response and state, and <a href="#Mem.ramC1"><code>Mem.ramC1</code></a>/<a href="#Mem.ramC2"><code>Mem.ramC2</code></a> answer in one or two cycles. The <a href="#W"><code>W</code></a> variants (<a href="#Mem.ramWC1"><code>Mem.ramWC1</code></a>/<a href="#Mem.ramWC2"><code>Mem.ramWC2</code></a>) take byte strobes. Both are plain <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a>s over bundles, so they simulate at values and synthesise like any other circuit; <code>ramC2</code> has the same state and timing as <a href="#Bus.ramC"><code>Bus.ramC</code></a>/<a href="#Bus.ramWC"><code>Bus.ramWC</code></a> (the one-cycle RAM takes <code>we</code> as its write enable; the two-cycle RAM gates the write with <code>valid</code>).</li></ul>
<p>The word and byte laws are proved; the byte-enable <em>mask</em> is a wiring function whose 32-bit closed cases are proved and whose strobe patterns are checked exhaustively in <code>examples/hdl-mem-laws.wiz</code> (test group <code>hdl</code>). The checks are marked as such: a law checked by evaluation is <em>tested</em>, not proved.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Netlist

<a id="module-Hdl.Netlist"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Netlist: the simulation theorem</h4>
<p>A <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> (<code>Hdl.Core</code>) has two simulations: the value simulation <a href="#Circuit.run"><code>Circuit.run</code></a> (the Mealy step at <a href="#HwTy.El"><code>HwTy.El</code></a> values) and the netlist simulation <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> (the synthesised netlist&#39;s nodes). They are different programs, so their agreement is a theorem, not a definition. This file proves it for the <em>Mealy core</em> subset:</p>
<ul><li>one clock (<code>Netlist.clocks = [ClockDomain.sys]</code>),</li><li>no memories (<code>Netlist.mems = []</code>),</li><li>no multi-clock design (<a href="#Multi"><code>Multi</code></a>/<code>Cdc</code>) and no primitive without a behavioural model,</li><li>the netlist&#39;s registers are exactly the state&#39;s leaves, in <a href="#HwTy.leaves"><code>HwTy.leaves</code></a> order.</li></ul>
<p>The proof is a cycle-indexed simulation relation, <a href="#Circuit.Simulates"><code>Circuit.Simulates</code></a>, with one state-step obligation (<code>stepOk</code>). <a href="#Circuit.Simulates.runFrom"><code>Circuit.Simulates.runFrom</code></a> is the induction and <a href="#Circuit.Simulates.simulate_eq_run"><code>Circuit.Simulates.simulate_eq_run</code></a> is the theorem:</p>
<pre><code>Netlist.simulate n (Hdl.map (HwTy.leaves i) xs) = Hdl.map (HwTy.leaves o) (Circuit.run c xs)</code></pre>
<p>for every finite input list <code>xs</code>. The obligations are <em>discharged</em>, not assumed, for a synthesised design: <code>examples/hdl-sim-theorem.wiz</code> proves them by <code>rfl</code> for a one-bit delay (<code>Circuit.netlist &quot;delay&quot;</code>), i.e. by kernel evaluation of the netlist&#39;s nodes.</p>
<p><a href="#Netlist.simFast"><code>Netlist.simFast</code></a> is the compiled fast simulator (<code>Hdl.Sim</code>); it computes the same function as <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> for a <a href="#Netlist.wellFormed"><code>Netlist.wellFormed</code></a> netlist (arguments to earlier nodes, registers/memories that exist, no primitive instances), and falls back to <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> otherwise. That agreement is checked by the executable differential tests (<code>examples/hdl-sim.wiz</code>, the <code>hdl</code> group); it is not proved here because <code>Hdl.Sim</code> uses <a href="#Array"><code>Array</code></a>, which the kernel does not reduce.</p>
<h5>Outside the theorem</h5>
<ul><li><strong>Multi-clock.</strong> A <a href="#Multi"><code>Multi</code></a> design, <a href="#ClockDomain.named"><code>ClockDomain.named</code></a> parts and <code>Cdc</code> cells have more than one <code>always</code> block; <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> is single-rate and <a href="#Netlist.domainRefusals"><code>Netlist.domainRefusals</code></a> refuses such a netlist (the event schedule, H10, is not implemented). Only the <code>sys</code>/one-domain case is related here.</li><li><strong>Memories.</strong> The theorem assumes <code>n.mems = []</code>. <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> also handles <a href="#NetMem"><code>NetMem</code></a> reads/writes (state <a href="#HTrie"><code>HTrie</code></a>s); proving their refinement needs the memory contents in the relation and is left to the memory interface&#39;s own laws.</li><li><strong>Resets.</strong> A synchronous reset is part of a step and may satisfy <code>stepOk</code> if the netlist&#39;s <a href="#NetReg.rst"><code>NetReg.rst</code></a> is what the step does; the theorem does not model reset <em>domains</em>, asynchronous assertion, or <code>Cdc.resetSync</code>/<code>Cdc.resetBridge</code>. Async reset crossings are outside.</li><li><strong>Uninterpreted primitives.</strong> <a href="#NetPrim.eval"><code>NetPrim.eval</code></a> is the primitive&#39;s <code>model</code>, or a default when <code>model = none</code>; a design whose primitive has no behavioural model is outside the theorem (and <a href="#Netlist.simFast"><code>Netlist.simFast</code></a> falls back). Vendor cells with a model are in the step relation only if <code>stepOk</code> is proved for them.</li><li><strong><code>simFast</code>.</strong> Covered by the executable differential tests and <a href="#Netlist.wellFormed"><code>Netlist.wellFormed</code></a>, not by this proof (see above).</li></ul>
</div>

<a id="Circuit.Simulates"></a>

structure · `Hdl/Netlist.wiz:173`

```text
{ω i : HwTy} → {ω o : HwTy} → Circuit i o → Netlist → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>The smallest simulation relation for the single-clock, memoryless Mealy core: the netlist&#39;s initial register leaves are the circuit&#39;s initial state leaves, and one netlist cycle implements one <a href="#Circuit.stepEl"><code>Circuit.stepEl</code></a>.</p>
</div>

**Constructors and fields**

- <a id="Circuit.Simulates.mk"></a>`mk` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → {c : Circuit i o} → {n : Netlist} → n.2.2.2.2.2.2.2.1 = [ClockDomain.sys] → n.2.2.2.2.2.2.1 = [] → Hdl.map NetReg Nat (fun r => r.2.2.1) n.2.2.1 = HwTy.leaves c.1 c.2.1 → ((s : HwTy.El c.1) → (x : HwTy.El i) → Netlist.StepOk i o c n s x) → Circuit.Simulates i o c n`
- <a id="Circuit.Simulates.oneClock"></a>`oneClock` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → {c : Circuit i o} → {n : Netlist} → Circuit.Simulates i o c n → n.2.2.2.2.2.2.2.1 = [ClockDomain.sys]` — the netlist has one clock domain (<a href="#ClockDomain.sys"><code>ClockDomain.sys</code></a>)
- <a id="Circuit.Simulates.memFree"></a>`memFree` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → {c : Circuit i o} → {n : Netlist} → Circuit.Simulates i o c n → n.2.2.2.2.2.2.1 = []` — the netlist has no memories
- <a id="Circuit.Simulates.initOk"></a>`initOk` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → {c : Circuit i o} → {n : Netlist} → Circuit.Simulates i o c n → Hdl.map NetReg Nat (fun r => r.2.2.1) n.2.2.1 = HwTy.leaves c.1 c.2.1` — the initial registers are the initial state&#39;s leaves
- <a id="Circuit.Simulates.stepOk"></a>`stepOk` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → {c : Circuit i o} → {n : Netlist} → Circuit.Simulates i o c n → (s : HwTy.El c.1) → (x : HwTy.El i) → Netlist.StepOk i o c n s x` — one netlist cycle is one circuit step


<a id="Circuit.Simulates.runFrom"></a>
### `Circuit.Simulates.runFrom`

def · `Hdl/Netlist.wiz:185`

```text
{ω i : HwTy} → {ω o : HwTy} → {c : Circuit i o} → {n : Netlist} → Circuit.Simulates i o c n → (s : HwTy.El c.1) → (xs : List (HwTy.El i)) → Netlist.runFrom n (HwTy.leaves c.1 s) (Hdl.map (HwTy.El i) (List Nat) (HwTy.leaves i) xs) = Hdl.map (HwTy.El o) (List Nat) (HwTy.leaves o) (Circuit.runFrom i o c s xs)
```
<div class="doc"><p>The state-step lemma: if the relation holds, <a href="#Netlist.runFrom"><code>Netlist.runFrom</code></a> from any state whose leaves are the state&#39;s leaves is the value run.</p>
</div>


<a id="Circuit.Simulates.simulate_eq_run"></a>
### `Circuit.Simulates.simulate_eq_run`

def · `Hdl/Netlist.wiz:208`

```text
{ω i : HwTy} → {ω o : HwTy} → {c : Circuit i o} → {n : Netlist} → Circuit.Simulates i o c n → (xs : List (HwTy.El i)) → Netlist.simulate n (Hdl.map (HwTy.El i) (List Nat) (HwTy.leaves i) xs) = Hdl.map (HwTy.El o) (List Nat) (HwTy.leaves o) (Circuit.run i o c xs)
```
<div class="doc"><p><strong>The simulation theorem.</strong> For a circuit and a netlist in the Mealy-core subset (<a href="#Circuit.Simulates"><code>Circuit.Simulates</code></a>), the netlist simulation of any finite input trace is the value simulation, cycle for cycle.</p>

## Hdl.Optic

<a id="module-Hdl.Optic"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Optic</h4>
<p>Optics for HDL bundles (<code>import Hdl.Optic</code>). Design: wiz-notes/cohesion-hardware.md, 2.2; the optics are lib/Optic.wiz&#39;s.</p>
<p>A bundle <code>structure Tx (r : HwTy → Type) where …</code> derives <a href="#Lens"><code>Lens</code></a> as any structure does (<code>deriving Bundle, Lens</code>): <code>Tx.lineL : Lens (Tx r) (r Bit)</code>, one lens at every representation, so a step can update one field (<code>Lens.over Tx.leftL dec s</code>) and a proof that the other fields are unchanged is <a href="#Lens.Indep"><code>Lens.Indep</code></a> (derived, by <code>rfl</code>) or <code>rfl</code> itself. This module adds what is specific to hardware:</p>
<ul><li><code>Hdl.zoom l g</code>: run a sub-step <code>g</code> on the part of the state that <code>l</code> selects; with <a href="#Hdl.zoom_frame"><code>Hdl.zoom_frame</code></a>, every place independent of <code>l</code> is unchanged (the frame rule).</li><li><code>Bundle.lens b</code>: a bundle&#39;s packed code and its structure, as a lens at values, and <code>Bundle.Lawful b</code> (derived bundles: by <code>rfl</code>).</li><li><a href="#HwTy.fstL"><code>HwTy.fstL</code></a>/<code>sndL</code>: the components of a product code at values.</li></ul>
</div>

## Hdl.Pipe

<a id="module-Hdl.Pipe"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Pipe: pipelines as arrows</h4>
<p>An <em>arrow</em> language for pipelines over <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> (<code>import Hdl.Pipe</code>). A <code>Pipe i o</code> is a <code>Circuit i o</code> with its latency in cycles; the combinators compose circuits and add the latencies. It is additive: <code>Hdl.Core</code>&#39;s <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a>/<a href="#Multi"><code>Multi</code></a> semantics are unchanged, and a <a href="#Pipe"><code>Pipe</code></a> lowers to a <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> (<a href="#Pipe.circuit"><code>Pipe.circuit</code></a>), so <a href="#Circuit.run"><code>Circuit.run</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.netlist"><code>Circuit.netlist</code></a>, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a>, <code>Hdl.Sim</code>&#39;s <code>simFast</code>, <a href="#Verilog.emit"><code>Verilog.emit</code></a> and all the <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> lemmas apply unchanged.</p>
<p>Why an arrow and not a monad? A state monad over <a href="#NetM"><code>NetM</code></a>/<a href="#MultiM"><code>MultiM</code></a> is the right shape for <em>building</em> a netlist (those monads accumulate nodes), but as the user-facing pipeline language it hides the state type and forces every sequential composition to agree on an existential state, which Wiz&#39;s dependent <a href="#HwTy"><code>HwTy</code></a> codes make unnecessarily awkward; an indexed monad would need a type-level latency <em>and</em> a type-level state to recover the <a href="#Circuit.seq"><code>Circuit.seq</code></a>/<a href="#Circuit.par"><code>Circuit.par</code></a> lemmas that already exist. The arrow keeps the two type parameters (<code>i</code>, <code>o</code>) first-class, so <code>i</code> and <code>o</code> are ordinary <a href="#HwTy"><code>HwTy</code></a> codes, quantities (<code>ω</code>) stay where Core puts them, and every combinator is a thin wrapper around a <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> combinator whose laws are already proved (<a href="#Circuit.run_seq"><code>Circuit.run_seq</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.run_par"><code>Circuit.run_par</code></a>, <a href="#Circuit.run_delay"><code>Circuit.run_delay</code></a>, <code>Circuit.run_loop</code>). Explicit <a href="#Circuit.seq"><code>Circuit.seq</code></a>/<code>par</code>/<code>loop</code> calls are the third option: they work, but a pipeline reads as a chain of stages, and the latency bookkeeping and the valid/ready discipline have nowhere to live.</p>
<h5>The data path (<a href="#Pipe"><code>Pipe</code></a>)</h5>
<pre><code>def alu3 : Pipe (HwTy.bits 8) (HwTy.bits 8) :=
  Pipe.pipe &quot;alu3&quot; (
    Pipe.stage &quot;add&quot; 0 (fun x =&gt; x + 3) |&gt;&gt;
    Pipe.stage &quot;mul&quot; 0 (fun x =&gt; x * 5) |&gt;&gt;
    Pipe.stage &quot;sub&quot; 0 (fun x =&gt; x - 2))</code></pre>
<p><code>Pipe.stage name init f</code> is combinational <code>f</code> followed by one register (<code>latency 1</code>). <code>|&gt;&gt;</code> is <a href="#Pipe.seq"><code>Pipe.seq</code></a>, <code>***</code> is <a href="#Pipe.par"><code>Pipe.par</code></a>, <code>&amp;&gt;</code> is <a href="#Pipe.fanout"><code>Pipe.fanout</code></a> (the arrow&#39;s <code>&amp;&amp;&amp;</code>; the HDL already spells bitwise-and <code>&amp;&amp;&amp;</code>, so this module keeps a distinct symbol). <a href="#Pipe.loop"><code>Pipe.loop</code></a> (or <a href="#Pipe.feedback"><code>Pipe.feedback</code></a>) closes a feedback path through a register. <a href="#Pipe.pipe"><code>Pipe.pipe</code></a> names a whole chain. The symbols are declared at precedence 20 (<code>|&gt;&gt;</code>) and 30 (<code>***</code>, <code>&amp;&gt;</code>), below function application and above the signal operators, and print back as written.</p>
<h5>The handshake path (<a href="#Flow"><code>Flow</code></a>)</h5>
<p>A <code>Flow i o</code> is an elastic (valid/ready) pipeline stage with a separate <em>ready</em> function, so sequential composition connects the backward ready wire without a combinational loop:</p>
<ul><li>input channel: <code>in_data</code>, <code>in_valid</code>, <code>out_ready</code>;</li><li>output channel: <code>out_data</code>, <code>out_valid</code>, <code>in_ready</code>;</li><li><code>ready st out_ready</code> is the stage&#39;s <code>in_ready</code> (it does not depend on <code>in_data</code> or <code>in_valid</code>, the AXI rule);</li><li><code>step st in_data in_valid out_ready</code> gives the next state, <code>out_data</code> and <code>out_valid</code>.</li></ul>
<p><a href="#Flow.seq"><code>Flow.seq</code></a> computes the downstream stage&#39;s ready first and feeds it to the upstream stage; <a href="#Flow.reg"><code>Flow.reg</code></a> is the one-register elastic buffer (<code>in_ready = ¬full ∨ out_ready</code>), and <code>Flow.stage name init f</code> is a combinational function followed by that register. <a href="#Flow.toCircuit"><code>Flow.toCircuit</code></a> lowers a flow to an ordinary <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> over <a href="#FlowIn"><code>FlowIn</code></a>/<a href="#FlowOut"><code>FlowOut</code></a>, so the same simulation, netlist, Verilog and temporal-logic tools apply.</p>
<p>Not here yet: multi-clock flows (a <a href="#Flow"><code>Flow</code></a> is one <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a>, one clock), memories in a flow, true fork/join of independent ready/valid channels (the data-path <a href="#Pipe"><code>Pipe</code></a> has <code>fanout</code>/<code>join</code>), and a proved throughput theorem (the latency is tracked; the one-item-per-cycle and no-loss properties are tested, and the <a href="#TL"><code>TL</code></a> protocol lemmas are the next step).</p>
</div>

<a id="Pipe"></a>
### `Pipe`

structure · `Hdl/Pipe.wiz:71`

```text
HwTy → HwTy → Type 1
```
<div class="doc"><p>A pipeline: a circuit and its latency in cycles. The circuit is the semantics; the latency is bookkeeping (it is what <a href="#Pipe.seq"><code>Pipe.seq</code></a> adds and <a href="#Pipe.par"><code>Pipe.par</code></a> takes the maximum of).</p>
</div>

- <a id="Pipe.latency"></a>`latency` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → Pipe i o → Nat`

<a id="Flow"></a>
### `Flow`

structure · `Hdl/Pipe.wiz:273`

```text
HwTy → HwTy → Type 1
```
<div class="doc"><p>An elastic pipeline stage: state, a <em>ready</em> function (which does not depend on the input data or valid, the AXI rule) and a step function. The step sees the downstream <code>ready</code> and returns the upstream <code>valid</code>; <a href="#Flow.seq"><code>Flow.seq</code></a> connects the two without a combinational loop.</p>
</div>

**Constructors and fields**

- <a id="Flow.mk"></a>`mk` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (st : HwTy) → HwTy.El st → ({r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r st → r HwTy.bit → r HwTy.bit) → ({r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r st → r i → r HwTy.bit → r HwTy.bit → r (HwTy.prod st (HwTy.prod o HwTy.bit))) → Flow i o`
- <a id="Flow.st"></a>`st` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → Flow i o → HwTy`
- <a id="Flow.init"></a>`init` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (self : Flow i o) → HwTy.El self.1`
- <a id="Flow.ready"></a>`ready` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (self : Flow i o) → {r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r self.1 → r HwTy.bit → r HwTy.bit` — The stage&#39;s <code>in_ready</code>, from the state and the downstream&#39;s <code>ready</code>.
- <a id="Flow.step"></a>`step` : `{i : HwTy} → {o : HwTy} → (self : Flow i o) → {r : HwTy → Type} → [inst✝ : Hw r] → r self.1 → r i → r HwTy.bit → r HwTy.bit → r (HwTy.prod self.1 (HwTy.prod o HwTy.bit))` — One cycle: state, input data, input valid, downstream ready → next state, output data, output valid.

## Hdl.Prim

<a id="module-Hdl.Prim"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Prim</h4>
<p>Primitive instances: vendor cells (an FPGA&#39;s I/O buffers, SERDES, PLLs, …) as black boxes in the HDL (<a href="#Hw.prim"><code>Hw.prim</code></a>; <a href="#Prim"><code>Prim</code></a> and the netlist&#39;s <a href="#NetOp.inst"><code>NetOp.inst</code></a> are in Hdl.Core, this module has the rest). A <code>Prim i o</code> declares one: its Verilog module name, parameters, a port name per leaf of its input and output codes, and optionally a behavioural model at values. At the wire instance a primitive is one netlist node (<a href="#NetOp.inst"><code>NetOp.inst</code></a>) that <a href="#Verilog.emit"><code>Verilog.emit</code></a> prints as a module instance; at values it is its model.</p>
<p>def oddr : Prim (HwTy.prod HwTy.clock (HwTy.prod Bit Bit)) Bit := Prim.decl &quot;ODDR&quot; (.cons (&quot;DDR_CLK_EDGE&quot;, PrimParam.str &quot;SAME_EDGE&quot;) .nil) (.cons &quot;C&quot; (.cons &quot;D1&quot; (.cons &quot;D2&quot; .nil))) (.cons &quot;Q&quot; .nil) .none … Hw.prim oddr (Hw.pair Hw.clock (Hw.pair a b)) … -- ODDR #(.DDR_CLK_EDGE(&quot;SAME_EDGE&quot;)) u7 (.C(clk), .D1(n3), .D2(n5), .Q(n7));</p>
<p>Kinds (Core&#39;s <a href="#PortKind"><code>PortKind</code></a>): a leaf under <a href="#HwTy.clock"><code>HwTy.clock</code></a> is a clock net, under <code>HwTy.pad n</code> a package pin an I/O buffer drives or reads, under <code>HwTy.inout n</code> a bidirectional one. They connect primitives only: a clock goes from a circuit&#39;s clock input, the implicit clock (<a href="#Hw.clock"><code>Hw.clock</code></a>) or a primitive&#39;s clock output to a primitive&#39;s clock input; a pad goes from a circuit&#39;s input to a buffer&#39;s input, or from a buffer&#39;s output to the circuit&#39;s output (a bidirectional one becomes an <code>inout</code> port). Anything else is an error of the netlist (<a href="#Netlist.errors"><code>Netlist.errors</code></a>, printed by <a href="#Verilog.emit"><code>Verilog.emit</code></a>).</p>
<p>Sharing: an instance is never hash-consed (two buffers with the same inputs are two buffers), so a primitive&#39;s result that is used more than once must be one value: bind it with <code>let</code> (auto-share), never pass the <code>Hw.prim …</code> expression to a function that reads it several times (each read would build another instance).</p>
<p>Simulation: a primitive without a model is 0 at values and in <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a>; <a href="#Netlist.unmodelled"><code>Netlist.unmodelled</code></a> names such instances and the checked runners (<a href="#Circuit.runModelled"><code>Circuit.runModelled</code></a>, <a href="#Netlist.simulateModelled"><code>Netlist.simulateModelled</code></a>) refuse to run a circuit with one. A netlist with more than one clock domain is refused too (<a href="#Netlist.domainRefusals"><code>Netlist.domainRefusals</code></a>): its registers tick at two rates, which the single-tick simulation cannot express.</p>
<p>Clocks: a circuit&#39;s registers stay on its one implicit clock. <a href="#Clocking"><code>Clocking</code></a> describes a generated top-level wrapper whose clock primitive (a PLL) turns the board&#39;s clock into that implicit clock (through a BUFG) and into the circuit&#39;s clock inputs. Data that crosses from one clock domain into another goes through a synchroniser (<a href="#Prim.declSync"><code>Prim.declSync</code></a>; <a href="#Cdc.sync2"><code>Cdc.sync2</code></a> in <code>Hdl.Cdc</code>), and <a href="#Netlist.domainErrors"><code>Netlist.domainErrors</code></a> rejects every other crossing.</p>
<p>A parameter&#39;s value, printed as Verilog.</p>
</div>

<a id="Prim.declSync"></a>
### `Prim.declSync`

def · `Hdl/Prim.wiz:75`

```text
{ω i : HwTy} → {ω o : HwTy} → String → List (String × PrimParam) → List String → List String → Option (HwTy.El i → HwTy.El o) → Prim i o
```
<div class="doc"><p>A synchroniser declaration (<a href="#Prim.decl"><code>Prim.decl</code></a> marked as a crossing): its output is in its clock input&#39;s domain and its data may come from one other domain (<a href="#Netlist.domainErrors"><code>Netlist.domainErrors</code></a>). Its clock input must be the only clock leaf of <code>i</code>; <a href="#Cdc.sync2"><code>Cdc.sync2</code></a> (<code>Hdl.Cdc</code>) is the two-flop one. A model, if any, is not a two-flop delay (a model is one total function from inputs to outputs), so the checked runners still refuse a multi-domain netlist (<a href="#Netlist.domainRefusals"><code>Netlist.domainRefusals</code></a>).</p>
</div>

## Hdl.ProtocolLaw

<a id="module-Hdl.ProtocolLaw"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.ProtocolLaw</h4>
<p>The obligations of the protocol bridges in <code>Hdl.Apb</code> and <code>Hdl.Wishbone</code>, plus the <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> (byte-strobe) form of the bus stability laws. Like <code>Hdl.BusLaw</code>, these are predicates over value traces and Boolean one-step forms; <code>examples/hdl-protocols.wiz</code> evaluates the Boolean forms on generated traces at the same time as it compares the value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a>. They are <strong>tested, not proved</strong> on those inputs.</p>
<p>The laws, by obligation:</p>
<ul><li><strong>Data/address stability.</strong> A bus source holds <code>valid</code>, <code>we</code>, <code>addr</code>, <code>wdata</code> and <code>wstrb</code> while stalled (<a href="#Bus.Law.ReqWStable"><code>Bus.Law.ReqWStable</code></a> and its components). An APB master holds <code>PSEL</code>, <code>PADDR</code>, <code>PWDATA</code>, <code>PWRITE</code> and <code>PSTRB</code> while <code>PSEL</code> is high and <code>PREADY</code> is low (<code>Apb.Law.Stable</code>); <code>PENABLE</code> may rise at the SETUP/ACCESS boundary, so it is not part of that law. A Wishbone master holds <code>CYC</code>, <code>STB</code>, <code>WE</code>, <code>ADR</code>, <code>DAT_W</code> and <code>SEL</code> until <code>ACK</code>/<code>ERR</code>/<code>RTY</code> (<code>Wishbone.Law.Stable</code>).</li><li><strong>Response ordering.</strong> The bridges are single outstanding, so an answer at cycle <code>t</code> belongs to the request offered in that same cycle (the source holds it while stalled): <code>Apb.Law.ResponseMatches</code> and <code>Wishbone.Law.ResponseMatches</code> require the request fields and the slave&#39;s protocol fields to agree, and <code>Apb.Law.AccessResp</code> / <code>Wishbone.Law.AckReq</code> require a response only in an access/request phase. Since there is only one transfer in flight, answers cannot overtake each other.</li><li><strong>No lost strobes.</strong> Every write&#39;s byte strobes arrive unchanged on the other side: <code>Apb.Law.StrobeToApb</code> (bus -&gt; APB <code>PSTRB</code>), <code>Apb.Law.StrobeToBus</code> (APB <code>PSTRB</code> -&gt; bus <code>wstrb</code>), and the two Wishbone <code>SEL</code> forms.</li></ul>
<p>The APB bundle&#39;s <code>PSTRB</code> is zero on reads (APB4), so the strobe laws are conditioned on a write. <code>Apb.Law.ApbResp</code> and <code>Wishbone.Law.WbResp</code> (reverse direction) require <code>PREADY</code>/<code>ACK</code> only in an ACCESS/request phase, and <code>Apb.Law.PreadyOnlyAccess</code> / <code>Wishbone.Law.AckOnlyReq</code> are the same obligation.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Sim

<a id="module-Hdl.Sim"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Sim</h4>
<p>Fast netlist simulation for compiled programs (<code>import Hdl.Sim</code>).</p>
<p><a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> (lib/Hdl/Core.wiz) is the netlist&#39;s semantics, written for the kernel: node values in a persistent random-access list, O(nodes · log nodes) per cycle with an allocation per node. <a href="#Circuit.run"><code>Circuit.run</code></a> (the value simulation) is the circuit&#39;s semantics; compiled, it runs the step function at <a href="#HwTy.El"><code>HwTy.El</code></a> every cycle, with every meta-level computation in it (table trees, constants computed from the configuration, bundle codes, dictionary calls) done again in each cycle.</p>
<p><a href="#Netlist.simFast"><code>Netlist.simFast</code></a> computes exactly what <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> computes (the same operations on the same numbers, node by node), but builds the netlist&#39;s program once and runs it over native arrays updated in place (<a href="#Array"><code>Array</code></a>, lib/Std.wiz): a value per node, the register values, the input values. The netlist is the step function with all the meta-level work done once (synthesis is partial evaluation), and hash-consed, so this is also the fast way to run a circuit&#39;s value simulation: <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a>, <a href="#Design.simFast"><code>Design.simFast</code></a> (on leaves, as <a href="#Circuit.runLeaves"><code>Circuit.runLeaves</code></a> and <a href="#Design.runLeaves"><code>Design.runLeaves</code></a>). Compiled code only: <a href="#Array"><code>Array</code></a> has no definition the kernel or <code>#eval</code> could run.</p>
<p>Agreement: <code>Netlist.simFast n xs = Netlist.simulate n xs</code> for every netlist whose node arguments refer to earlier nodes, whose registers, memory reads and writes and ports refer to nodes and memories that exist, and which has no vendor primitive (every netlist <a href="#Circuit.netlist"><code>Circuit.netlist</code></a> builds from code without primitives; <a href="#Netlist.wellFormed"><code>Netlist.wellFormed</code></a> checks it), and <a href="#Netlist.simFast"><code>Netlist.simFast</code></a> falls back to <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> on any other (primitive instances included). The <code>hdl</code> test group checks both against <a href="#Circuit.run"><code>Circuit.run</code></a> cycle for cycle.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Spi

<a id="module-Hdl.Spi"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Spi</h4>
<p>A mode 0 SPI master (<code>import Hdl.Spi</code>): CPOL = 0 (the clock idles low) and CPHA = 0 (data is sampled on the rising edge and shifted out on the falling edge), an 8-bit transfer, and a configurable divider. One bit takes <code>2 * div</code> clock cycles: <code>div</code> with the clock low, then <code>div</code> with it high. <code>div</code> is a meta-level <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> (1 … 65536) and only reaches the netlist as the constant the half-period counter is compared with.</p>
<p>The signals are a bundle (<a href="#Spi.Out"><code>Spi.Out</code></a>), so the module&#39;s ports are <code>sclk</code>, <code>mosi</code>, <code>cs</code>, <code>busy</code>, <code>done</code> and <code>data</code>; the input is <a href="#Spi.In"><code>Spi.In</code></a> (<code>miso</code>, <code>start</code>, <code>data</code>). The outputs are registers, so the pins cannot glitch. <code>start</code> with <code>data</code> is taken when idle and ignored otherwise; <code>busy</code> is high from that cycle until the last falling edge; <code>done</code> is high for one cycle then (in the same cycle <code>data</code> is the byte shifted in from <code>miso</code>). The first bit (the most significant one) is on <code>mosi</code> in the cycle <code>cs</code> goes low, so a mode 0 slave sees it before the first rising edge.</p>
<p>Clock domains: the master is a synchronous circuit in one clock domain. For a MISO pin from another domain, put a two-flip-flop synchroniser in front of it (as <a href="#Uart.rxC"><code>Uart.rxC</code></a> does for its line); the SPI clock is generated in this domain, so <code>sclk</code> is not a clock here: no logic is clocked by it, which keeps the whole master on one clock.</p>
<p><code>Spi.loopC div</code> is the loopback example: <code>mosi</code> is wired to <code>miso</code>, so the byte received is the byte sent. That checks the shift order and the sampling edges without a slave.</p>
<p>The generic master (<code>Spi.masterCW w cw ncs div</code>) keeps the same protocol but makes three things meta-level parameters: the transfer width <code>w</code> (8 bits below), the width <code>cw</code> of the half-period counter (16 bits below) and the number of chip selects <code>ncs</code> (one below). Its input <a href="#Spi.InW"><code>Spi.InW</code></a> adds <code>sel</code>, the index of the selected slave, and its output <a href="#Spi.OutW.cs"><code>Spi.OutW.cs</code></a> is <code>ncs</code> lines, all high when idle and bit <code>sel</code> low while a transfer runs. The original <code>masterC</code>/<code>loopC</code> API names are unchanged. One behaviour changed intentionally: <a href="#Spi.shiftIn8"><code>Spi.shiftIn8</code></a> used to shift a received bit in at the top (<code>cat b (slice 1 7 x)</code>), which reverses the byte; it now shifts like the generic path (<code>x &lt;&lt; 1 | b</code>), so the first (most significant) bit sampled ends at the top. The old 8-bit loopback did not show the reversal because its test bytes 0xA5 and 0x3C are palindromes; <code>examples/rune-spi.wiz</code> now uses 0x81 and 0x01, which distinguishes them.</p>
<p>What remains (see <code>wiz-notes/rune.md</code>): modes 1 … 3 (CPOL/CPHA), a <code>cs</code> decoder with active-high selects or per-slave timing, and a <code>miso</code> input synchroniser as a separate part.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Temporal

<a id="module-Hdl.Temporal"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Temporal</h4>
<p>Temporal logic for circuits (<code>import Hdl.Temporal</code>): properties over unbounded time, in the style of LTL, SVA and TLA+, with the proof rules to establish them. Design notes: docs/libraries.md (&quot;H14 T&quot;) and wiz-notes/hdl-temporal.md.</p>
<ul><li>A trace is a function <code>Nat → A</code> (not a ν-stream: equality at ν is stuck, while equality of functions is pointwise). A formula <code>TL A</code> is a proposition about a trace at a time: <code>φ σ t</code> says that <code>φ</code> holds of <code>σ</code> at cycle <code>t</code> (the anchored semantics). <code>□φ</code> at <code>t</code> is &quot;φ at <code>k + t</code> for every k&quot;, <code>◇φ</code> &quot;for some k&quot;.</li><li>Two layers: cycle-level operators (○, <code>##n</code>, bounded <code>◇</code>/<code>□</code>, <code>|-&gt;</code>, <code>|=&gt;</code>) for properties of one circuit, and actions with stuttering (<a href="#TL.stut"><code>TL.stut</code></a>, TLA&#39;s <code>□[N]_v</code>) for refinement of an abstract specification.</li><li>The semantic object is a Mealy machine <code>S → I → S × O</code>; <code>Circuit.stepEl c</code> is one. <a href="#Mealy.stateAt"><code>Mealy.stateAt</code></a>/<a href="#Mealy.outAt"><code>Mealy.outAt</code></a> run it along an input trace, and <a href="#Mealy.runFrom_take"><code>Mealy.runFrom_take</code></a> says that the finite simulation <a href="#Circuit.runFrom"><code>Circuit.runFrom</code></a> is a prefix.</li></ul>
<p>Proof rules: invariance (<a href="#Mealy.invariant"><code>Mealy.invariant</code></a>), induction on time (<a href="#TL.always_ind"><code>TL.always_ind</code></a>), bounded checks by evaluation (<a href="#Mealy.checkFrom_spec"><code>Mealy.checkFrom_spec</code></a>, <a href="#Mealy.findFrom_spec"><code>Mealy.findFrom_spec</code></a>), a transient phase followed by an invariant (<a href="#TL.splitAt"><code>TL.splitAt</code></a>), refinement by a representation map (<a href="#Mealy.simulates"><code>Mealy.simulates</code></a>) and with stuttering (<a href="#Mealy.refinesStut"><code>Mealy.refinesStut</code></a>), liveness from fairness (<a href="#TL.fairStep"><code>TL.fairStep</code></a>) and from a ranking function (<a href="#TL.rank"><code>TL.rank</code></a>).</p>
</div>

