<a id="TL.fairStepAux"></a>
### `TL.fairStepAux`

def · `Hdl/Temporal.wiz:175`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : TL A) → (q : TL A) → (h : Nat → Bool) → (σ : Trace A) → (v : Nat) → ((u : Nat) → p σ u → h u = Bool.false → p σ (Nat.succ u)) → ((u : Nat) → p σ u → h u = Bool.true → q σ u) → p σ v → (j : Nat) → p σ (Nat.add j v) ∨ (◇ q) σ v
```
<div class="doc"><p>Liveness from fairness: while <code>p</code> holds and the fair event <code>h</code> (a Boolean, e.g. a consumer&#39;s <code>ready</code>) is absent, <code>p</code> persists; when <code>h</code> comes, <code>q</code> happens; <code>h</code> comes infinitely often. Then <code>p</code> leads to <code>q</code>. (TLA&#39;s WF1 for a deterministic step.)</p>
</div>


<a id="TL.fairStep"></a>
### `TL.fairStep`

def · `Hdl/Temporal.wiz:188`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : TL A) → (q : TL A) → (h : Nat → Bool) → (σ : Trace A) → ((u : Nat) → p σ u → h u = Bool.false → p σ (Nat.succ u)) → ((u : Nat) → p σ u → h u = Bool.true → q σ u) → ((u : Nat) → (∃ k, h (Nat.add k u) = Bool.true)) → (v : Nat) → p σ v → (◇ q) σ v
```
<div class="doc"><p>Liveness from fairness: while <code>p</code> holds and the fair event <code>h</code> is absent, <code>p</code> persists; when <code>h</code> comes, <code>q</code> happens; <code>h</code> comes infinitely often. Then <code>p</code> leads to <code>q</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="TL.rank"></a>
### `TL.rank`

def · `Hdl/Temporal.wiz:201`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : TL A) → (q : TL A) → (rk : Nat → Nat) → (σ : Trace A) → ((u : Nat) → (r : Nat) → p σ u → rk u = Nat.succ r → q σ u ∨ p σ (Nat.succ u) ∧ rk (Nat.succ u) = r) → ((u : Nat) → p σ u → rk u = 0 → q σ u) → (r : Nat) → (v : Nat) → p σ v → rk v = r → TL.within A (Nat.succ r) q σ v
```
<div class="doc"><p>Liveness from a ranking function: while <code>p</code> holds and <code>q</code> has not happened, the rank goes down by one per cycle; at rank 0 <code>q</code> happens. Then <code>q</code> happens within <code>r + 1</code> cycles of a time where <code>p</code> holds with rank <code>r</code> (a bound as well as liveness).</p>
</div>


<a id="Mealy.refinesStut"></a>
### `Mealy.refinesStut`

def · `Hdl/Temporal.wiz:220`

```text
{S : Type} → {I : Type} → {O : Type} → {T : Type} → (m : Mealy S I O) → (s0 : S) → (xs : Trace I) → (f : S → T) → (next : T → T → Prop) → (inv : S → Prop) → ((t : Nat) → inv (Mealy.stateAt S I O m s0 xs t)) → ((s : S) → (x : I) → inv s → next (f s) (f (m s x).1) ∨ f s = f (m s x).1) → (t : Nat) → TL.stut T next (Trace.map S T f (Mealy.stateAt S I O m s0 xs)) t
```
<div class="doc"><p>Refinement with stuttering (TLA): if, on the states the run can reach (<code>inv</code>), every step is a step of the abstract relation <code>next</code> or leaves the abstraction <code>f</code> unchanged, the abstract trace satisfies <code>□[next]_f</code>.</p>
</div>

<a id="Mealy.settles"></a>

def · `Hdl/Temporal.wiz:286`

```text
{S : Type} → {I : Type} → {O : Type} → (m : Mealy S I O) → (s0 : S) → (xs : Trace I) → (F : Nat) → (c : S) → Mealy.stateAt S I O m s0 xs F = c → ((j : Nat) → (m c (xs (Nat.add j F))).1 = c) → (j : Nat) → Mealy.stateAt S I O m s0 xs (Nat.add j F) = c
```
<div class="doc"><p>A transient phase, then rest: if the run is in state <code>c</code> at cycle <code>F</code> and <code>c</code> is fixed under the inputs from then on, it stays in <code>c</code>; a property checked for the first <code>F</code> cycles and true of <code>c</code> (with those inputs) then holds at every cycle.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Uart

<a id="module-Hdl.Uart"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Uart</h4>
<p>A reusable 8N1 UART (<code>import Hdl.Uart</code>): a baud generator, a transmitter and a receiver with a configurable number of clock cycles per bit, and a loopback circuit that wires the transmitter&#39;s line into the receiver. It is the UART of the iCEstick project (<code>wiz-icestick-uart/src/Icestick/Uart.wiz</code>) with the board-specific parts removed, so that other designs can instantiate it: every part is a <a href="#Circuit"><code>Circuit</code></a> over bundles, polymorphic in the representation like the rest of the HDL, so the same definition simulates at values and synthesises to a netlist.</p>
<p>Layout of one frame, least significant data bit first, line idle high:</p>
<pre><code>idle  start  d0  d1  d2  d3  d4  d5  d6  d7  stop  idle
 1      0     …                                  1     1</code></pre>
<p><code>n</code> is the number of clock cycles per bit, a meta-level <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> (1 … 2^w): it only ends up in the netlist as the constants the counters are compared with. <code>w</code> is the width of the clocks-per-bit counter: the default <a href="#Uart.cntW"><code>Uart.cntW</code></a> is 16 bits, so <code>n</code> ranges over 1 … 65536; <a href="#Uart.cntW7"><code>Uart.cntW7</code></a> (7 bits, 1 … 128) is the iCEstick&#39;s counter and <a href="#Uart.cntW10"><code>Uart.cntW10</code></a> (10 bits, 1 … 1024) is the Arty&#39;s and the OLED designs&#39;. The <code>…w</code> circuits take the width as their first argument; the named configurations (<a href="#Uart.tx7C"><code>Uart.tx7C</code></a>, <a href="#Uart.tx10C"><code>Uart.tx10C</code></a>, …) fix it. The counter is the only width that changes: the phase, the bit periods left and the shift registers are the same in every configuration. <code>n = 104</code> turns the iCEstick&#39;s 12 MHz clock into 115384.6 baud (0.16 % above 115200); the Arty&#39;s 100 MHz clock with <code>n = 866</code> gives 115473.4 baud (0.006 % above 115200).</p>
<p>Clock domains: the receiver&#39;s input goes through two flip-flops inside the receiver (the <code>Rx</code> state&#39;s <code>ff1</code>/<code>ff2</code>), so a pin in another clock domain is synchronised before any logic looks at it. The transmitter&#39;s line is a register of its own, so the pin cannot glitch. Both parts are ordinary synchronous circuits with a plain state, so <a href="#Circuit.withReset"><code>Circuit.withReset</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.withResetEnable"><code>Circuit.withResetEnable</code></a> put a reset (and an enable) around an instantiation without changing it; the example simulates the receiver under a reset with a line whose phase is not aligned to the local clock. Use <code>n ≥ 5</code>: the two synchroniser flip-flops delay the start edge by two cycles, and the receiver samples at the middle of each bit (see <a href="#Uart.rxStep"><code>Uart.rxStep</code></a>).</p>
<p>The width families:</p>
<ul><li><code>Uart.baudCw w n</code> / <code>Uart.txCw w n</code> / <code>Uart.rxCw w n</code> / <code>Uart.loopbackCw w n</code>: the generic circuits, for a counter of <code>w</code> bits and <code>1 ≤ n ≤ 2^w</code>;</li><li><code>Uart.baudC n</code>, <code>Uart.txC n</code>, <code>Uart.rxC n</code>, <code>Uart.loopbackC n</code>: the 16-bit defaults (<a href="#Uart.cntW"><code>Uart.cntW</code></a>, 1 … 65536), the original rune configuration;</li><li><code>Uart.baud7C n</code>, <code>Uart.tx7C n</code>, <code>Uart.rx7C n</code>, <code>Uart.loop7C n</code>: the iCEstick&#39;s 7-bit counter (<a href="#Uart.cntW7"><code>Uart.cntW7</code></a>, 1 … 128);</li><li><code>Uart.baud10C n</code>, <code>Uart.tx10C n</code>, <code>Uart.rx10C n</code>, <code>Uart.loop10C n</code>: the 10-bit counter (<a href="#Uart.cntW10"><code>Uart.cntW10</code></a>, 1 … 1024) of the Arty and the OLED designs.</li></ul>
<p>The parts:</p>
<ul><li><code>Uart.baudCw w n</code>: a free-running baud generator (input <code>ce</code>, output <code>tick</code>) whose tick is high one cycle in every <code>n</code>;</li><li><code>Uart.txCw w n</code>: input <code>start</code>/<code>data</code>, output <code>line</code>/<code>busy</code>, 8N1, <code>start</code> taken when idle;</li><li><code>Uart.rxCw w n</code>: input <code>line</code>, output <code>valid</code>/<code>data</code>/<code>busy</code>; <code>valid</code> is high for one cycle at the sample of a stop bit that is high, with the byte in <code>data</code>;</li><li><code>Uart.loopbackCw w n</code>: <code>txCw</code> and <code>rxCw</code> with the line wired from the transmitter to the receiver (the loopback example), input <code>start</code>/<code>data</code>, output <code>busy</code>/<code>valid</code>/<code>data</code>.</li></ul>
</div>

## Hdl.Wishbone

<a id="module-Hdl.Wishbone"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Wishbone</h4>
<p>A thin classic Wishbone B4 bridge for <code>Hdl.Bus</code> (<code>import Hdl.Wishbone</code>), in both directions over the existing <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> valid/ready model. It is deliberately the single-transfer, non-pipelined Wishbone subset (<code>CYC</code>/<code>STB</code>/<code>ACK</code>/<code>ERR</code>), not a new protocol:</p>
<ul><li><code>Wishbone.busToWbC aw dw</code>: a <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> master on a Wishbone slave. It maps <code>valid</code> to <code>CYC</code> and <code>STB</code>, <code>we</code> to <code>WE</code>, <code>addr</code> to <code>ADR</code>, <code>wdata</code> to <code>DAT_W</code> and <code>wstrb</code> to <code>SEL</code>; <code>ACK</code> (or <code>ERR</code>) is the bus answer, <code>DAT_R</code> is <code>rdata</code>, and <code>RTY</code> is folded into <code>err</code> because the wiz bus has no retry. <code>STALL</code> is passed through in the bundle but is not needed for this classic subset: a stalled slave simply does not assert <code>ACK</code>, so the bus waits and the master holds the request.</li><li><code>Wishbone.wbToBusC aw dw</code>: a Wishbone master on a <a href="#Bus.ReqW"><code>Bus.ReqW</code></a> slave. <code>CYC &amp;&amp; STB</code> is the bus <code>valid</code>, <code>WE</code>/<code>ADR</code>/<code>DAT_W</code>/<code>SEL</code> the payload, and the bus answer drives <code>ACK</code>/<code>ERR</code>/<code>DAT_R</code>; <code>RTY</code> and <code>STALL</code> are low because the bus has no retry/stall phase.</li></ul>
<p>Both directions are combinational, pass every byte strobe through unchanged, and never answer without a request. <code>examples/hdl-protocols.wiz</code> (test group <code>bus-protocol</code>) checks the stability, response-order and strobe laws on generated traces and compares the value simulation, <a href="#Netlist.simulate"><code>Netlist.simulate</code></a> and <a href="#Circuit.simFast"><code>Circuit.simFast</code></a>.</p>
<p>Wishbone B4 is the OpenCores specification; <code>SEL</code> here is the per-byte select, as in Wishbone B4, so it lines up with <a href="#Bus.ReqW.wstrb"><code>Bus.ReqW.wstrb</code></a>.</p>
</div>

<a id="Wishbone.busToWbComb"></a>
### `Wishbone.busToWbComb`

def · `Hdl/Wishbone.wiz:86`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p>One cycle of the bus-to-Wishbone bridge: the request is forwarded combinationally and a Wishbone <code>ACK</code>/<code>ERR</code>/<code>RTY</code> answers the bus. <code>RTY</code> becomes <code>err</code> (no retry on the bus), and every response is gated by <code>valid</code>, so a stray slave response cannot answer a request that is not there.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Xdc

<a id="module-Hdl.Xdc"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Xdc</h4>
<p>Pin constraints for Xilinx 7-series FPGAs (the XDC of Vivado, read also by nextpnr-xilinx): a package pin and an I/O standard for every port, by the port&#39;s name in the netlist, and the clock&#39;s period.</p>
<p>A board is its clock and a table of resources (<a href="#XPin"><code>XPin</code></a>: a port name and its package pins, bit 0 first). A design&#39;s ports are looked up in the table by name, so the table can list the whole board and a design uses part of it (<a href="#Xdc.check"><code>Xdc.check</code></a> reports ports without a resource and widths that differ; unused resources are fine).</p>
<p>Port names as <a href="#Verilog.emit"><code>Verilog.emit</code></a> declares them: a one-bit port is <code>[0:0]</code> there, and nextpnr names its pin by the bare port name (<code>uart_tx</code>), wider ones by bit (<code>led[0]</code>), as <a href="#Pcf.emit"><code>Pcf.emit</code></a> does for nextpnr-ice40.</p>
</div>

## Hdl.Xilinx7

<a id="module-Hdl.Xilinx7"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hdl.Xilinx7</h4>
<p>Xilinx 7-series primitives (UG953, &quot;7 Series FPGA Libraries Guide&quot;), as <a href="#Prim"><code>Prim</code></a> declarations and typed functions over them. These are the cells a DDR3 PHY on an Artix-7 needs (I/O buffers, ODDR, OSERDESE2, ISERDESE2, IDELAYE2, IDELAYCTRL, BUFG) and PLLE2_BASE as a <a href="#Clocking"><code>Clocking</code></a>. openXC7 (yosys synth_xilinx, nextpnr-xilinx, Project X-Ray) supports all of them.</p>
<p>Port lists name only the ports the functions use; the others are left unconnected, which takes their defaults (UG953). Models: the buffers have one (a buffer is its input; a bidirectional one reads back what it drives, and 0 while it is in tristate); IDELAYCTRL is ready at once. The clocked cells (ODDR, the SERDES, IDELAYE2) have none: their outputs change faster than the circuit&#39;s clock, so the checked simulations refuse a circuit with one (<a href="#Circuit.runModelled"><code>Circuit.runModelled</code></a>).</p>
</div>

## HeapBorrow

<a id="module-HeapBorrow"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>HeapBorrow</h4>
<p>Feral&#39;s borrows on heap cells: the bridge between the functional model of owned data (lib/Region.wiz, lib/Optic.wiz: a <code>&amp;mut A</code> is a value handed in and handed back) and the model heap of separation logic (lib/HProp.wiz, lib/Hoare.wiz: an owned cell is <code>l ↦ v</code>). docs/resources.md tells the whole story; wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md has the design.</p>
<p>A Feral function taking <code>&amp;mut A</code> lowers to a function of the value, <code>A → Result (B × A)</code> (the borrow&#39;s final value comes back with the result; <a href="#Uniq.borrow"><code>Uniq.borrow</code></a> wraps exactly this shape around a call). On a heap whose cell <code>l</code> holds the lender, the same call is: read <code>l</code>, run the function, write the final value back — a fault if the function panicked. That is <a href="#Prog.borrowMut"><code>Prog.borrowMut</code></a>. Its specification comes from the function&#39;s <em>functional</em> specification (decision CS9: safe Feral code is verified in the functional model, as in Aeneas): if <code>f a</code> succeeds with <code>(b, a&#39;)</code> satisfying <a href="#Q"><code>Q</code></a>, then</p>
<p>{l ↦ a} Prog.borrowMut l f {b. ∃a&#39;. \[Q b a&#39;] ⋆ l ↦ a&#39;}</p>
<p>and the frame rule (<a href="#Triple.frame"><code>Triple.frame</code></a>, or <code>xapp</code>&#39;s inferred frame) adds every other cell: the cells a Feral function is not given are the ones it can&#39;t touch. <a href="#Result.Holds"><code>Result.Holds</code></a> (total correctness: an <code>err</code> satisfies nothing) is the reading that lines up with <a href="#Triple"><code>Triple</code></a>, where a fault (<a href="#Prog.fail"><code>Prog.fail</code></a>) satisfies nothing either.</p>
</div>

<a id="Prog.handBack_spec"></a>
### `Prog.handBack_spec`

def · `HeapBorrow.wiz:40`

```text
{V : Type} → {B : Type} → (l : Nat) → (a : V) → (Q : B → V → Prop) → (r : Result (B × V)) → Result.Holds (B × V) (fun p => Q p.1 p.2) r → ⦃l ↦ a⦄ Prog.handBack V B l r ⦃b, ∃ʰ v, ⌜Q b v⌝ ⋆ l ↦ v⦄
```
<div class="doc"><p>After the value-level function ran: the cell holds the final value (or the program faulted, and nothing holds).</p>
</div>


<a id="Prog.handBack_ok"></a>

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p>a call whose result is known (<code>f a</code> computes to it, or a lemma says so): the cell holds the final value</p>

<a id="Prog.handBack2_ok"></a>
### `Prog.handBack2_ok`

def · `HeapBorrow.wiz:79`

```text
{V : Type} → {B : Type} → (p : Nat) → (q : Nat) → (a : V) → (b : V) → (c : B) → (v : V) → (w : V) → ⦃p ↦ a ⋆ q ↦ b⦄ Prog.handBack2 V B p q (Result.ok (B × V × V) (c, v, w)) ⦃r, ⌜r = c⌝ ⋆ p ↦ v ⋆ q ↦ w⦄
```

## Hoare

<a id="module-Hoare"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Hoare: Hoare triples over a model heap, with the frame rule</h4>
<p>Stage 24c. Programs that read, write, allocate and free cells of a model heap, a weakest precondition for them, Hoare triples defined from it, and the structural rules (the frame rule among them), all proved by the kernel. The heap predicates come from <a href="#HProp"><code>HProp</code></a> (lib/HProp.wiz); the tactics that make the proofs short are in <code>HoareTactics</code>, and the worked examples (swap, in-place list reversal, …) in <code>HoareExamples</code>.</p>
<p>The presentation is SLF&#39;s (Software Foundations vol. 6, chapters WPsem and WPgen): a weakest precondition <code>wp c Q</code> for each command, triples defined from it, and the structural rules derived. It is shaped as an instance of <em>Dijkstra monads for all</em> (Maillard et al., ICFP 2019), so that other effects can be added later without changing the logic:</p>
<ul><li>the computational monad is <code>Prog V</code>, a tree of heap operations (a free monad: an action tree in the sense of SteelCore, Swamy et al., ICFP 2020, with the continuations in the nodes);</li><li>the specification monad is <code>W V A := (A → HProp V) → HProp V</code>, predicate transformers over heap predicates, ordered by <code>w₁ ≤ w₂ := ∀ Q, w₂ Q ⊢ w₁ Q</code> (DM4All §3.1: <code>w₂</code> is the weaker specification), restricted to monotone ones (<a href="#W.Mono"><code>W.Mono</code></a>), and for separation logic also to frame-preserving ones (<a href="#W.Frame"><code>W.Frame</code></a>, SteelCore §3.2&#39;s <code>preserves_frame</code> at the level of transformers);</li><li>the effect observation <code>wp : Prog V A → W V A</code> is a monad morphism (DM4All Definition 1): <a href="#wp.ret"><code>wp.ret</code></a> holds by computation, <a href="#wp.bind_l"><code>wp.bind_l</code></a>/<a href="#wp.bind_r"><code>wp.bind_r</code></a> by induction;</li><li>a triple is <code>{P} c {Q} := P ⊢ wp c Q</code> (<a href="#Triple"><code>Triple</code></a>), i.e. <code>c</code> lies in the Dijkstra monad at the specification <code>fun Q&#39; =&gt; P ⋆ …</code> (we don&#39;t build <code>D A w</code> as a type: the triples are all the examples need).</li></ul>
<p>The structural rules (<a href="#Triple.conseq"><code>Triple.conseq</code></a>, <a href="#Triple.frame"><code>Triple.frame</code></a>, <a href="#Triple.bind"><code>Triple.bind</code></a>, …) follow from the monad laws, monotonicity and frame preservation. <a href="#adequacy"><code>adequacy</code></a> ties <a href="#wp"><code>wp</code></a> to an interpreter <a href="#Prog.run"><code>Prog.run</code></a> on concrete heaps: if <code>wp c Q</code> holds of the heap, running <code>c</code> doesn&#39;t fault and ends in a heap satisfying <a href="#Q"><code>Q</code></a>. Nothing here is an axiom.</p>
<p>Programs are total, so a loop takes fuel; running out is a fault (<a href="#Prog.fail"><code>Prog.fail</code></a>), and <code>wp Prog.fail Q = \[False]</code>, so a proved triple also proves there was enough fuel.</p>
<pre><code>-- read a cell and write it back, incremented
def incr (l : Nat) : Prog Nat Unit := do
  v ← Prog.read l;
  Prog.write l (Nat.succ v)
-- its specification: {l ↦ v} incr l {l ↦ v + 1}
def incrSpec (l v : Nat) : Prop := Triple (l ↦ v) (incr l) (fun _ =&gt; l ↦ Nat.succ v)</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="Triple.run"></a>

def · `Hoare.wiz:532`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p>The triple form of <a href="#adequacy"><code>adequacy</code></a>: a proved triple, run from any heap satisfying its precondition (with anything else alongside, by the frame rule), doesn&#39;t fault and ends in its postcondition.</p>

## HoareExamples

<a id="module-HoareExamples"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>HoareExamples: verified programs over the model heap</h4>
<p>Stages 24c–24d. Small heap programs (<a href="#Prog"><code>Prog</code></a>, lib/Hoare.wiz) with their specifications, proved with the <code>x</code>-tactics of <code>HoareTactics</code>: swapping two cells, a counter, and loops over mutable lists (<a href="#MList"><code>MList</code></a>): in-place reversal, length, incrementing every element, freeing. Every specification is a <a href="#Triple"><code>Triple</code></a>, so <a href="#adequacy"><code>adequacy</code></a> applies to it: the program runs without a fault on any heap satisfying the precondition. <a href="#Prog.show"><code>Prog.show</code></a> runs a program on a concrete heap.</p>
<pre><code>def Prog.swap_spec (p q a b : Nat) :
    Triple ((p ↦ a) ⋆ (q ↦ b)) (Prog.swap p q) (fun _ =&gt; (p ↦ b) ⋆ (q ↦ a)) := by
  xgo
-- [1, 2] at 0 and 1, swapped: some ((), [some 2, some 1])
#eval Prog.show (Prog.swap 0 1) (Heap.ofList [1, 2] 0) 2 2</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="Prog.revLoop.spec"></a>
### `Prog.revLoop.spec`

def · `HoareExamples.wiz:65`

```text
(L : List Nat) → (f : Nat) → Nat.lt (List.length Nat L) f = Bool.true → (p : Nat) → (q : Nat) → (L₂ : List Nat) → ⦃MList L p ⋆ MList L₂ q⦄ Prog.revLoop f p q ⦃r, MList (List.revApp Nat L L₂) r⦄
```
<div class="doc"><p>The loop invariant of <a href="#Prog.revLoop"><code>Prog.revLoop</code></a>: with more fuel than cells, <code>MList L p ⋆ MList L₂ q</code> becomes <code>MList (revApp L L₂)</code>. Where the precondition is contradictory (<code>MList [] (p + 1)</code> is <code>\[p + 1 = 0]</code>), <code>xunfold</code> pulls the fact and that closes the goal; <code>xstep</code> names the next pointer <code>n</code> after the binder of <a href="#MList"><code>MList</code></a>&#39;s <code>∃</code>, and the fact it pulls <code>hp</code>.</p>

## HoareTactics

<a id="module-HoareTactics"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>HoareTactics: proof automation for separation logic</h4>
<p>Stage 24d, after SLF&#39;s <code>xsimpl</code>, <code>xpull</code> and the <code>x</code>-tactics of chapter WPgen. With these, a triple of <code>Hoare</code> is usually proved by naming the steps rather than writing the proof term:</p>
<ul><li><code>xsimpl</code> simplifies an entailment <code>L ⊢ R</code>: it flattens both sides, pulls pure facts and existentials on the left, instantiates existentials on the right, cancels matching atoms and unfolds representation predicates; <code>xpull</code> only does the left side;</li><li><code>xstep</code> takes one command of the program (read, write, allocate, free, return); <code>xval</code>, <code>xseq</code>, <code>xwp</code> the other small steps;</li><li><code>xapp t</code> uses a proved triple <code>t</code> for a call, framing the rest;</li><li><code>xchange e</code> rewrites an atom of the precondition by an entailment, <code>xunfold</code> unfolds the precondition&#39;s atoms;</li><li><code>xgo</code> runs <code>xstep</code> until it can&#39;t, then <code>xsimpl</code>.</li></ul>
<p>The design is <em>small reflection plus tactics</em>. The tactics (Wiz functions, see lib/Prelude.wiz) read the goal, decide what to do, and build proof terms out of a handful of lemmas proved once, here, about <strong>star lists</strong>: <code>starL [H₁, …, Hₙ]</code> is <code>H₁ ⋆ (… ⋆ Hₙ)</code>, definitionally. Rearranging a <code>⋆</code> chain is then a matter of list positions (<a href="#starL.pick"><code>starL.pick</code></a>, by induction on the position), and flattening an arbitrary tree of <code>⋆</code> and <a href="#emp"><code>emp</code></a> is one lemma about a reflected tree (<a href="#HTree.flat_eq"><code>HTree.flat_eq</code></a>). The kernel checks every step by computing the lists, so the tactics are not trusted.</p>
<pre><code>def Prog.incr (p : Nat) : Prog Nat Unit := .get p (fun n =&gt; .set p (Nat.succ n) (.ret ()))
def Prog.incr_spec (p n : Nat) : Triple (p ↦ n) (Prog.incr p) (fun _ =&gt; p ↦ Nat.succ n) := by
  xgo</code></pre>
<p>More in <code>HoareExamples</code>.</p>
</div>

<a id="XT.simp"></a>
### `XT.simp`

def · `HoareTactics.wiz:849`

```text
Nat → Bool → Nat → List Nat → List String → TacticM (List Nat × List String)
```
<div class="doc"><p>The loop of <code>xpull</code> and <code>xsimpl</code> (fuel, full?, goal, side goals, names): the goals left (the main one first) and the names left. A step reads the goal, and either replaces it by one new goal (with side goals: witnesses of existentials, pure side conditions) or stops. In order:</p>
<ol><li>flatten both sides into star lists (<a href="#xs.flat"><code>xs.flat</code></a>);</li><li>on the left, a pure fact becomes a hypothesis (<code>hp</code>; if it is contradictory, it closes the goal), an existential a variable (named after its binder; names can be given: <code>xpull as n, h</code>); <code>xpull</code> stops here;</li><li>a goal <code>… ⊢ wp c Q</code> is left for the program tactics;</li><li>an existential on the right gets a metavariable as its witness;</li><li>a right atom equal (argument by argument, up to conversion, solving metavariables) to a left atom is cancelled;</li><li>a pure fact on the right becomes a side goal (closed if <code>rfl</code>, an assumption or <code>fun e =&gt; e</code> proves it);</li><li><code>emp ⊢ emp</code> and <code>… ⊢ htop</code> are closed; <code>… ⊢ ∀x. J x</code> and <code>… ⊢ H₁ −∗ H₂</code> are introduced;</li><li>an atom whose head is a definition that computes (a representation predicate applied to a constructor, <code>MList (x :: L) p</code>) is unfolded once (<a href="#TacticM.unfold"><code>TacticM.unfold</code></a>, which folds the recursive occurrences back), right atoms first.</li></ol>
</div>

## IO

<a id="module-IO"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>IO</h4>
<p>Effects through a linear world token (stage 9), and the C foreign function interface.</p>
<p>An <code>IO A</code> is a function that takes the <a href="#World"><code>World</code></a> exactly once and gives it back with an <code>A</code>. Because the world is a quantity-1 argument, the kernel&#39;s usage checking forces the actions into a single order: there is no way to run an action twice or to drop the world. At runtime the token is a scalar and an <a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a> action is an ordinary function.</p>
<p>Main definitions:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a>, <a href="#IO.pure"><code>IO.pure</code></a>, <a href="#IO.bind"><code>IO.bind</code></a> (and the <code>Monad IO</code> instance, for <code>do</code> blocks);</li><li>output and input: <a href="#IO.println"><code>IO.println</code></a>, <a href="#IO.print"><code>IO.print</code></a>, <a href="#IO.readFile"><code>IO.readFile</code></a>, <a href="#IO.args"><code>IO.args</code></a>;</li><li>machine numbers: <a href="#UInt64"><code>UInt64</code></a> and <a href="#Float64"><code>Float64</code></a>, with numerals and <code>+ - * / %</code>;</li><li>byte buffers: <a href="#Bytes"><code>Bytes</code></a>, with UTF-8 (<a href="#Bytes.ofUtf8"><code>Bytes.ofUtf8</code></a>, <a href="#Bytes.toUtf8"><code>Bytes.toUtf8</code></a>) and Latin-1 (<a href="#Bytes.ofLatin1"><code>Bytes.ofLatin1</code></a>, <a href="#Bytes.toLatin1"><code>Bytes.toLatin1</code></a>) encodings;</li><li><a href="#Callback"><code>Callback</code></a>, for Wiz functions that C code keeps.</li></ul>
<p>Foreign functions run only in compiled code (<code>wiz run</code>), not under <code>#eval</code>.</p>
<pre><code>import IO

def main : IO Unit := do
  args ← IO.args;
  IO.println (String.append &quot;hello, &quot; (Nat.toString (List.length args)))</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="IO.bind"></a>
### `IO.bind`

def · `IO.wiz:46`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (1 x : IO A) → (1 f : A → IO B) → IO B
```
<div class="doc"><p>Run <code>x</code>, then run <code>f</code> on its result.</p>
<p>The action and the continuation are used once, so both are quantity-1 parameters (L6): the continuation may capture linear resources, and an action that consumes one may be sequenced. (Unrestricted arguments are fine too.) <code>do</code> blocks in <a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a> come down to this.</p>
</div>

<a id="IO1"></a>
### `IO1`

def · `IO.wiz:67`

```text
Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>IO1 A</code>: an action whose result is used once (cohesion M6 part 2), for actions that hand back a linear value (a token, a handle) in direct style instead of to a continuation. <code>IO A</code>&#39;s result is unrestricted, so a linear value can&#39;t come out of it; this one&#39;s can. Additive: <a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a> is unchanged, and unifying the two is a later design question (wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md §10). In <code>do1</code>, <code>x ⇐ e;</code> binds the result of an <a href="#IO1"><code>IO1</code></a> action at quantity 1 and goes on in <a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a> (<code>(x, y) ⇐ e;</code> takes a pair apart).</p>
</div>

## Infoview

<a id="module-Infoview"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Infoview</h4>
<p>The infoview&#39;s model and its two renderers (stages 11m–n): goals as the language server sends them (<code>wiz/interactiveGoals</code>, <code>wiz/interactiveInfo</code>), laid out for a terminal (SGR colours, wrapped to a width, one selected subterm in reverse video) and for a browser (HTML with <code>data-ref</code> attributes). Pure functions; the terminal program (infoview/Tui.wiz) and the browser (web/) do the input and output. Tagged text itself (its JSON, flattening, navigation, HTML) is lib/Tagged.wiz, shared with the documentation&#39;s pages (11s).</p>
<ul><li>Reading the server&#39;s answers: <a href="#Goals.ofJson"><code>Goals.ofJson</code></a>, <a href="#TacView.ofJson"><code>TacView.ofJson</code></a>, <a href="#Items.ofJson"><code>Items.ofJson</code></a>.</li><li>The terminal: <a href="#View.ofInfo"><code>View.ofInfo</code></a> lays everything out as lines of <a href="#Piece"><code>Piece</code></a>s; <a href="#Infoview.ansiLines"><code>Infoview.ansiLines</code></a> (or <a href="#Infoview.plainLines"><code>Infoview.plainLines</code></a>) turns them into text, and <a href="#View.navigate"><code>View.navigate</code></a> / <a href="#Infoview.tagAt"><code>Infoview.tagAt</code></a> move and find the selection.</li><li>The browser: <a href="#Infoview.htmlInfo"><code>Infoview.htmlInfo</code></a>, numbered the same way, so selections agree.</li><li>The protocol around it: <a href="#Rpc.frame"><code>Rpc.frame</code></a>, <a href="#Rpc.unframe"><code>Rpc.unframe</code></a>, <a href="#Rpc.request"><code>Rpc.request</code></a>, and <a href="#Key.decode"><code>Key.decode</code></a> for the terminal&#39;s keys and mouse.</li></ul>
<pre><code>def show (width : Nat) (answer : Json) : List String :=
  Infoview.plainLines (View.lines (View.ofGoals width (Goals.ofJson answer)))
-- one goal `n : Nat ⊢ n = n` shows as [&quot;n : Nat&quot;, &quot;⊢ n = n&quot;]</code></pre>
</div>

## Int

<a id="module-Int"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Int</h4>
<p>Integers (<code>import Int</code>): a natural number or the negative of a successor, as in Lean.</p>
<p>Arithmetic is defined by cases on the natively computed <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> operations, so the kernel computes it on numerals and compiled code runs <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a>&#39;s natives on the magnitudes. <code>#eval</code> prints <code>-5</code>, not <code>.negSucc 4</code> (<code>builtin int</code>).</p>
<p>Main definitions: the type <a href="#Int"><code>Int</code></a>, its arithmetic (<a href="#Int.add"><code>Int.add</code></a>, <a href="#Int.mul"><code>Int.mul</code></a>, <a href="#Int.div"><code>Int.div</code></a>, <a href="#Int.mod"><code>Int.mod</code></a>, …) with the usual operator instances, comparisons (<a href="#Int.lt"><code>Int.lt</code></a>, <a href="#Int.le"><code>Int.le</code></a>, <a href="#Int.beq"><code>Int.beq</code></a>) and a few lemmas (<a href="#Int.neg_neg"><code>Int.neg_neg</code></a>, <a href="#Int.add_zero"><code>Int.add_zero</code></a>, …).</p>
<pre><code>import Int

def ex : (-3 : Int) * 4 + 2 = -10 := rfl   -- the kernel computes it
#eval Int.div (-7) 2   -- -3</code></pre>
</div>

## IntOrder

<a id="module-IntOrder"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>IntOrder</h4>
<p>The order of the integers (<code>import IntOrder</code>): <code>a ≤ b</code> when <code>b - a</code> is not negative, <code>a &lt; b</code> when <code>a + 1 ≤ b</code>; the absolute value and the triangle inequality.</p>
<p><code>a ≤ b</code> and <code>a &lt; b</code> (lib/Order.wiz) are <code>Int.Le a b</code> and <code>Int.Lt a b</code>. Most facts are proved by moving to <a href="#Int.NonNeg"><code>Int.NonNeg</code></a> of a difference and rewriting the difference with <code>int_ring!</code> (<a href="#Int.NonNeg.congr"><code>Int.NonNeg.congr</code></a>), so new ones are easy to add in the same way.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#Int.NonNeg"><code>Int.NonNeg</code></a>, <a href="#Int.Le"><code>Int.Le</code></a>, <a href="#Int.Lt"><code>Int.Lt</code></a>; reflexivity, transitivity, antisymmetry and totality (<a href="#Int.le_total"><code>Int.le_total</code></a>, <a href="#Int.le_or_lt"><code>Int.le_or_lt</code></a>); monotonicity of <code>+</code> and of multiplication by a non-negative or positive number, and cancellation of a positive factor; <a href="#Int.abs"><code>Int.abs</code></a> facts: <a href="#Int.le_abs"><code>Int.le_abs</code></a>, <a href="#Int.abs_le"><code>Int.abs_le</code></a>, the triangle inequality <a href="#Int.abs_add"><code>Int.abs_add</code></a> and <a href="#Int.abs_sub_le"><code>Int.abs_sub_le</code></a>.</p>
<pre><code>import IntOrder

def ex (a b : Int) (h : a ≤ b) : a + 1 ≤ b + 1 := Int.add_le_add_right 1 a b h
def tri (a b : Int) : Int.abs (a + b) ≤ Int.abs a + Int.abs b := Int.abs_add a b</code></pre>
</div>

## IntRing

<a id="module-IntRing"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>IntRing</h4>
<p>Equations of commutative rings at <a href="#Int"><code>Int</code></a>, decided by reflection, and the ring laws of the integers (<code>import IntRing</code>):</p>
<pre><code>import IntRing

def ex (a b : Int) : (a - b) * (a + b) = a * a - b * b :=
  int_ring! (a - b) * (a + b) = a * a - b * b
def comm (a b : Int) : a * b = b * a := Int.mul_comm a b</code></pre>
<p><code>int_ring! lhs = rhs</code> reads both sides as <a href="#IntExpr"><code>IntExpr</code></a>s (<code>+</code>, <code>*</code>, binary and unary <code>-</code>, parentheses, ascriptions and numerals; every other subterm is an atom, compared by its syntax) and normalises them to polynomials with integer coefficients (<a href="#IntPoly"><code>IntPoly</code></a>).</p>
<p>Its soundness needs the ring laws of <a href="#Int"><code>Int</code></a>, which are proved through the pair representation: <code>Int.ofPair a b</code> is <code>a - b</code> for natural numbers <code>a</code>, <code>b</code>; every integer is one (<a href="#Int.pair"><code>Int.pair</code></a>), the operations act on pairs as on formal differences (<a href="#Int.ofPair_add"><code>Int.ofPair_add</code></a>, <a href="#Int.ofPair_mul"><code>Int.ofPair_mul</code></a>, …), and equal differences are equal integers (<a href="#Int.ofPair_eq"><code>Int.ofPair_eq</code></a>). So an identity of integers becomes one of naturals, which <code>nat_ring!</code> proves. <code>int_pair_ring!</code> does this by reflection; it is the slower bootstrap that proves the lemmas behind <code>int_ring!</code>.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <code>int_ring!</code>; the laws <a href="#Int.add_comm"><code>Int.add_comm</code></a>, <a href="#Int.add_assoc"><code>Int.add_assoc</code></a>, <a href="#Int.mul_comm"><code>Int.mul_comm</code></a>, <a href="#Int.mul_assoc"><code>Int.mul_assoc</code></a>, <a href="#Int.mul_add"><code>Int.mul_add</code></a>, <a href="#Int.add_mul"><code>Int.add_mul</code></a>, <a href="#Int.add_neg"><code>Int.add_neg</code></a>, <a href="#Int.sub_self"><code>Int.sub_self</code></a>, <a href="#Int.neg_mul"><code>Int.neg_mul</code></a>, …; <a href="#Int.beq_eq"><code>Int.beq_eq</code></a>; the pair representation <a href="#Int.ofPair"><code>Int.ofPair</code></a>. The order is in lib/IntOrder.wiz.</p>
</div>

## Intern

<a id="module-Intern"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Intern</h4>
<p>Interned strings (<code>import Intern</code>): an <a href="#InternTable"><code>InternTable</code></a> gives each distinct string a small id, a <a href="#U32"><code>U32</code></a>, so that strings compare and hash as words (equal ids, equal strings, within one table). Ids are stable: a string keeps its id as more are interned, and ids are handed out in order, 0, 1, 2, … A table is a functional value, updated in place when it is unique (as <a href="#StrMap"><code>StrMap</code></a>); keep one per program or per analysis, and key <a href="#U64Map"><code>U64Map</code></a>s (lib/WordMap.wiz) or index <a href="#U32Array"><code>U32Array</code></a>s by the ids.</p>
<p>The model. A table is the list of its strings, by id, all distinct (<code>mk (strs : List String)</code>): <code>intern</code> gives a string&#39;s index, appending it if it is new. The module keeps the strings distinct (the constructor is private). The kernel computes with the definitions, and <code>#eval</code>/<code>#run</code> run them.</p>
<p>Compiled code runs natives instead (<code>runtime/</code>, <code>wiz_itab_*</code>): the strings by id (each <a href="#String"><code>String</code></a> value kept as it is, so <code>lookup</code> copies nothing) and a hash index from a string to its id, so <code>intern</code> and <code>find</code> take time proportional to the string&#39;s length, and <code>lookup</code> constant time.</p>
<p>Trust. The natives are trusted to agree with the definitions (<code>#print axioms</code> lists them, marked <code>native</code>, 22f). They abort when memory runs out or a table would hold 2^32 - 1 strings (the model&#39;s ids wrap around there). The tests (group <code>natives</code>) run the same programs under the interpreter and compiled, C and LLVM.</p>
<p>the index of the first string equal to <code>s</code></p>
</div>

## Json

<a id="module-Json"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Json</h4>
<p>JSON (RFC 8259) in Wiz: values (<a href="#Json"><code>Json</code></a>), a parser (<a href="#Json.parse"><code>Json.parse</code></a>) and a printer (<a href="#Json.render"><code>Json.render</code></a>). The infoview clients use it to speak the language server&#39;s protocol.</p>
<p>Strings are code points throughout: <code>\uXXXX</code> escapes (with surrogate pairs) are decoded on input, and the printer either keeps non-ASCII characters as they are (they become UTF-8 at the C boundary) or escapes them (<a href="#Json.renderAscii"><code>Json.renderAscii</code></a>). Integers are kept exactly; other numbers keep their text (<a href="#Json.dec"><code>Json.dec</code></a>).</p>
<ul><li>Building: <a href="#Json.mkObj"><code>Json.mkObj</code></a>, <a href="#Json.mkArr"><code>Json.mkArr</code></a>, <a href="#Json.mkStr"><code>Json.mkStr</code></a>, <a href="#Json.ofNat"><code>Json.ofNat</code></a>, <a href="#Json.mkBool"><code>Json.mkBool</code></a>, <a href="#Json.mkNull"><code>Json.mkNull</code></a>.</li><li>Taking apart: <a href="#Json.get"><code>Json.get</code></a>, <a href="#Json.getPath"><code>Json.getPath</code></a>, <a href="#Json.asString"><code>Json.asString</code></a>, <a href="#Json.asNat"><code>Json.asNat</code></a>, <a href="#Json.asList"><code>Json.asList</code></a>, and the defaulting <a href="#Json.getStr"><code>Json.getStr</code></a>, <a href="#Json.getNat"><code>Json.getNat</code></a>, <a href="#Json.getList"><code>Json.getList</code></a>.</li></ul>
<p>Everything is pure, so <code>#eval</code> runs it:</p>
<pre><code>#eval Json.render (Json.mkObj [(&quot;id&quot;, Json.ofNat 1), (&quot;ok&quot;, Json.mkBool .true)])
-- {&quot;id&quot;:1,&quot;ok&quot;:true}
#eval match Json.parse &quot;{\&quot;a\&quot;: [1, 2]}&quot; with
  | .ok j =&gt; Json.render j
  | .error e =&gt; e
-- {&quot;a&quot;:[1,2]}</code></pre>
</div>

```text
Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A JSON value. Arrays and objects hold values, so <a href="#Json"><code>Json</code></a>, <a href="#Jsons"><code>Jsons</code></a> (the elements of an array) and <a href="#JFields"><code>JFields</code></a> (the fields of an object) are mutual: Wiz has no nested inductive types. <code>int neg n</code> is the integer <code>n</code>, negative when <code>neg</code>; <code>dec text</code> is any other number, as its text.</p>
</div>

## ListLemmas

<a id="module-ListLemmas"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>List lemmas</h4>
<p>Lemmas about the list functions of <code>lib/Text.wiz</code> (<code>import ListLemmas</code>): how <code>map</code>, <code>filter</code>, <code>any</code>, <code>all</code>, <code>append</code>, <code>reverse</code> and <code>length</code> interact, and membership.</p>
<p>Membership is the proposition <a href="#List.Mem"><code>List.Mem</code></a> (<code>x ∈ l</code>, and <code>∀ x ∈ l, P x</code> with the binder notation), not a Boolean test: <a href="#List.any"><code>List.any</code></a>/<a href="#List.all"><code>List.all</code></a> are the Boolean versions, and <a href="#List.any_eq_true"><code>List.any_eq_true</code></a>/<a href="#List.all_eq_true"><code>List.all_eq_true</code></a> are the bridge between them.</p>
<p>The lemmas are ordinary definitions, proved by structural recursion (no axiom and no <code>sorry</code>; the trust ledger is unchanged). There is no <code>simp</code> tactic in Wiz, so there is no <code>[simp]</code> attribute to mark them with: they are stated left to right, the way <code>rw</code> uses them (<code>rw h; rfl</code>). The <code>_cons_true</code>/<code>_cons_false</code> lemmas are the equations <code>filter</code>, <code>any</code> and <code>all</code> need for a case split on their predicate.</p>
<pre><code>import ListLemmas

def mapMap (f g : Nat → Nat) (l : List Nat) :
    List.map f (List.map g l) = List.map (fun x =&gt; f (g x)) l :=
  List.map_map f g l

def allThree : (3 ∈ [1, 2, 3]) := Or.inr (Or.inr (Or.inl (refl 3)))</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="List.mem_cons_iff"></a>
### `List.mem_cons_iff`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:66`

```text
{A : Type} → (x : A) → (y : A) → (xs : List A) → (x ∈ List.cons A y xs ↔ x = y ∨ x ∈ xs)
```

<div class="doc"><p><code>x</code> is in <code>y :: xs</code> exactly when it is <code>y</code> or in <code>xs</code>.</p>

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:70`

</div>

<a id="List.map_cons"></a>

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:91`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (x : A) → (xs : List A) → List.map A B f (List.cons A x xs) = List.cons B (f x) (List.map A B f xs)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>map f (x :: xs) = f x :: map f xs</code>.</p>

<a id="List.map_map"></a>

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:98`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → {C : Type} → (g : B → C) → (f : A → B) → (l : List A) → List.map B C g (List.map A B f l) = List.map A C (fun x => g (f x)) l
```

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:117`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p><code>++</code> is associative.</p>
</div>

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:122`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → List.append A l [] = l
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>l ++ [] = l</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.nil_append"></a>
### `List.nil_append`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:126`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → List.append A [] l = l
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>[] ++ l = l</code>, by computation.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.length_append_eq"></a>
### `List.length_append_eq`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:129`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → (m : List A) → List.length A (List.append A l m) = Nat.add (List.length A l) (List.length A m)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>length (l ++ m) = length l + length m</code>. (<code>lib/WordArray.wiz</code> has the same fact as <a href="#List.length_append"><code>List.length_append</code></a>; this name lets both modules be imported.)</p>
</div>


<a id="List.revApp_append"></a>
### `List.revApp_append`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:138`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → (m : List A) → (acc : List A) → List.revApp A (List.append A l m) acc = List.revApp A m (List.revApp A l acc)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>revApp</code> is <code>reverse</code> with an accumulator: <code>revApp l m</code> appends the reverse of <code>l</code> to <code>m</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.length_revApp"></a>
### `List.length_revApp`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:144`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → (acc : List A) → List.length A (List.revApp A l acc) = Nat.add (List.length A l) (List.length A acc)
```
<div class="doc"><p>The length of <code>revApp l acc</code> is <code>length l + length acc</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.length_reverse"></a>
### `List.length_reverse`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:151`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → List.length A (List.reverse A l) = List.length A l
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>reverse</code> keeps the length.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.map_revApp"></a>
### `List.map_revApp`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:156`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (l : List A) → (acc : List A) → List.map A B f (List.revApp A l acc) = List.revApp B (List.map A B f l) (List.map A B f acc)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>map</code> commutes with <code>revApp</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.map_reverse"></a>
### `List.map_reverse`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:161`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (l : List A) → List.map A B f (List.reverse A l) = List.reverse B (List.map A B f l)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>map</code> commutes with <code>reverse</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.revApp_eq_append"></a>
### `List.revApp_eq_append`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:166`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → (acc : List A) → List.revApp A l acc = List.append A (List.reverse A l) acc
```

<a id="List.reverse_cons"></a>
### `List.reverse_cons`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:176`

```text
{A : Type} → (x : A) → (xs : List A) → List.reverse A (List.cons A x xs) = List.append A (List.reverse A xs) [x]
```

<a id="List.reverse_append"></a>
### `List.reverse_append`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:180`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p><code>reverse</code> turns <code>++</code> around: <code>reverse (l ++ m) = reverse m ++ reverse l</code>.</p>

<a id="List.reverse_reverse"></a>
### `List.reverse_reverse`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:187`

```text
{A : Type} → (l : List A) → List.reverse A (List.reverse A l) = l
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>reverse</code> is an involution.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.mem_map_of_mem"></a>
### `List.mem_map_of_mem`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:202`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (x : A) → (l : List A) → x ∈ l → f x ∈ List.map A B f l
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>x ∈ l</code> gives <code>f x ∈ map f l</code>.</p>

<a id="List.ex_mem_cons"></a>
### `List.ex_mem_cons`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:210`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (y : A) → (ys : List A) → (z : B) → (∃ w, w ∈ ys ∧ f w = z) → (∃ w, w ∈ List.cons A y ys ∧ f w = z)
```
<div class="doc"><p>Carry an existential membership proof past a <code>cons</code> (a helper for <code>mem_of_mem_map</code>).</p>
</div>


<a id="List.mem_of_mem_map"></a>
### `List.mem_of_mem_map`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:217`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (z : B) → (l : List A) → z ∈ List.map A B f l → (∃ y, y ∈ l ∧ f y = z)
```
<div class="doc"><p>An element of a mapped list is the image of an element of the list.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.mem_map"></a>
### `List.mem_map`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:226`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (z : B) → (l : List A) → (z ∈ List.map A B f l ↔ (∃ x, x ∈ l ∧ f x = z))
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>z ∈ map f l</code> exactly when <code>z = f x</code> for some <code>x ∈ l</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.filter_cons_true"></a>
### `List.filter_cons_true`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:236`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : A → Bool) → (x : A) → (xs : List A) → p x = Bool.true → List.filter A p (List.cons A x xs) = List.cons A x (List.filter A p xs)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>filter p (x :: xs) = x :: filter p xs</code> when <code>p x</code> is true.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.filter_cons_false"></a>
### `List.filter_cons_false`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:240`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : A → Bool) → (x : A) → (xs : List A) → p x = Bool.false → List.filter A p (List.cons A x xs) = List.filter A p xs
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>filter p (x :: xs) = filter p xs</code> when <code>p x</code> is false.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.filter_sound"></a>
### `List.filter_sound`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:245`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : A → Bool) → (x : A) → (l : List A) → x ∈ List.filter A p l → x ∈ l ∧ p x = Bool.true
```
<div class="doc"><p>Everything <code>filter</code> keeps was in the list and satisfies the predicate.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.filter_complete"></a>
### `List.filter_complete`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:264`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : A → Bool) → (x : A) → (l : List A) → x ∈ l → p x = Bool.true → x ∈ List.filter A p l
```
<div class="doc"><p>An element of the list that satisfies the predicate survives <code>filter</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.mem_filter"></a>
### `List.mem_filter`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:284`

```text
{A : Type} → (p : A → Bool) → (x : A) → (l : List A) → (x ∈ List.filter A p l ↔ x ∈ l ∧ p x = Bool.true)
```
<div class="doc"><p>Membership after <code>filter</code>, both directions: soundness and completeness.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.filter_map"></a>
### `List.filter_map`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:289`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (f : A → B) → (q : B → Bool) → (l : List A) → List.filter B q (List.map A B f l) = List.map A B f (List.filter A (fun x => q (f x)) l)
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>filter</code> commutes with <code>map</code> when the predicate is pulled back along the map.</p>
</div>


<a id="List.filter_filter"></a>
### `List.filter_filter`

def · `ListLemmas.wiz:305`


## Logic

<a id="module-Logic"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Logic</h4>
<p>Propositional logic over the impredicative <code>Prop</code> (stage 24a).</p>
<p>Wiz has no inductive propositions (<code>μ</code> always lives in <code>Type</code>), so the connectives are built from what the kernel has: <code>True</code>, <code>False</code>, <code>absurd</code>, Σ and Π, and observational equality (CoreSpec §7–8).</p>
<ul><li><code>∧</code> is a Σ of two propositions, so it is itself a proposition, with projections and η.</li><li><code>↔</code> is the pair <code>(P → Q) × (Q → P)</code>. An equation of propositions computes to almost the same type (propext, CoreSpec §8.2), <code>(0 _ : (0 _ : P) → Q) × ((0 _ : Q) → P)</code>, with erased binders, so <a href="#Iff.toEq"><code>Iff.toEq</code></a> and <a href="#Iff.ofEq"><code>Iff.ofEq</code></a> are one-liners (and no axiom). The two differ in the Σ binder&#39;s quantity: the first field of a computed equation can&#39;t be projected outside erased code, so <a href="#Iff.ofEq"><code>Iff.ofEq</code></a> gets it from <a href="#Eq.symm"><code>Eq.symm</code></a>.</li><li><code>∨</code> and <code>∃</code> are Church encodings (the impredicative ones: <code>∀ R, (… → R) → R</code>). A Σ over a <code>Type</code> would land in <code>Type</code>, and there are no inductive propositions to define them with. Their eliminators only go into propositions, which is all a logic needs (and is what Lean&#39;s <code>Or.elim</code>/<code>Exists.elim</code> allow too). The eliminated proposition <code>R</code> is bound at quantity 0.</li></ul>
<p>The names are Lean&#39;s, so that the library can switch to native inductive propositions later (plan D4) without renaming.</p>
<p>What is here: <a href="#Not"><code>Not</code></a> (<code>¬</code>), <a href="#And"><code>And</code></a> (<code>∧</code>), <a href="#Or"><code>Or</code></a> (<code>∨</code>), <a href="#Iff"><code>Iff</code></a> (<code>↔</code>), <a href="#Ex"><code>Ex</code></a> (<code>∃</code>, with binder notation), the equality lemmas <a href="#Eq.symm"><code>Eq.symm</code></a>, <a href="#Eq.trans"><code>Eq.trans</code></a>, <a href="#Eq.congrArg"><code>Eq.congrArg</code></a>, <a href="#Eq.substProp"><code>Eq.substProp</code></a>, the definitional <a href="#propext"><code>propext</code></a> and <a href="#funext"><code>funext</code></a>, and the Boolean algebra (<a href="#Bool.and_comm"><code>Bool.and_comm</code></a>, <a href="#Bool.or_assoc"><code>Bool.or_assoc</code></a>, <a href="#Bool.and_absorb"><code>Bool.and_absorb</code></a>, the De Morgan laws, …) with its bridges from <code>b = true</code> to <code>∧</code>, <code>∨</code> and <code>¬</code> (<a href="#Bool.and_eq_true"><code>Bool.and_eq_true</code></a>, <a href="#Bool.or_eq_true"><code>Bool.or_eq_true</code></a>, <a href="#Bool.not_eq_true"><code>Bool.not_eq_true</code></a>).</p>
<pre><code>import Logic

def swap {P Q : Prop} (h : P ∧ Q) : Q ∧ P := And.intro h.2 h.1
def orSwap {P Q : Prop} (h : P ∨ Q) : Q ∨ P := Or.elim h Or.inr Or.inl
def ex3 : ∃ n : Nat, n = 3 := Ex.intro (fun n =&gt; n = 3) 3 rfl</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="Eq.substProp"></a>
### `Eq.substProp`

def · `Logic.wiz:216`

```text
{A : Type} → (0 P : A → Prop) → {a : A} → {b : A} → a = b → P a → P b
```
<div class="doc"><p>Transport a proof of <code>P a</code> along <code>a = b</code> to a proof of <code>P b</code>, for a family of propositions <code>P</code>.</p>
<p>(It goes through <a href="#congrArg"><code>congrArg</code></a>: a motive <code>fun b _ =&gt; P b</code> would use <code>b</code>, which <code>transp</code> binds at 0; an equation of propositions computes to the pair of implications, whose second field is the direction we want.)</p>
</div>

def · `Logic.wiz:224`


<a id="funext"></a>
### `funext`

def · `Logic.wiz:230`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → {f : A → B} → {g : A → B} → ((x : A) → f x = g x) → f = g
```
<div class="doc"><p>Function extensionality is definitional: an equation of functions <em>is</em> pointwise, <code>(0 x : A) → f x = g x</code>. Its binder is erased, so a proof that uses <code>x</code> (passes it to a lemma that matches on it) can&#39;t be written against it directly; <a href="#funext"><code>funext</code></a> takes the unerased form and lets subtyping (quantities don&#39;t matter in a Π that is a proposition, CoreSpec §11.5) do the rest.</p>
</div>


<a id="congrFun"></a>

def · `Logic.wiz:232`

<div class="doc"><p>Equal functions agree at every argument: from <code>f = g</code>, <code>f x = g x</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="Trans"></a>
### `Trans`

class · `Logic.wiz:249`

```text
Prop → Prop → outParam Prop → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>Trans p q r</code>: a proof of <code>p</code> and one of <code>q</code> give one of <code>r</code>. <code>calc</code> (stage 13s) composes adjacent steps with an instance of it: the relations may differ (<code>a ≤ b</code> then <code>b &lt; c</code> gives <code>a &lt; c</code>), and the last step&#39;s relation is the chain&#39;s.</p>
<p><code>r</code> is an <a href="#outParam"><code>outParam</code></a>, so instance search finds it from <code>p</code> and <code>q</code>. A library registers a relation by adding instances (<code>lib/Nat.wiz</code>, <code>lib/IntOrder.wiz</code>, <code>lib/Rat.wiz</code>), and so can a program:</p>
<pre><code>def MyRel (a b : Nat) : Prop := a = b
infix:50 &quot; ~ &quot; =&gt; MyRel
instance {a b c : Nat} : Trans (a ~ b) (b ~ c) (a ~ c) := Trans.mk (fun h h&#39; =&gt; Eq.trans h h&#39;)</code></pre>
</div>

- <a id="Trans.trans"></a>`trans` : `{p : Prop} → {q : Prop} → {r : outParam Prop} → [self : Trans p q r] → p → q → r` — Compose a proof of <code>p</code> and one of <code>q</code> into a proof of <code>r</code>.

## MVar

<a id="module-MVar"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>MVar</h4>
<p>Shared state between threads: <code>import MVar</code> (stage 25d, docs/stages/25-concurrency.md).</p>
<p>A peer of the session-typed channels in lib/Session.wiz (decision CS1), for the programs channels don&#39;t fit: many threads sharing one cell, a work queue, a lock around output. What each API guarantees (25d has the table):</p>
<ul><li><code>MVar A</code>: a cell that is empty or holds an <code>A</code> (Haskell&#39;s <a href="#MVar"><code>MVar</code></a>). <code>take</code> waits until it is full and empties it, <a href="#put"><code>put</code></a> waits until it is empty and fills it. Values are immutable, so there are no data races; values cross threads safely (the runtime marks them shared, 25a). <strong>No deadlock freedom</strong>: two threads can each wait for the other&#39;s <a href="#put"><code>put</code></a>.</li><li><a href="#MVar.borrow"><code>MVar.borrow</code></a>/<a href="#MVar.fill"><code>MVar.fill</code></a>: the linear discipline. <code>borrow</code> takes the value and hands out a <code>Hole m</code>, a linear obligation to refill <code>m</code>: it can&#39;t be dropped or used twice, so a borrower refills the cell exactly once on every path (no cell left empty for ever by a forgotten <a href="#put"><code>put</code></a>). Still no deadlock freedom.</li><li><a href="#Lock"><code>Lock</code></a>: a mutex with a linear <code>Guard</code>. <code>acquire</code> gives a guard, <code>release</code> consumes it: every acquisition is released exactly once (no leaked lock, no double unlock), from any thread. <strong>No deadlock freedom</strong>: lock order is up to the program.</li></ul>
<p>Programs that use these are outside the deadlock-freedom claim of lib/Session.wiz. In compiled code the natives are <code>wiz_mvar_*</code> and <code>wiz_lock_*</code> in runtime/; the interpreters (<code>#eval</code>, <code>#run</code>) can&#39;t run them.</p>
<pre><code>def counter : IO Nat := do
  m ← MVar.newFull 0;
  MVar.modify m Nat.succ;
  MVar.take m</code></pre>
</div>

## Nat

<a id="module-Nat"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Nat</h4>
<p>Natural numbers (<code>import Nat</code>): the commutative semiring laws, subtraction, and the order, proved by hand from <code>0</code> and <code>succ</code>.</p>
<p>The order is the Prelude&#39;s Boolean <a href="#Nat.le"><code>Nat.le</code></a>, made a proposition by <code>= .true</code> (<code>Nat.Le m n := Nat.le m n = .true</code>). An equation of Booleans computes, so <code>Nat.Le (succ m) (succ n)</code> <em>is</em> <code>Nat.Le m n</code> and <code>Nat.Le 0 n</code> is <code>True</code>: many order facts hold by <code>rfl</code>, and case splits use <a href="#Bool.cases"><code>Bool.cases</code></a>. <code>m ≤ n</code> and <code>m &lt; n</code> (lib/Order.wiz) are <a href="#Nat.Le"><code>Nat.Le</code></a> and <a href="#Nat.Lt"><code>Nat.Lt</code></a>.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#congrArg"><code>congrArg</code></a>, <a href="#congrArg2"><code>congrArg2</code></a>; the laws <a href="#Nat.add_comm"><code>Nat.add_comm</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.add_assoc"><code>Nat.add_assoc</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.mul_comm"><code>Nat.mul_comm</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.mul_assoc"><code>Nat.mul_assoc</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.mul_add"><code>Nat.mul_add</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.add_mul"><code>Nat.add_mul</code></a>, …; cancellation (<a href="#Nat.add_left_cancel"><code>Nat.add_left_cancel</code></a>); <a href="#Nat.Le"><code>Nat.Le</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.Lt"><code>Nat.Lt</code></a> with reflexivity, transitivity, antisymmetry, totality (<a href="#Nat.le_cases"><code>Nat.le_cases</code></a>) and monotonicity of <code>+</code> and <code>*</code>; <a href="#Nat.cmp"><code>Nat.cmp</code></a>, a three-way comparison. Identities of <code>+</code> and <code>*</code> are better proved by <code>nat_ring!</code> (lib/Ring.wiz).</p>
<pre><code>import Nat

def ex (a b : Nat) : a + b + 0 = b + a :=
  Eq.trans (Nat.add_zero (a + b)) (Nat.add_comm a b)
def le : Nat.Le 2 5 := rfl</code></pre>
</div>

## Optic

<a id="module-Optic"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Optic</h4>
<p>Optics for borrows (RD11): the target library of Feral&#39;s lowering of mutable borrows. See wiz-notes/borrows-as-optics.md.</p>
<p>A Feral function that returns <code>&amp;mut A</code> borrowed from a lender <code>S</code> lowers (Aeneas style) to a forward value and a backward closure: <code>S → Result (A × (A → S))</code>. That is a (partial) costate coalgebra <code>S → Result (Store A S)</code>, and when its body is a place expression (fields, indices, variant payloads) it is a lawful partial lens. This file names the pieces and states the laws. The representation stays the closure form, which is what reference counting with reuse wants.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#Store"><code>Store</code></a> (a borrowed value and how to put it back), <a href="#Lens"><code>Lens</code></a> and <a href="#PLens"><code>PLens</code></a> (total and partial places), <a href="#zoom"><code>zoom</code></a> (run a <code>&amp;mut</code> function on a sub-place), <a href="#Affine"><code>Affine</code></a> (<code>Option&lt;&amp;mut A&gt;</code>), <a href="#TraverseMut"><code>TraverseMut</code></a> (<code>iter_mut</code>), the lens laws (<a href="#Lens.Lawful"><code>Lens.Lawful</code></a>, <a href="#PLens.Lawful"><code>PLens.Lawful</code></a>, <a href="#Lens.Indep"><code>Lens.Indep</code></a>) and proofs that composition keeps them (<a href="#Lens.comp_lawful"><code>Lens.comp_lawful</code></a>, <a href="#List.atL_lawful"><code>List.atL_lawful</code></a>). <a href="#Result"><code>Result</code></a>, <a href="#Error"><code>Error</code></a> and their specification predicates are in lib/Result.wiz.</p>
<pre><code>import Optic

def p : Pair2 Nat Nat := Pair2.mk 1 2
#eval Lens.get Pair2.fstL p                    -- 1
#eval (Lens.set Pair2.sndL p 5).snd            -- 5
#eval Result.map Store.pos (List.atL 1 (List.cons 7 (List.cons 8 List.nil)))   -- .ok 8</code></pre>
</div>

## OpticDerive

<a id="module-OpticDerive"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>OpticDerive</h4>
<p><code>deriving Lens</code> (<code>import OpticDerive</code>): a lens per field of a structure, its laws, and the independence of every two distinct fields. For <code>structure S Δ where f₁ : T₁ … fₙ : Tₙ</code> it defines, with the parameters Δ implicit,</p>
<p>S.fL         : Lens (S Δ) T                       get <code>s.f</code>, put by rebuilding <code>S.mk …</code> S.fL_lawful  : Lens.Lawful S.fL                    by <code>rfl</code> S.f_g_indep  : Lens.Indep S.fL S.gL                for f before g, by <code>rfl</code></p>
<p>the same names and statements as Feral&#39;s lowering of <code>struct</code> (lib/Feral.wiz, <code>Fe.lensDefs</code>), so lowered code can use the deriver. The lenses are ordinary values: for an HDL bundle (<code>structure Tx (r : HwTy → Type)</code>) <code>Tx.lineL : Lens (Tx r) (r Bit)</code> is one lens at every representation, on values (proofs) and on wires (synthesis); see lib/Hdl/Optic.wiz. Fields whose types depend on earlier fields are not supported (a put would have to change the type). Design: wiz-notes/cohesion-hardware.md 2.2.</p>
</div>

## Order

<a id="module-Order"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Order</h4>
<p>Notation for orders and equivalences (<code>import Order</code>): <code>a ≤ b</code>, <code>a &lt; b</code> and <code>a ≈ b</code>, each a class with one instance per type. The relations are propositions.</p>
<p>Instances: <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> (lib/Nat.wiz), <a href="#Int"><code>Int</code></a> (lib/IntOrder.wiz), and the rationals <a href="#Q"><code>Q</code></a> (lib/Rat.wiz, where <code>≈</code> is the equality of fractions).</p>
<pre><code>import Nat

def ex (n : Nat) : n ≤ n + 1 := Nat.le_add_right n 1</code></pre>
</div>

## PMap

<a id="module-PMap"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>PMap</h4>
<p>Persistent (immutable, structurally shared) maps and sets (<code>import PMap</code>): <code>PMap K V</code> and <code>PSet K</code>. Every update returns a new value and leaves the old one valid; the two share all the nodes the update did not touch, so an update allocates only the O(log n) nodes on the path from the root to the changed leaf (plus a constant number for rebalancing rotations).</p>
<p>The representation is a size-balanced binary search tree (a weight-balanced tree, after Adams; the same scheme as Haskell&#39;s <code>Data.Map</code>), with the subtree size stored in each node. Keys are ordered by a <a href="#Compare"><code>Compare</code></a> instance: <code>compare k k&#39;</code> is <code>.lt</code>, <code>.eq</code> or <code>.gt</code>. Instances are provided for <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> (through the builtin <a href="#Nat.lt"><code>Nat.lt</code></a>/<a href="#Nat.beq"><code>Nat.beq</code></a>) and <a href="#U64"><code>U64</code></a> (unsigned); any other key type gets one by defining its <a href="#Compare"><code>Compare</code></a> instance. (<a href="#U64Map"><code>U64Map</code></a> in lib/WordMap.wiz is the specialised, in-place when unique map with a native hash-table backend; <a href="#PMap"><code>PMap</code></a> is the pure model a future <a href="#U64Map"><code>U64Map</code></a> can be defined against, see <code>wiz-notes/persistent-data.md</code>.)</p>
<pre><code>import PMap

def m : PMap Nat String := PMap.fromList [(2, &quot;two&quot;), (1, &quot;one&quot;)]
def m&#39; : PMap Nat String := PMap.insert m 3 &quot;three&quot;
-- PMap.toList m  = [(1, &quot;one&quot;), (2, &quot;two&quot;)]
-- PMap.toList m&#39; = [(1, &quot;one&quot;), (2, &quot;two&quot;), (3, &quot;three&quot;)]</code></pre>
<p>The balance condition is a weight balance: with <code>sl</code> and <code>sr</code> the sizes of the children, a node is balanced when <code>sl + sr ≤ 1</code> or both <code>sl ≤ 3 sr</code> and <code>sr ≤ 3 sl</code>; otherwise a single or double rotation restores it. This bounds the height by about <code>2 log₂ n</code> and keeps every operation O(log n) in the worst case, unlike an unbalanced BST, which degenerates to a list on sorted keys.</p>
<p><code>toList</code> is in key order and <code>fromList</code> accepts entries in any order. <code>foldl</code> visits the entries in key order. The map keeps its invariant (one entry per key, the tree in order and weight-balanced) internally: the constructor of <a href="#PMap"><code>PMap</code></a> is private, and the module&#39;s operations preserve it.</p>
<p>Laws (<code>find_empty</code>, <code>size_empty</code>) are proved on the definitions. The other expected laws (<code>find_insert</code>, <code>find_erase</code>, <code>size_insert</code>) depend on the tree invariant surviving rotations; they are checked by the tests (group <code>persistent</code>) rather than proved here.</p>
</div>

## Prelude

<a id="module-Prelude"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Prelude</h4>
<p>The Wiz prelude (<code>import Prelude</code>): the basic types, notation, classes and metaprogramming that every other library module builds on.</p>
<p>It has:</p>
<ul><li>the basic data types: <a href="#Bool"><code>Bool</code></a>, <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> (unary to the kernel, native at runtime), <a href="#List"><code>List</code></a>, <a href="#Option"><code>Option</code></a>, <a href="#Except"><code>Except</code></a>, <a href="#Char"><code>Char</code></a> and <a href="#String"><code>String</code></a>, with their basic functions (<a href="#Nat.add"><code>Nat.add</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.div"><code>Nat.div</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.land"><code>Nat.land</code></a>, <a href="#List.append"><code>List.append</code></a>, …);</li><li>transport along equations (<a href="#Eq.cast"><code>Eq.cast</code></a>, <a href="#Eq.subst"><code>Eq.subst</code></a>) and the regularity axiom <a href="#castRefl"><code>castRefl</code></a>;</li><li>the numeric classes <a href="#Add"><code>Add</code></a>, <a href="#Sub"><code>Sub</code></a>, <a href="#Mul"><code>Mul</code></a>, <a href="#Div"><code>Div</code></a>, <a href="#Mod"><code>Mod</code></a>, <a href="#Neg"><code>Neg</code></a> and <a href="#OfNat"><code>OfNat</code></a> behind <code>+ - * / %</code> and numerals, and <a href="#Append"><code>Append</code></a> behind <code>++</code>;</li><li>notation: <code>if … then … else</code>, <code>&amp;&amp;</code>, <code>||</code>, <code>!</code>, <code>|&gt;</code>, list literals <code>[a, b]</code>, and <code>do</code>/<code>do1</code> blocks over <a href="#Monad"><code>Monad</code></a>/<a href="#Monad1"><code>Monad1</code></a>;</li><li>metaprogramming: reflected terms (<a href="#Expr"><code>Expr</code></a>, <a href="#ExprView"><code>ExprView</code></a>), syntax trees (<a href="#Syntax"><code>Syntax</code></a>), the monads <a href="#TacticM"><code>TacticM</code></a> and <a href="#MacroM"><code>MacroM</code></a>, reflection of inductive types (<a href="#IndView"><code>IndView</code></a>), and the basic tactics <code>intro</code>, <code>exact</code>, <code>rfl</code>, <code>assumption</code>, <code>apply</code>, <code>try</code>, <code>first</code>, <code>repeat</code>, <code>intros</code>, <code>rename_i</code>, <code>unfold</code>, <code>whnf</code>, <code>change</code> and <code>rw</code>.</li></ul>
<pre><code>def sumTo : Nat → Nat
  | .zero =&gt; 0
  | .succ n =&gt; Nat.succ n + sumTo n

def sumTo_three : sumTo 3 = 6 := by rfl</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="castRefl"></a>
### `castRefl`

axiom · `Prelude.wiz:37`

```text
{A : Type u} → (0 e : A = A) → (0 a : A) → (cast e a : A) = a
```
<div class="doc"><p>Propositional regularity: a cast along a proof of <code>A = A</code> is the identity, up to equality. An axiom (it doesn&#39;t compute), consistent in the setoid model. Wiz has no definitional regularity (D1: with an impredicative <code>Prop</code> it makes checking loop), so a cast at a type variable stays stuck; this axiom is how proofs get rid of one (<a href="#Vec.map_cons"><code>Vec.map_cons</code></a> in lib/Vec.wiz).</p>
</div>


<a id="Eq.cast"></a>
### `Eq.cast`

def · `Prelude.wiz:45`

```text
{A : Type u} → {B : Type u} → (0 e : A = B) → (1 a : A) → B
```
<div class="doc"><p>Transport along an equation, for linear values too (L4). The transported value is a quantity-1 parameter: a linear value (a channel endpoint, a token) can be passed, and so can an unrestricted one (an ω variable may be used once). <code>cast</code> itself passes its argument&#39;s usage through; these just state it in their types.</p>
<p><code>Eq.cast e a</code> turns <code>a : A</code> into a <code>B</code>, given <code>e : A = B</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="Eq.subst"></a>
### `Eq.subst`

def · `Prelude.wiz:52`

```text
{A : Type u} → (0 P : A → Type v) → {a : A} → {b : A} → (0 e : a = b) → (1 pa : P a) → P b
```
<div class="doc"><p>Substitution: from <code>e : a = b</code> and <code>pa : P a</code>, a <code>P b</code> (the transported value is linear, as in <a href="#Eq.cast"><code>Eq.cast</code></a>).</p>
<pre><code>Eq.subst (fun n =&gt; Vec A n) e v : Vec A m   -- for v : Vec A n, e : n = m</code></pre>
</div>


<a id="Eq.substBack"></a>
### `Eq.substBack`

def · `Prelude.wiz:55`

```text
{A : Type u} → (0 P : A → Type v) → {a : A} → {b : A} → (0 e : a = b) → (1 pb : P b) → P a
```
<div class="doc"><p>Substitution backwards, without <a href="#Eq.symm"><code>Eq.symm</code></a>: from <code>e : a = b</code> and <code>pb : P b</code>, a <code>P a</code>.</p>
</div>

<a id="Nat"></a>
### `Nat`

inductive · `Prelude.wiz:68`

```text
Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>The natural numbers, in unary: <code>zero</code> and <code>succ n</code>. The kernel computes with these definitions; at runtime (and on numerals in the kernel) numbers are native (<code>builtin nat</code>), so <code>1000000 * 1000000</code> is fast. A numeral at <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> is a native literal that computes like <code>Nat.succ (Nat.succ (Nat.succ Nat.zero))</code> (for <code>3</code>).</p>
</div>

<div class="doc"><p>Bitwise classes (H14 S2), as in Lean: <code>a &amp;&amp;&amp; b</code>, <code>a ||| b</code>, <code>a ^^^ b</code>, <code>~~~a</code>, and the shifts <code>a &lt;&lt;&lt; k</code>, <code>a &gt;&gt;&gt; k</code> by a number of places <code>k : Nat</code> (Lean&#39;s take it at the operand&#39;s type; a fixed amount is what hardware shifts by wiring). Type

<a id="TacticM"></a>
### `TacticM`

def · `Prelude.wiz:612`

```text
Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>The metaprogramming monad: requests to the elaborator (<a href="#Tac"><code>Tac</code></a>) in continuation-passing style, so <code>bind</code> is just composition. Macros (<a href="#MacroM"><code>MacroM</code></a>) and tactics (<a href="#Tactic"><code>Tactic</code></a>) both use it.</p>
<pre><code>def Tactic.myExact : Tactic := fun stx =&gt; do
  g ← TacticM.mainGoal;
  TacticM.exact g (Syntax.getArg stx 1);
  TacticM.replaceMainGoal .nil</code></pre>
</div>

## Rat

<a id="module-Rat"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Rat</h4>
<p>Rational numbers as an ordered field, up to an equivalence (<code>import Rat</code>).</p>
<p>A rational <a href="#Q"><code>Q</code></a> is a numerator and a positive denominator, <strong>not reduced</strong>, and <code>p ≈ q</code> (lib/Order.wiz) is the equality of fractions <code>p.num · q.den = q.num · p.den</code>: a setoid, not a quotient (Wiz has no quotient types). Reducing by gcd would keep the numbers small, but every law would then need facts about gcd; with unreduced fractions every law is an identity of integers. Every operation respects <code>≈</code> (<a href="#Q.add_congr"><code>Q.add_congr</code></a>, …), and the laws hold up to <code>≈</code>.</p>
<p><code>q_ring! lhs ≈ rhs</code> proves identities of commutative rings at <a href="#Q"><code>Q</code></a>: the numerator and denominator of each side are integer expressions in the atoms&#39; numerators and denominators, and <code>lhs ≈ rhs</code> is one integer identity, which <code>int_ring!</code>&#39;s normaliser decides.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#Q"><code>Q</code></a> with <code>+ - *</code>, <a href="#Q.inv"><code>Q.inv</code></a>, <code>/</code> and numerals; <code>≈</code>, <code>≤</code>, <code>&lt;</code>; <code>q_ring!</code>; the ring laws (<a href="#Q.add_comm"><code>Q.add_comm</code></a>, …, <a href="#Q.mul_add"><code>Q.mul_add</code></a>) and congruences; the order (<a href="#Q.le_trans"><code>Q.le_trans</code></a>, <a href="#Q.le_total"><code>Q.le_total</code></a>, <a href="#Q.le_or_lt"><code>Q.le_or_lt</code></a>, monotonicity of <code>+</code> and <code>*</code>); <a href="#Q.abs"><code>Q.abs</code></a> and the triangle inequality (<a href="#Q.abs_add"><code>Q.abs_add</code></a>, <a href="#Q.abs_sub_le"><code>Q.abs_sub_le</code></a>); the field law <a href="#Q.mul_inv"><code>Q.mul_inv</code></a>; and the archimedean property <a href="#Q.lt_ceil"><code>Q.lt_ceil</code></a>.</p>
<pre><code>import Rat

def half : Q := Q.mk 1 2 rfl
def ex : half + half ≈ 1 := rfl
def sq (p q : Q) : (p + q) * (p + q) ≈ p * p + 2 * p * q + q * q :=
  q_ring! (p + q) * (p + q) ≈ p * p + 2 * p * q + q * q</code></pre>
</div>

</div>

## Ref

<a id="module-Ref"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Ref</h4>
<p>Mutable cells owned by linear points-to tokens (<code>import Ref</code>; plan CS7b/S4, cohesion step M5, wiz-notes/cohesion-resources.md; docs/resources.md).</p>
<p>A location <code>l : Loc V</code> is an ordinary (ω) value: it can be copied, stored in data, and sent anywhere. Owning the cell is a separate value, the token <code>Pts l v</code>: &quot;<code>l</code> holds <code>v</code>, and I am the only one who may read or write it&quot;. Tokens are used at quantity 1, which is exact in Wiz, so</p>
<ul><li>a token can&#39;t be copied: one owner per cell (no aliasing of mutable state);</li><li>a token can&#39;t be dropped: every cell is freed exactly once (<a href="#Ref.free"><code>Ref.free</code></a>), no leaks, no double free;</li><li>reading or writing needs the token: no use after free, and a function can&#39;t touch a cell it isn&#39;t given (the frame rule, by typing).</li></ul>
<p>The token&#39;s second index is the cell&#39;s current value, as a ghost (erased) index, so a function&#39;s type is its Hoare triple: <code>Ref.set l w : (1 t : Pts l v) → … Pts l w …</code> is <code>{l ↦ v} set l w {l ↦ w}</code> (lib/Hoare.wiz, <a href="#Triple.write"><code>Triple.write</code></a>), and <a href="#Ref.get"><code>Ref.get</code></a> returns the value with an erased proof that it is the token&#39;s index (<a href="#Triple.read"><code>Triple.read</code></a>).</p>
<p><strong>What is trusted.</strong> The four natives <code>wiz_ref_*</code> (runtime/, over the MVar cells of 25d) and the types given to them below; the kernel checks everything else. The one type that asserts a fact is <code>Ref.readRaw</code>&#39;s: the value read equals the token&#39;s index. It holds by an invariant the API keeps: a cell is created with its token (<a href="#Ref.new"><code>Ref.new</code></a>, index = the value stored), the only write (<a href="#Ref.set"><code>Ref.set</code></a>) consumes the token and returns one indexed by the value written, nothing else reaches the cell (<a href="#Loc"><code>Loc</code></a> and <a href="#Pts"><code>Pts</code></a> are opaque, their natives private), and a token can&#39;t be duplicated. So the value in the cell is always the index of its one token. This is the meaning of the token in lib/HProp.wiz&#39;s model, <code>Pts l v</code> ↔ <code>l ↦ v</code>; a mechanised adequacy proof against <a href="#Prog.run"><code>Prog.run</code></a> (lib/Hoare.wiz) is future work. <code>#print axioms</code> lists the natives. Extern privacy is by name only: another module could bind <code>wiz_ref_new</code> with any type (it would show in <code>#print axioms</code>), the same gap as MVar.Hole, Lock.Guard and Chan.</p>
<p>Tokens are boxed units at run time (a zero-size representation is plan L5). In compiled code only: the interpreters (<code>#eval</code>, <code>#run</code>) don&#39;t run these natives.</p>
</div>

<a id="Pts"></a>
### `Pts`

axiom · `Ref.wiz:47`

```text
{V : Type} → Loc V → V → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>Owning the cell <code>l</code>, which holds <code>v</code>: no constructor and no ω producer, so a token is used at quantity 1 (exactly once).</p>
</div>


<a id="Ref.new"></a>
### `Ref.new`

def · `Ref.wiz:63`

```text
{V : Type} → {B : Type} → (v : V) → (1 k : (l : Loc V) → (1 t : Pts V l v) → IO B) → IO B
```
<div class="doc"><p>A new cell holding <code>v</code>, and its token (<code>{emp} new v {l. l ↦ v}</code>).</p>
</div>


<a id="Ref.get"></a>
### `Ref.get`

def · `Ref.wiz:72`

```text
{V : Type} → {B : Type} → (l : Loc V) → {v : V} → (1 t : Pts V l v) → (1 k : (a : V) → (0 e : a = v) → (1 t' : Pts V l v) → IO B) → IO B
```
<div class="doc"><p>The value, with an erased proof that it is the token&#39;s index, and the token back (<code>{l ↦ v} get l {a. [a = v] ⋆ l ↦ v}</code>). Reading takes the token: an erased use would let a stale token, kept past a <code>set</code>, read the new value with a proof that it is the old one.</p>
</div>


<a id="Ref.set"></a>
### `Ref.set`

def · `Ref.wiz:76`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p>Write <code>w</code>; the token comes back indexed by <code>w</code> (<code>{l ↦ v} set l x {l ↦ x}</code>).</p>
</div>


<a id="Ref.free"></a>
### `Ref.free`

def · `Ref.wiz:80`

</div>
