## Region

<a id="module-Region"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Region</h4>
<p>Regions (Rust lifetimes) and borrow handles for Feral&#39;s lowering (RD12). Plan: wiz-notes/rust-dsl-plan.md; rules: drafts/feral/LOWERING.md (L1, L3, L4, L12, L17, L20–L22); hand-lowered programs: drafts/feral/lowered/.</p>
<p>A lifetime <code>&#39;a</code> lowers to an erased variable <code>ρ : Region</code>. Every handle type below is a <code>structure</code> or an <code>inductive</code> with <code>ρ</code> as a parameter, so <code>ρ</code> is part of the type&#39;s identity (phantom parameters, docs/stages/22-numbers.md, 22e): <code>Shr ρ A</code> and <code>Shr ρ&#39; A</code> are different types, and <code>ρ</code> is inferred from a handle&#39;s type. Nothing of it reaches run time.</p>
<p>Borrow checking is typing: a borrow scope (<a href="#Shr.borrow"><code>Shr.borrow</code></a>, <a href="#Uniq.borrow"><code>Uniq.borrow</code></a>, <a href="#Uniq.reborrow"><code>Uniq.reborrow</code></a>, <a href="#Uniq.share"><code>Uniq.share</code></a>, <a href="#Uniq.zoom"><code>Uniq.zoom</code></a>, <a href="#Region.scope"><code>Region.scope</code></a>) takes a body that is polymorphic in a fresh region <code>ρ</code>, and its result type <code>B</code> is chosen outside, so no handle at <code>ρ</code> can leave the scope (as <code>runST</code>). Inside a mutable borrow the lender&#39;s name is rebound to a <code>Lent ρ S</code> token that has no operations, so using the lender while it is borrowed is a type mismatch. Mutable borrows (<a href="#Uniq"><code>Uniq</code></a>, <a href="#Mut"><code>Mut</code></a>, <a href="#MutOpt"><code>MutOpt</code></a>) are used at quantity 1: the kernel rejects passing one twice and keeping one past its scope. A reference flows to a longer-lived place only through <a href="#Shr.weaken"><code>Shr.weaken</code></a> or <a href="#Mut.weaken"><code>Mut.weaken</code></a>, which need <a href="#Outlives"><code>Outlives</code></a> evidence, and that evidence comes only from scopes (or from a function&#39;s <code>&#39;a : &#39;b</code> bounds, passed as erased proof arguments).</p>
</div>

<a id="ResultH"></a>
### `ResultH`

inductive · `Region.wiz:117`

```text
Qty → Type → Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>The quantity-polymorphic form of <a href="#Result1"><code>Result1</code></a>: the handle <code>H</code> is carried on <strong>both</strong> branches at <code>%q</code>, and the value <code>B</code> is unrestricted. At <code>q = 1</code> this is exactly <a href="#Result1"><code>Result1</code></a> (definitionally; <a href="#Result1.toResultH"><code>Result1.toResultH</code></a>/<a href="#ResultH.toResult1"><code>ResultH.toResult1</code></a> are the identity), which is the only useful instance: at <code>q = ω</code> the handle may be dropped or duplicated, and at <code>q = 0</code> it cannot be handed back. Use <code>q = 1</code> for the scope discipline, or <a href="#Result1"><code>Result1</code></a> directly. The ordinary <a href="#Result"><code>Result</code></a> is not an instance: its <code>err</code> has no handle. <code>wiz-notes/result-q.md</code>.</p>
</div>

**Constructors**

- <a id="ResultH.ok"></a>`ok` : `{q : Qty} → {B : Type} → {H : Type} → B → (%q h : H) → ResultH q B H`
- <a id="ResultH.err"></a>`err` : `{q : Qty} → {B : Type} → {H : Type} → Error → (%q h : H) → ResultH q B H`

<a id="ResultH.map"></a>
### `ResultH.map`

def · `Region.wiz:129`

```text

```
<div class="doc"><p>Map the value, keeping the handle on both branches. The mapping function is unrestricted because the <code>err</code> branch drops it; the handle itself stays at <code>q</code>.</p>

<a id="ResultH.bind"></a>
### `ResultH.bind`

def · `Region.wiz:138`

```text
{q : Qty} → {A : Type} → {B : Type} → {H : Type} → (1 x : ResultH q A H) → (A → (%q h : H) → ResultH q B H) → ResultH q B H
```
<div class="doc"><p>Sequence two handle-threading results: on success, <code>f</code> gets the value and the handle at <code>%q</code> and returns the next result; on error the handle is returned unchanged. The handle stays at the same quantity <code>q</code> (it cannot move to a different one), and <code>f</code> is unrestricted because the error branch drops it, so it must not capture a linear resource: thread resources through the handle, as <a href="#Result1"><code>Result1</code></a> does.</p>
</div>

<a id="Mut"></a>
### `Mut`

inductive · `Region.wiz:288`

```text
Region → Type → Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>Mut ρ A S</code> is a returned <code>&amp;&#39;a mut A</code> borrowed from a lender <code>S</code>, used at quantity 1: the borrow&#39;s value and the backward function that rebuilds the lender (<code>Store A S</code>, an ω field: the handle is what is linear). <a href="#MutOpt"><code>MutOpt</code></a> is <code>Option (&amp;&#39;a mut A)</code>: a borrow, or the lender&#39;s handle back. ## Result

<a id="module-Result"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Result</h4>
<p>The result monad of Feral&#39;s lowered code (RD7), shared by lib/Optic.wiz and lib/Region.wiz: a value (<code>ok a</code>) or a panic (<code>err e</code>).</p>
<p>Two readings of a specification over a <a href="#Result"><code>Result</code></a>: <a href="#Result.All"><code>Result.All</code></a> (partial correctness: a failure satisfies everything) and <a href="#Result.Holds"><code>Result.Holds</code></a> (total correctness: a failure satisfies nothing). <a href="#Result.Holds"><code>Result.Holds</code></a> is the one that lines up with separation logic&#39;s <a href="#Triple"><code>Triple</code></a>, where a fault (<a href="#Prog.fail"><code>Prog.fail</code></a>) satisfies nothing either.</p>
<p><code>ResultQ q A</code> is the quantity-polymorphic form: <code>ResultQ ω A</code> is <code>Result A</code> (definitionally), and <code>ResultQ 1 A</code> has a linear success value. <a href="#Result1"><code>Result1</code></a> (lib/Region.wiz) is its resource-threading sibling <code>ResultH 1</code>, not an instance of <a href="#ResultQ"><code>ResultQ</code></a>: its error branch carries a handle. See <code>wiz-notes/result-q.md</code>.</p>
</div>

<a id="ResultQ"></a>
### `ResultQ`

inductive · `Result.wiz:64`

```text
Qty → Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A result whose success value is used at quantity <code>q</code>: <code>ok</code> carries the value at <code>%q</code>, <code>err</code> carries only the <a href="#Error"><code>Error</code></a> (no payload). At <code>q = ω</code> this is exactly <a href="#Result"><code>Result</code></a> (definitionally; <a href="#Result.toResultQ"><code>Result.toResultQ</code></a>/<a href="#ResultQ.toResult"><code>ResultQ.toResult</code></a> are the identity), and at <code>q = 1</code> the success value is linear. It is <strong>not</strong> <a href="#Result1"><code>Result1</code></a>: an <code>err</code> has no value, so a linear resource cannot be threaded through the error path (see <a href="#ResultH"><code>ResultH</code></a> in lib/Region.wiz, whose <code>err</code> carries a handle).</p>
<p><code>q = 0</code>: the value is at quantity 0, so it may not be used by a consumer (<code>ResultQ.elim</code> takes it at <code>%0</code> and the branch may ignore it); constructing <code>.ok a</code> needs <code>a</code> at 0. The generic compiled representation still keeps the field (erasure is compiled once at a quantity variable), as for any q-polymorphic type: <code>wiz-notes/result-q.md</code> §3.</p>
</div>

**Constructors**

- <a id="ResultQ.ok"></a>`ok` : `{q : Qty} → {A : Type} → (%q a : A) → ResultQ q A`
- <a id="ResultQ.err"></a>`err` : `{q : Qty} → {A : Type} → Error → ResultQ q A`

## Ring

<a id="module-Ring"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Ring</h4>
<p>Equations of commutative semirings at <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a>, decided by reflection (<code>import Ring</code>):</p>
<pre><code>import Ring

def ex (a b c : Nat) : (a + b) * (a + c) = a * a + a * c + b * a + b * c :=
  nat_ring! (a + b) * (a + c) = a * a + a * c + b * a + b * c</code></pre>
<p><code>nat_ring! lhs = rhs</code> is a proof of <code>lhs = rhs</code>. It reads the syntax of both sides as expressions <a href="#NatExpr"><code>NatExpr</code></a> over atoms: <code>+</code>, <code>*</code>, parentheses, ascriptions, numerals and <a href="#Nat.succ"><code>Nat.succ</code></a> are understood, and every other subterm is an atom (two atoms are the same when their syntax is, so <code>f x</code> and <code>f (x)</code> are two atoms). <a href="#NatExpr.norm"><code>NatExpr.norm</code></a> puts an expression in a normal form, a sorted list of monomials (<a href="#NatPoly"><code>NatPoly</code></a>), and the kernel checks that the two normal forms agree by computing them. Only soundness is proved (<a href="#NatExpr.eval_norm"><code>NatExpr.eval_norm</code></a>: the normal form has the value of the expression); that the normal form is canonical is what makes the procedure complete for commutative semirings, not what makes it correct.</p>
<p>The equation is written twice, in the statement and in the proof: a term macro sees only its own syntax. The tactic <code>by ring</code> (lib/RingTactic.wiz) reads the goal instead.</p>
<p>The reifier (<code>Ring.Reify</code>) and the keys of monomials (<code>Ring.Key</code>) are shared with <code>int_ring!</code> (lib/IntRing.wiz) and <code>q_ring!</code> (lib/Rat.wiz).</p>
</div>

## RingTactic

<a id="module-RingTactic"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>RingTactic</h4>
<p><code>ring</code>: prove an equation of commutative (semi)rings by reading the goal (<code>import RingTactic</code>).</p>
<pre><code>import RingTactic

def ex (a b : Int) : (a - b) * (a + b) = a * a - b * b := by ring
def nat (a b c : Nat) : (a + b) * c = c * b + a * c := by ring
def rat (p q : Q) : (p + q) * (p - q) ≈ p * p - q * q := by ring
def all : (a b : Nat) → a + b = b + a := by ring   -- the binders are introduced</code></pre>
<p>The goal (after introducing its <code>∀</code>s) is <code>lhs = rhs</code> at <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> or <a href="#Int"><code>Int</code></a>, or <code>lhs ≈ rhs</code> at <a href="#Q"><code>Q</code></a> (lib/Rat.wiz). The tactic looks inside the equation with <a href="#TacticM.eqView"><code>TacticM.eqView</code></a>, reifies both sides as expressions over atoms (<a href="#NatExpr"><code>NatExpr</code></a>, <a href="#IntExpr"><code>IntExpr</code></a>, <a href="#QExpr"><code>QExpr</code></a>: the normalisers of <code>nat_ring!</code>, <code>int_ring!</code> and <code>q_ring!</code>), compares their normal forms itself, so that a false equation gets a clear error, and closes the goal with the normaliser&#39;s soundness lemma (<code>NatExpr.prove ρ e₁ e₂ Ring.trivial</code>), which the kernel checks by computing the normal forms again.</p>
<p>Reification reads elaborated terms, not syntax: <code>+</code>, <code>*</code>, <code>-</code> (binary and unary, not at <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a>) through their classes (<a href="#Add.add"><code>Add.add</code></a>, …, and the heterogeneous <a href="#HAdd.hAdd"><code>HAdd.hAdd</code></a>, …, once they exist) or as <a href="#Nat.add"><code>Nat.add</code></a>/<a href="#Int.add"><code>Int.add</code></a>/<a href="#Q.add"><code>Q.add</code></a> …; numerals (<a href="#OfNat.ofNat"><code>OfNat.ofNat</code></a>, literals); <a href="#Nat.succ"><code>Nat.succ</code></a>. Every other subterm is an atom, and two atoms are the same when their terms are equal (<a href="#Expr.beq"><code>Expr.beq</code></a>), so <code>f x</code> and <code>f (x)</code> are one atom, unlike in <code>nat_ring!</code>.</p>
</div>

## Sat

<a id="module-Sat"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Sat</h4>
<p>Certified SAT (<code>import Sat</code>): an LRAT proof checker proved sound, Boolean formulas with a Tseitin translation proved sound, and the theorem that puts them together:</p>
<p>Sat.decide_sound : IsTrue (Sat.checkAll f nodes cert) → ∀ σ, BForm.eval σ f = .true</p>
<p>and its dag version (28c: one node per distinct subterm, <a href="#Sat.Gate"><code>Sat.Gate</code></a>/<a href="#Sat.GNode"><code>Sat.GNode</code></a>, closed by <a href="#Sat.dag_sound"><code>Sat.dag_sound</code></a>/<a href="#Sat.dag_eq"><code>Sat.dag_eq</code></a>), which the tactic uses. A SAT solver (CaDiCaL, untrusted) finds <code>cert</code>; the kernel runs the check (<code>refl</code>), so a proof made this way trusts nothing new. The tactic that drives it is <code>sat_decide</code> (lib/SatTactic.wiz). Design: wiz-notes/smt.md §4; docs/stages/28-solvers.md, 28b.</p>
</div>

<div class="doc"><p><code>a = b</code>.</p>
</div>


## SatTactic

<a id="module-SatTactic"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>SatTactic</h4>
<p><code>sat_decide</code> (stage 28b): decide a Boolean goal with a SAT solver, <strong>without trusting it</strong>. <code>import SatTactic</code>.</p>
<p>def demorgan (a b : Bool) : Bool.not (Bool.and a b) = Bool.or (Bool.not a) (Bool.not b) := by sat_decide</p>
<p>The goal (after introducing its <code>∀</code>s) is <code>e = .true</code> or <code>e₁ = e₂</code> at <a href="#Bool"><code>Bool</code></a>, where <code>e</code> is built from <code>Bool.and/or/not/xor</code>, <a href="#Sat.boolEq"><code>Sat.boolEq</code></a> and <code>.true</code>/<code>.false</code>; every other Bool subterm is an atom (a variable of the formula), and an application of a definition that unfolds to one of those is unfolded at its head. The tactic</p>
<ol><li>reflects <code>e</code> into a dag of <a href="#Sat.Gate"><code>Sat.Gate</code></a>s, one node per distinct subterm (28c: the subterms are shared, so a big formula is checked once per node), with the atoms as <code>σ := Sat.envOf [t₀, …]</code>;</li><li>builds the dag&#39;s CNF, with the output negated (<a href="#Sat.dagFull"><code>Sat.dagFull</code></a>);</li><li>asks the SAT solver (CaDiCaL, <code>--sat-solver</code>) for an LRAT refutation (<a href="#TacticM.satSolve"><code>TacticM.satSolve</code></a>; a model is shown as a counterexample, its inputs printed);</li><li>closes the goal with <a href="#Sat.dag_sound"><code>Sat.dag_sound</code></a> (or <a href="#Sat.dag_eq"><code>Sat.dag_eq</code></a> for an equation): it defines <code>σ</code> and the node list, passes <code>Sat.trivial : IsTrue (Sat.checkAll …)</code> and a proof that every gate holds (<a href="#SatT.holdsE"><code>SatT.holdsE</code></a>: <code>refl</code> at each node&#39;s own subterm, or a lemma, as in lib/BitBlast.wiz, 28d), and the kernel checks both by conversion.</li></ol>
<p>Neither the solver, nor this tactic, nor the host&#39;s DIMACS/LRAT plumbing is trusted. The kernel runs the checker (slow for big proofs; kernel evaluation, wiz-notes/smt.md).</p>
</div>

## Scry.Ai

<a id="module-Scry.Ai"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Ai: the abstract-interpretation core</h4>
<p>The parser-free core of stage S5 (design <code>wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md</code> §4.6, §5.3): lattice/domain/transfer interfaces, unsigned machine intervals with constants and nullness, a widening worklist, narrowing, overflow/out-of-bounds/nullness alarms, and the post-fixpoint checker. See <code>wiz-notes/scry-ai.md</code>.</p>
<p><code>import Scry.Ai</code> gives the interfaces and the engine; tests and examples use <code>Scry.AiExamples</code> (<code>lib/Scry/AiExamples.wiz</code>). Nothing here imports Wil or tree-sitter.</p>
<pre><code>import Scry.Ai

#eval accepts (AiMach.mk 8) cfg inv   -- the checker&#39;s verdict on a post-fixpoint</code></pre>
</div>

No public declarations.

## Scry.AiCfg

<a id="module-Scry.AiCfg"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.AiCfg: a tiny three-address language, CFG and transfer functions</h4>
<p>The frontend-independent half of the abstract-interpretation core: a small language (<a href="#AExpr"><code>AExpr</code></a>/<a href="#ACond"><code>ACond</code></a>/<a href="#AStmt"><code>AStmt</code></a>), a CFG (<a href="#ACfg"><code>ACfg</code></a>/<a href="#AEdge"><code>AEdge</code></a>), and the concrete-ish transfer functions for the <a href="#Value"><code>Value</code></a> domain of <code>Scry.AiDomain</code>. There is no parser and no Wil dependency: a Wil lowering will construct these values in stage S2/S5.</p>
<p>The language has the operations the S5 alarms need: machine-width <code>add</code>/<code>sub</code>/<code>mul</code>, array <code>load</code> with an explicit static length, <code>alloc</code>, and <code>null</code>. The transfer functions are width-aware: an operation whose exact range could leave <code>[0, 2^w)</code> becomes <code>Top</code> (unsigned wrap-around is never ignored). Soundness obligations are the <code>Prop</code> statements at the end of the module.</p>
<pre><code>import Scry.AiCfg

#eval (AExpr.eval (AiMach.mk 8) [] (.lit 7)).itv</code></pre>
</div>

## Scry.AiDomain

<a id="module-Scry.AiDomain"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.AiDomain: lattices and abstract domains</h4>
<p>The domain half of scry&#39;s abstract-interpretation core (design <code>wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md</code> §4.6, §5.3, stage S5). This module is independent of the Wil frontend: it defines the interfaces, the small numerical and nullness domains, and their <em>soundness obligations</em>. The obligations are <code>Prop</code>-valued statements, not proofs; §5.3&#39;s <code>check_sound</code> is conditional on them (the checker itself does not call them, which is the point of result checking).</p>
<p>Main definitions:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#Lattice"><code>Lattice</code></a>, <a href="#Widen"><code>Widen</code></a>, <a href="#Narrow"><code>Narrow</code></a>, <a href="#AbsDomain"><code>AbsDomain</code></a>, <a href="#Transfer"><code>Transfer</code></a>: the interfaces. The computational fields are what the engine runs; γ and the transfer relation live in <a href="#AbsDomain"><code>AbsDomain</code></a>/<a href="#Transfer"><code>Transfer</code></a>, and the laws are separate <code>Prop</code> statements below.</li><li><a href="#Interval"><code>Interval</code></a>: unsigned machine intervals <code>[lo, hi]</code>, <code>Top</code>, and <code>Bot</code>, with a width supplied by the transfer functions (<a href="#AiMach"><code>AiMach</code></a>).</li><li><a href="#Const"><code>Const</code></a>: a constant domain (<code>known n</code>, <code>unknown</code>, <code>cbot</code>).</li><li><a href="#Null"><code>Null</code></a>: <code>nul</code>, <code>nonNull</code>, <code>maybe</code>, <code>nbot</code>.</li><li><a href="#Value"><code>Value</code></a>: the simple reduced product <code>Interval × Const × Null</code>.</li><li><a href="#AiEnv"><code>AiEnv</code></a>: a non-relational environment <code>Var → Value</code>, as an association list.</li></ul>
<p>The product is reduced in one direction: a known constant tightens the interval to a point (<a href="#Value.norm"><code>Value.norm</code></a>). Nothing here is relational (no octagons yet, §4.6).</p>
<pre><code>import Scry.AiDomain

#eval Interval.contains (Interval.range 2 4) 3   -- true</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="Lattice"></a>
### `Lattice`

class · `Scry/AiDomain.wiz:43`

```text
Type → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A lattice with a decidable order: <code>le</code> is the concrete order, <code>join</code> the least upper bound, <code>bot</code> the least element. The laws are <a href="#Lattice.le_refl_stmt"><code>Lattice.le_refl_stmt</code></a>, … below; they are not fields, so an engine can run an instance whose proofs are still open (result checking).</p>

## Scry.AiExamples

<a id="module-Scry.AiExamples"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.AiExamples: the small programs S5&#39;s tests and docs run</h4>
<p>Hand-built CFGs, so that the engine and the checker can be exercised without a parser or a Wil frontend. <code>Tests/Scry.lean</code> evaluates the functions below; <code>wiz-notes/scry-ai.md</code> reproduces the same programs.</p>
<ul><li><code>loopCfg</code>: a counter loop that needs widening (16-bit, bound 1000).</li><li><code>constCfg</code>: <code>x := 2; y := 3; z := x * y</code>, an interval/constant proof.</li><li><code>nullCfg</code>: dereference a null pointer, a nullness alarm.</li><li><code>safeArrayCfg</code>: an in-bounds load from a fresh array, no alarm.</li><li><code>oobCfg</code>: <code>load p 8 4</code> on a fresh array of length 4, an out-of-bounds alarm.</li><li><code>ovfCfg</code>: <code>x := x + 1</code> with <code>x</code> unknown at 8 bits, an overflow alarm.</li></ul>
</div>

## Scry.AiFixpoint

<a id="module-Scry.AiFixpoint"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.AiFixpoint: worklist engine, narrowing, alarms and the post-fixpoint checker</h4>
<p>Stage S5&#39;s untrusted fast path and its result checker.</p>
<ul><li><a href="#AState"><code>AState</code></a> is the invariant map <code>block → AiEnv</code>.</li><li><code>solve</code> is a chaotic-iteration worklist: edges are queued when their source state grows, and a block that is reached again is widened. It is a <code>partial def</code>; nothing about termination is proved (widening makes it terminate for the finite-height domains here, but the engine is outside the trusted base).</li><li><a href="#narrowOnce"><code>narrowOnce</code></a> improves a widened post-fixpoint once, as §4.6 describes.</li><li><a href="#check"><code>check</code></a> is the §5.3 certificate checker: every edge must satisfy <code>transfer (inv p) ⊑ inv q</code>, the entry must be covered, and every statement&#39;s alarm condition must be discharged by the invariant. It reports <a href="#Alarm"><code>Alarm</code></a>s; an empty list is acceptance. The checker never trusts the engine.</li></ul>
<pre><code>import Scry.AiFixpoint

#eval check (AiMach.mk 8) exampleCfg (fixpoint (AiMach.mk 8) exampleCfg)  -- []</code></pre>
</div>

## Scry.Analysis

<a id="module-Scry.Analysis"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Analysis</h4>
<p>The <strong>intraprocedural graph layer</strong> over <code>Scry.Wil</code> (<code>import Scry.Analysis</code>): the CFG, dominators, reaching definitions, and the PDG&#39;s data-dependence (def-use) edges. There is no parser and no C lowering here; the input is a hand-built or lowered <a href="#Wil.Func"><code>Wil.Func</code></a>.</p>
<h5>Program points</h5>
<p>A Wil function is a list of basic blocks. Analysis needs a <em>program point</em> for every statement <strong>and</strong> every terminator, so an empty block still has a place in the CFG:</p>
<ul><li>block <code>b</code> with <code>n</code> statements owns points <code>base(b) … base(b)+n</code>; points <code>0 … n-1</code> are its statements and point <code>n</code> (the terminator point) executes <code>blk.term</code>;</li><li><code>base(b+1) = base(b) + n + 1</code>, so the points of a function are a contiguous range <code>0 … count-1</code>;</li><li>a statement point steps to the next point; a terminator point steps to the first point of each target block (<code>goto</code> one, <code>br</code> two, <code>ret</code>/<code>unreachable</code> none).</li></ul>
<p>This is the smallest encoding that keeps <code>br</code>/<code>goto</code> edges honest without inventing extra nodes per block.</p>
<h5>What is computed</h5>
<ul><li><a href="#Scry.cfgEdges"><code>Scry.cfgEdges</code></a> — the CFG as <code>(from, to)</code> pairs over program points.</li><li><a href="#Scry.dominators"><code>Scry.dominators</code></a> — the classic iterative dominator sets over the CFG. Unreachable points get <code>{self}</code> by convention.</li><li><a href="#Scry.rdIn"><code>Scry.rdIn</code></a> — <strong>reaching definitions</strong>: for each point, the set of definition points that may reach it. A definition is a statement point that writes a register (<code>assign</code> or a call&#39;s result variable). The transfer is <code>gen ∪ (in − kill)</code>, where <code>kill</code> removes the other definitions of the variables this point writes.</li><li><a href="#Scry.dataDeps"><code>Scry.dataDeps</code></a> — flow-dependence edges <code>(defPoint, usePoint, var)</code>: a definition point <code>d</code> reaches a use of <code>var</code> at <code>u</code>. These are the PDG data edges taint consumes.</li></ul>
<p>The fixpoints are ordinary <code>partial def</code> loops (the design&#39;s engine is deliberately executable, not proved here); the inputs are tiny per-function graphs. Anti-dependence, output-dependence and control-dependence edges are not computed: taint needs flow dependence only, and the rest belongs to the S4 remainder (<code>wiz-notes/scry-taint.md</code>).</p>
<p>Every set is a <code>List Nat</code> with membership-based dedup, and every map is an association list, so the representation is the same as the rest of scry&#39;s pure list model.</p>
</div>

## Scry.Cert

<a id="module-Scry.Cert"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Cert</h4>
<p><strong>Derivation certificates</strong> for scry&#39;s Datalog (<code>import Scry.Cert</code>): a finding is a fact plus a finite, acyclic derivation tree, and <code>Derivation.check</code> decides whether the tree is a valid rule instance by rule instance from the EDB.</p>
<p>This is the S8 slice of <code>wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md</code>: §4.5&#39;s <code>Derivation p db fact</code> and §5.1&#39;s &quot;the kernel evaluates <code>Derivation.check prog db tree = .true</code>&quot;. The design notes are in <code>wiz-notes/scry-derivation.md</code>.</p>
<h5>Shape</h5>
<p>Wiz has no nested inductive types (an inductive&#39;s fields may not mention the type being defined, not even under <a href="#List"><code>List</code></a>), so the tree is <strong>flat</strong>: <code>Derivation</code> is a list of <code>ProofNode</code>s in premise-first order, and a node names its premises by their position. A node is one of</p>
<ul><li><code>edb</code> — a fact of the input database;</li><li><code>rule ri env pids</code> — the rule <code>p.rules[ri]</code> instantiated at <code>env</code>, reading the non-negated body atoms from the facts at positions <code>pids</code> (in body order; a negated atom consumes none and is checked against <code>db</code>); the node&#39;s <code>fact</code> must be the instance&#39;s head fact;</li><li><code>join a b</code> — a lattice fact whose value is the join of the values at <code>a</code> and <code>b</code> (same relation and key). This is how a fixpoint value that is the join of several rule instances is certified.</li></ul>
<p><code>env</code> is stored in the certificate, but the checker verifies it against every body atom and the premises, so an untrusted producer cannot use it to smuggle in a fact it has no premise for. Premise positions must be smaller than the node&#39;s position, so the certificate is acyclic by construction.</p>
<h5>Soundness</h5>
<p><a href="#Scry.inLfp"><code>Scry.inLfp</code></a> is the semantic statement &quot;the fact is entailed by the least fixpoint&quot;: it holds in every database that contains the EDB and is closed under the program&#39;s rules. Three theorems are proved below, all by induction over the flat node list:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#Scry.check_sound_posTuple"><code>Scry.check_sound_posTuple</code></a> for the <strong>positive tuple fragment</strong> (no negation; tuple heads; no <code>join</code> node), from the program&#39;s shape alone;</li><li><a href="#Scry.check_sound_negFree"><code>Scry.check_sound_negFree</code></a> for <strong>negation-free programs</strong> (lattice heads, lattice body atoms and <code>join</code> nodes included), in the original <a href="#Scry.inLfp"><code>Scry.inLfp</code></a> sense, under the <a href="#Scry.LatLaws"><code>Scry.LatLaws</code></a> of the program&#39;s lattice (<code>eq_refl</code>, <code>eq_sound</code>, join idempotence, commutativity and associativity);</li><li><a href="#Scry.check_sound"><code>Scry.check_sound</code></a> for <strong>all node kinds</strong>, in the absence-preserving semantics <code>Scry.inLfpNeg p frozen db</code>: for a frozen set of relations that contains every relation the program negates, extensions may not add an absent tuple of a frozen relation. That is the stratified reading at one stratum (the lower relations are frozen; current-stratum facts may still be derived); the remaining obligation is to instantiate <code>frozen</code> with the program&#39;s lower strata and prove the side condition from <code>Program.check</code> (see <code>wiz-notes/scry-derivation.md</code>).</li></ul>
</div>

## Scry.Datalog

<a id="module-Scry.Datalog"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Datalog</h4>
<p>The <strong>deep embedding</strong> of scry&#39;s lattice-valued Datalog (<code>import Scry.Datalog</code>), with no surface syntax and no parser. A program is a value of <code>Program L</code>:</p>
<ul><li><code>Term</code> is a variable (<code>var n</code>) or a literal (<code>lit v</code>); every column is a <a href="#U64"><code>U64</code></a>, as in <code>Scry.Store</code>;</li><li><code>Atom</code> is a positive relation atom (<code>pos</code>), a negated one (<code>neg</code>), or a lattice-valued atom (<code>lat rel key valueVar</code>, which reads the relation&#39;s value for a key and binds it to lattice variable <code>valueVar</code>);</li><li><code>Head</code> is a tuple head or a lattice head whose value is an <code>LExpr</code> (<code>lit</code>, a lattice variable, <code>join</code>, or a Wiz function from <code>Program.funcs</code> applied to an expression);</li><li>a <code>Rule</code> is a head and a body; a <code>Program</code> adds the lattice operations, the arities, which relations are lattice-valued, and the transfer-function table.</li></ul>
<p><code>Program.check</code> is the macro&#39;s job done as a function of the deep embedding: <strong>range restriction</strong> (every head variable and every negated variable is bound by a positive body atom; every lattice head variable by a lattice body atom) and <strong>stratification</strong> (a negated atom&#39;s relation must be in a strictly lower stratum than the rule&#39;s head). <a href="#check"><code>check</code></a> returns the stratum of every relation, or <code>.none</code>.</p>
<p>The evaluator is in <code>Scry.Eval</code>. The theorems a later stage wants (<code>Program.sem</code> is the least fixpoint, <code>Derivation.check</code>) are not here: this stage is the executable semantics and its reference implementation.</p>
</div>

## Scry.Egraph

<a id="module-Scry.Egraph"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Egraph</h4>
<p>A native e-graph engine for scry (<code>import Scry.Egraph</code>), with no egglog and no foreign dependency. It is the S12 slice of <code>wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md</code> §10: an equality-saturated term store with a union-find, congruence closure by rebuilding, a hash-consed e-node table, extraction, and a small pattern/rewrite loop with a fuel bound. A Datalog relation of equalities can feed it with <code>mergeFacts</code>/<code>mergeRows</code>.</p>
<h5>Representation</h5>
<ul><li><strong>E-node.</strong> <code>ENode</code> is an operator (<code>op : Nat</code>) and the e-class ids of its children (<code>args : List Nat</code>). Leaves are nodes with no arguments. The op is an uninterpreted symbol number; scry&#39;s IR assigns the numbers.</li><li><strong>E-class.</strong> A union-find over dense ids <code>0 … next - 1</code>. <code>parent</code> and <code>rank</code> are lists indexed by id (union by rank; <code>find</code> follows parent pointers). <code>nodes</code> is the flat e-node table: <code>(class id, node)</code>, most recently added first. <code>etable</code> is the hash cons: canonical e-node → class id. Both lists are association lists; the interface is the same one a native table (<a href="#U64Array"><code>U64Array</code></a>/<a href="#U64Map"><code>U64Map</code></a>) would implement.</li><li><strong>Canonical form.</strong> After <code>rebuild</code>, every stored class id is a root and every child id in a stored node is a root. <code>canonical</code> checks that invariant.</li><li><strong>Merge.</strong> <code>union</code> links two roots (by rank). <code>merge</code> unions and rebuilds, so the result is closed under congruence. <code>mergeFacts</code> does a batch of unions and one rebuild, which is the operation a Datalog stratum calls after deriving equality facts.</li><li><strong>Rebuild.</strong> Congruence closure: repeatedly canonicalise every node, hash-cons it into a fresh table, and union the classes of two nodes that became identical. Each pass removes at least one class when it changes anything, so <code>next + 1</code> passes suffice. The final pass writes a canonical, duplicate-free node table.</li></ul>
<h5>Saturation, extraction</h5>
<p><code>Rewrite</code> is a pair of patterns (<code>Pat</code>); a pattern is a variable or a node whose children are patterns. Matching is relational e-matching: a node pattern is matched against every e-node of the class, and variables bind e-class ids (non-linear patterns compare roots). Applying a rewrite instantiates the right-hand side (hash-consing its nodes) and unions the two classes. <code>saturate g rules fuel</code> runs all rules, rebuilds, and repeats while something changed and fuel remains; the fuel bound is what makes a non-terminating system (e.g. <code>f x → f (f x)</code>) usable. A rewrite adds no new equality when the right-hand side already lives in the left-hand side&#39;s class, so a saturated graph stops early rather than burning the whole budget.</p>
<p>Extraction is bottom-up dynamic programming: <code>costs</code> relaxes a cost per class for <code>next + 1</code> rounds (each node costs <code>1 + weight op + the children&#39;s costs</code>), then <code>buildTerm</code> picks a cheapest node per class, with the class cost as a depth bound so a cyclic e-class cannot loop. <code>extract</code> is unit cost; <code>extractWith</code> takes a weight table.</p>
<p>The engine is ordinary Wiz, so the same examples run under the interpreter (<code>#eval</code>) and compiled (C and LLVM). It is untrusted, like the rest of the fast engine: nothing here is proved about terms or rewrites.</p>
</div>

## Scry.Eval

<a id="module-Scry.Eval"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Eval</h4>
<p>A semi-naive evaluator for <code>Scry.Datalog.Program</code> (<code>import Scry.Eval</code>), with a delta loop and provenance.</p>
<ul><li><strong>Strata are evaluated in order</strong>, so a negated atom reads a relation that is already complete (that is what <code>Program.check</code>&#39;s stratification buys). Within one stratum every rule is evaluated once without a delta if none of its body atoms is in the stratum, then a delta loop runs the rules that are recursive in the stratum: for each body position in the stratum, that atom is matched against the previous round&#39;s delta and the other atoms against the current database. A round&#39;s new tuples, and the keys whose lattice value moved, become the next delta; the loop stops when the delta is empty.</li><li><strong>Lattice relations</strong> keep one value per key. A key that is absent has <code>bot</code>; a new value is <code>join</code>ed in, and the key joins the delta only when the joined value differs. Values must therefore move up a finite lattice (the engine is a <code>partial def</code>: it does not prove termination, and a non-monotone transfer function can loop, as the design intends for an untrusted fast engine).</li><li><strong>Provenance</strong> is a flat heap of <code>ProofStep</code>s: each step has an id, the fact it derived, the rule (<code>.none</code> for an EDB fact), and the ids of the premises it used. <code>State.whyTuple</code>/<code>State.whyLat</code> return a fact&#39;s step, and <code>State.expandWitness</code> unfolds it into the reachable steps (a derivation tree with sharing). A negation has no premise id: the witness certifies the positive part of the derivation; an absence certificate is future work (<code>wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md</code> §5.1).</li></ul>
</div>

## Scry.Store

<a id="module-Scry.Store"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Store</h4>
<p>The relation store for scry&#39;s Datalog engine (<code>import Scry.Store</code>): a <strong>pure list model</strong> of the relations a Datalog program derives.</p>
<p>A <code>Db L</code> has one <code>TupleRel</code> for each ordinary (set-valued) relation and one <code>LatRel L</code> for each lattice-valued relation, both looked up by the relation&#39;s number (the schema&#39;s <code>arities</code> list fixes the arities; nothing here checks them). A tuple is a <code>List U64</code>, so ids, <a href="#U32"><code>U32</code></a>/<a href="#U64"><code>U64</code></a> columns and interned-string ids all use one representation.</p>
<p>The model keeps each tuple relation as a list of distinct rows, and each lattice relation as one entry per key. <code>insert</code> is linear (<code>memRow</code>), which is the right model for the kernel and the interpreter and for small inputs; the interface is the set of functions below, so a native backend (a hash set over <a href="#U64Array"><code>U64Array</code></a> for tuples and a <a href="#U64Map"><code>U64Map</code></a> from a key&#39;s hash to its value for lattice entries, both stage S0, <code>lib/WordArray.wiz</code> and <code>lib/WordMap.wiz</code>) can replace it without touching the evaluator. This module does not provide that backend.</p>
<p>The constructor of each relation is private, so the model is the only accessor and a user cannot break the distinctness invariant.</p>
</div>

## Scry.Taint

<a id="module-Scry.Taint"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry.Taint</h4>
<p>Intraprocedural <strong>taint analysis as Datalog</strong> (<code>import Scry.Taint</code>), over the def-use edges of <code>Scry.Analysis</code> and a small source/sink/sanitiser specification.</p>
<h5>The spec</h5>
<p><a href="#Scry.TaintSpec"><code>Scry.TaintSpec</code></a> names:</p>
<ul><li><code>sources</code> — direct calls whose <strong>result</strong> is attacker-controlled (<code>getenv</code>, <code>recv</code>, …);</li><li><code>sanitisers</code> — direct calls whose <strong>result</strong> is clean (<code>sanitize</code>, <code>escape_shell</code>, …); a sanitiser is a kill for its own result, not for its arguments;</li><li><code>sinks</code> — direct calls and the argument index to check (<code>(&quot;system&quot;, 0)</code>, <code>(&quot;printf&quot;, 0)</code>, …).</li></ul>
<p>The spec can be written as a Wiz value (<code>Scry.TaintSpec.mk …</code>) or parsed from the small line format in <a href="#Scry.parseTaintSpec"><code>Scry.parseTaintSpec</code></a>:</p>
<pre><code>source getenv
source recv
sanitise sanitize
sink system 0
sink printf 0</code></pre>
<p>Blank lines and lines with an unknown first word are ignored. The format is deliberately tiny: S4&#39;s rule pack will replace it with a real <code>.scry</code> spec file.</p>
<h5>The Datalog program</h5>
<p>Relations (all columns are <a href="#U64"><code>U64</code></a> in <code>Scry.Store</code>):</p>
<p>| # | relation | arity | kind | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | <code>flow (def, use)</code> | 2 | EDB, from reaching definitions | | 1 | <code>src (def)</code> | 1 | EDB, a source call with a result | | 2 | <code>sink (call, arg)</code> | 2 | EDB, a sink call and the checked argument | | 3 | <code>san (def)</code> | 1 | EDB, a sanitiser call with a result | | 4 | <code>tainted (def)</code> | 1 | IDB | | 5 | <code>alert (call, arg)</code> | 2 | IDB |</p>
<p>Rules:</p>
<pre><code>tainted s      :- src s.
tainted b      :- tainted a, flow a b, !san b.
alert s arg    :- tainted d, flow d s, sink s arg.</code></pre>
<p>The negation is stratified (<code>san</code> is EDB, <code>tainted</code> is one stratum up), so <a href="#Scry.Program.check"><code>Scry.Program.check</code></a> accepts the program. <code>!san b</code> blocks taint at a sanitiser&#39;s <strong>result definition</strong>: a sanitiser&#39;s argument may be tainted (it is a normal use), but the value it returns is not. Because every Wil statement writes at most one register, <code>tainted b</code> means &quot;the register defined at <code>b</code> is tainted&quot;, and a <code>flow</code> edge is per-register, so a branch merge with one tainted arm is tainted (union at the merge).</p>
<h5>Findings and paths</h5>
<p><a href="#Scry.findingsInFunc"><code>Scry.findingsInFunc</code></a> evaluates the program with the semi-naive engine, reads the <code>alert</code> relation, and rebuilds a <strong>source -&gt; sink path</strong> from the engine&#39;s provenance: the alert&#39;s <code>tainted</code> premise is walked back through <code>tainted</code>/<code>flow</code> premises until a <code>src</code> seed, then the sink call point is appended. A finding is one <code>(sink call, arg)</code> tuple; if several definitions reach the same argument the engine reports one path (the first derivation in provenance order).</p>
<h5>What this prototype does not model</h5>
<ul><li><strong>Memory</strong>: <code>store</code>/<code>load</code> do not carry taint, so <code>*p = getenv(); system(*p)</code> is a false negative (tested, and named in <code>wiz-notes/scry-taint.md</code>).</li><li><strong>Calls</strong>: an ordinary call does not propagate taint from arguments to its result, and there are no interprocedural summaries (S7). Sources, sanitisers and sinks are the only calls the spec interprets.</li><li><strong>Terminator uses</strong>: <code>ret</code>/<code>br</code> conditions are CFG edges but not data edges yet.</li></ul>
</div>

## Scry.TaintExamples

<a id="module-Scry.TaintExamples"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>A hand-built taint corpus</h4>
<p>The programs here are written with <code>Scry.Wil</code>&#39;s builder, not lowered from C. They are the golden corpus for the <code>scry-taint</code> test group (<code>Tests/ScryTaint.lean</code>) and exercise one feature of the prototype each:</p>
<ul><li><code>directFn</code> — taint through copies and arithmetic (<code>getenv</code> -&gt; <code>copy</code> -&gt; <code>add</code> -&gt; <code>system</code>);</li><li><code>sanitisedFn</code> — a sanitiser kills the flow (no finding, although a source reaches the sink along the CFG);</li><li><code>cleanFn</code> — a source and a sink with no data path between them (no finding);</li><li><code>branchFn</code> — a branch merge: one arm copies the source, the other assigns a constant; the merge is tainted through the source arm;</li><li><code>loopFn</code> — the only path to the sink goes around the back edge (the sink is at the loop head, before the source in program order), so reaching definitions and taint need a fixpoint;</li><li><code>fpFn</code> / <code>fnFn</code> — the false-positive / false-negative pair: the first is the sanitiser case (a naive &quot;source reaches sink&quot; analysis would flag it), the second stores the source through a pointer and reloads it (this prototype&#39;s memory blind spot, so it misses it);</li><li><code>directFn</code> again is the positive control for the pair: the same shape without a sanitiser or memory is reported.</li></ul>
<p>The comments give each statement&#39;s program point (<code>Scry.Analysis</code> numbers statements and terminators per block), so the expected paths in the tests can be read off by hand.</p>
</div>

## Scry.Wil

<a id="module-Scry.Wil"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Scry&#39;s common IR: Wil</h4>
<p>Wil is the small three-address IR the <code>scry</code> analyser (design: <code>wiz-notes/code-analysis-design.md</code>, §4.3) lowers C, C# and Python into. It is deliberately smaller than a compiler IR: enough to state a concrete semantics, so the abstract domains of stage S5 can be proved sound against it, and enough for the graph layers (CFG, dominators, CDG, def-use) of S2/S4.</p>
<p>This module has <strong>no parser and no C lowering</strong>. It fixes the grammar of Wil and gives it a concrete, fuel-bounded semantics over a block memory:</p>
<ul><li><a href="#Wil.Ty"><code>Wil.Ty</code></a> — the types (integers of a width and signedness, pointers, function types, records, <code>dyn</code> and <code>unknown</code>);</li><li><a href="#Wil.Val"><code>Wil.Val</code></a> — concrete values (an integer bit pattern, a pointer into a block, null, undefined);</li><li><a href="#Wil.Rhs"><code>Wil.Rhs</code></a> and <a href="#Wil.Stmt"><code>Wil.Stmt</code></a> — three-address right-hand sides and statements, and the terminators (<a href="#Wil.Term"><code>Wil.Term</code></a>) of a basic block;</li><li><a href="#Wil.Block"><code>Wil.Block</code></a>, <a href="#Wil.Func"><code>Wil.Func</code></a>, <a href="#Wil.Program"><code>Wil.Program</code></a> — basic blocks, functions (an entry block and a list of blocks) and a program (a list of functions);</li><li><a href="#Wil.step"><code>Wil.step</code></a>, <a href="#Wil.Step"><code>Wil.Step</code></a>, <a href="#Wil.run"><code>Wil.run</code></a> — the small-step concrete semantics and its fuel-bounded driver. Memory is CompCert style (blocks × offsets), so <code>lib/Hoare.wiz</code>&#39;s heap predicates can be given to a function&#39;s Wil form later.</li></ul>
<p>Every statement will carry an <em>origin</em> (a span/CST node), so findings point at source and CST queries can join Wil facts. The field is not in this stage: the C frontend adds it in S2, and adding <code>origin</code> to <a href="#Wil.Stmt"><code>Wil.Stmt</code></a> and <a href="#Wil.Term"><code>Wil.Term</code></a> is a mechanical change.</p>
<h5>What is deliberately not here yet</h5>
<ul><li>C lowering, origins, the CFG/dominator/CDG passes and the call graph (S2 rest);</li><li>indirect calls and function pointers (<code>Callee.direct</code> is implemented; <code>.indirect</code> faults);</li><li>floating point, aggregates and unions (<code>dyn</code> carries an unknown value);</li><li>nondeterministic <code>havoc</code> (the concrete interpreter picks the type&#39;s zero);</li><li>C undefined behaviour as alarms: an out-of-bounds or dangling access faults the machine, and a division by zero follows <code>lib/Word.wiz</code> (x/0 = 0).</li></ul>
</div>

<div class="doc"><p>One concrete step. It is total: a missing block, an unbound register, a bad memory access or an unimplemented indirect call is a <code>fault</code>, never a stuck function.</p>
</div>


<a id="Wil.Step"></a>
### `Wil.Step`

def · `Scry/Wil.wiz:688`

```text
Wil.Config → Wil.Config → Prop
```
<div class="doc"><p>The concrete one-step relation: <code>c</code> steps to <code>c&#39;</code> when the step function says so. <a href="#Wil.step"><code>Wil.step</code></a> is the executable form; <a href="#Wil.Step"><code>Wil.Step</code></a> is the proposition S5&#39;s soundness statements are about (<code>Transfer.sound : … → Wil.StepStmt s σ σ&#39; → …</code>).</p>
</div>

def · `Scry/Wil.wiz:693`

<div class="doc"><p>Run a configuration for at most <code>fuel</code> steps. Fuel is consumed by every step (statement, terminator, call and return), so recursion and loops both end in <code>outOfFuel</code>.</p>

## Scry.WilExamples

<a id="module-Scry.WilExamples"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>A hand-built Wil corpus</h4>
<p>The programs below are the golden corpus of the Wil stage: they are written with <code>Scry.Wil</code>&#39;s builder (<a href="#Wil.func"><code>Wil.func</code></a>, <a href="#Wil.block"><code>Wil.block</code></a>, <a href="#Wil.num"><code>Wil.num</code></a>, <a href="#Wil.binop"><code>Wil.binop</code></a>, …) rather than lowered from C. Their expected results are in <code>Tests/Scry.lean</code>, and they exercise the features the concrete semantics claims:</p>
<ul><li><code>arith</code> — constants, <code>mul</code>, <code>add</code>;</li><li><code>maxOf</code> — a two-way branch on <code>&lt;</code>;</li><li><code>incTwice</code> — direct calls, a return value used by the caller;</li><li><code>sumTo</code> — direct recursion (the callee is the caller);</li><li><code>facLoop</code> — a back edge, and a loop that terminates;</li><li><code>storeLoad</code> / <code>gepLoad</code> — <code>alloc</code>, <code>store</code> and <code>load</code> through a block pointer;</li><li><code>oobLoad</code>, <code>danglingLoad</code> — the two memory faults;</li><li><code>assumeFalse</code> — an infeasible path;</li><li><code>spin</code> — a <code>goto</code> that never leaves, so only fuel stops it.</li></ul>
<p>The tests run these with <a href="#Wil.runFunction"><code>Wil.runFunction</code></a> and compare the result against a direct Wiz computation (a differential check) or against the exact fault. When the C frontend lands (S2), the same corpus gains a third column: the value compiled C prints for the same source.</p>
</div>

## Serial

<a id="module-Serial"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Serial</h4>
<p>Serial ports and pseudo-terminals (sys-bytes): termios through <code>serial.c</code>.</p>
<p>A port is an <a href="#Fd"><code>Fd</code></a> (lib/Sys): <a href="#Serial.open"><code>Serial.open</code></a> opens and configures one, and every <a href="#Fd"><code>Fd</code></a> operation works on it (<a href="#Fd.write"><code>Fd.write</code></a>, <a href="#Fd.readWithin"><code>Fd.readWithin</code></a>, <a href="#Fd.readExactlyWithin"><code>Fd.readExactlyWithin</code></a>, …). Configuration is always raw: bytes go through untouched (no echo, no line editing, no CR/LF translation, no signals), and a read waits for at least one byte; time limits are the <code>…Within</code> reads&#39;.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#Serial.open"><code>Serial.open</code></a>/<a href="#Serial.withPort"><code>Serial.withPort</code></a> (open and configure a port), <a href="#SerialConfig"><code>SerialConfig</code></a> (rate, data bits, parity, stop bits, flow control; <a href="#SerialConfig.raw8N1"><code>SerialConfig.raw8N1</code></a> for the usual 8N1), <a href="#Serial.settings"><code>Serial.settings</code></a> (read back what a terminal is set to), and <a href="#Pty"><code>Pty</code></a> (a pseudo-terminal, to play a device in tests). This is host code: it runs on the machine the device is plugged into.</p>
<pre><code>import Serial

def main : IO Unit := EIO.toIO (Serial.withPort &quot;/dev/ttyUSB1&quot; (SerialConfig.raw8N1 .b115200)
  (fun f =&gt; Fd.writeUtf8 f &quot;hello&quot;))</code></pre>
</div>

## Session

<a id="module-Session"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Session</h4>
<p>Session-typed linear channels: <code>import Session</code> (stage 25b–c, docs/stages/25-concurrency.md).</p>
<p>A protocol <a href="#Proto"><code>Proto</code></a> says what happens on a channel, step by step, from one end&#39;s point of view; what comes next may depend on the value just exchanged (dependent session types, Toninho–Caires–Pfenning 2011). The other end follows the <code>dual</code>. Two layers:</p>
<ol><li>A pure semantics: a process following <code>p</code> is a <code>Proc R p</code>, and <a href="#link"><code>link</code></a> runs a process against one following the dual, to completion. <a href="#link"><code>link</code></a> is total (structural on <code>p</code>): two processes on the two ends of one channel can&#39;t get stuck.</li><li>Linear channels in <a href="#IO"><code>IO</code></a>: <code>Chan p</code> is one end of a channel whose remaining protocol is <code>p</code>. Endpoints are used exactly once (quantity 1, which is exact in Wiz: an endpoint can be neither dropped nor copied), so every step of the protocol happens, in order, and the channel is closed at the end. <a href="#Chan.fork"><code>Chan.fork</code></a> is the only way to make a channel, and it hands the two ends to two different threads. In compiled code a channel is a native queue and <code>fork</code> starts a thread (runtime/, <code>wiz_chan_*</code>, 25a); <code>#eval</code>/<code>#run</code> can&#39;t run threads, and run <a href="#Proc.runLinked"><code>Proc.runLinked</code></a>&#39;s model (<a href="#link"><code>link</code></a>) instead.</li></ol>
<p>Sequence linear steps with <code>do1</code> or <a href="#IO.bind"><code>IO.bind</code></a> (both take the action and the continuation at quantity 1, 9e); plain <code>do</code> can&#39;t capture an endpoint.</p>
<p>The API is in continuation-passing style (decision CS3): every operation takes the rest of the program as a function of the endpoint&#39;s next state, so no linear value has to sit in a data structure (Σ fields are ω, and <code>match</code> can&#39;t bind fields linearly yet).</p>
<p><strong>Deadlock freedom by construction</strong> (decision CS2; the argument and its scope are in docs/stages/25-concurrency.md, 25c): a program that uses only this API — no <a href="#MVar"><code>MVar</code></a>, no <a href="#Lock"><code>Lock</code></a> (lib/MVar.wiz), no other blocking primitive, no <code>partial</code> definitions — can&#39;t deadlock: channels form a forest (each <code>fork</code> adds one channel between a new thread and its parent, and an endpoint moves only into the child a <code>fork</code> starts), endpoints are linear (nobody waits for an end that was dropped), and every process is total. The claim is a meta-theorem from the literature (Wadler 2012, Lindley–Morris 2015, Jacobs– Balzer–Krebbers 2022), not a proof in Wiz.</p>
<p>For example, a client that sends a number and receives its double, and the matching server, run against each other by the pure semantics:</p>
<pre><code>def P : Proto := .send Nat (fun _ =&gt; .recv Nat (fun _ =&gt; .done))
def client : Proc Nat P := (3, fun r =&gt; r)
def server : Proc Unit (Proto.dual P) := fun n =&gt; (n + n, ())
-- link P client server = (6, ())</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="Proto"></a>
### `Proto`

inductive · `Session.wiz:60`

```text
Type 1
```
<div class="doc"><p>A session protocol, seen from one end of a channel: <code>send A k</code> sends a value <code>a : A</code> and continues as <code>k a</code>, <code>recv A k</code> receives one and continues as <code>k a</code>, <code>done</code> ends the session. What comes next may depend on the value exchanged.</p>
<pre><code>-- send a number, receive a number back, done
.send Nat (fun _ =&gt; .recv Nat (fun _ =&gt; .done))</code></pre>
</div>

- <a id="Proto.recv"></a>`recv` : `(A : Type) → (A → Proto) → Proto`
- <a id="Proto.done"></a>`done` : `Proto`


<a id="Proto.dual"></a>
### `Proto.dual`

def · `Session.wiz:67`

```text
Proto → Proto
```
<div class="doc"><p>The other end&#39;s view of a protocol: every <a href="#send"><code>send</code></a> becomes a <code>recv</code> and vice versa. <code>Proto.dual (Proto.dual p)</code> behaves like <code>p</code>.</p>
</div>


<a id="Proc"></a>
### `Proc`

def · `Session.wiz:76`

```text
Type → Proto → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>A process that follows <code>p</code> and returns <code>R</code>: sending is choosing a value (Σ), receiving is being ready for any value (Π). This is the &quot;propositions as sessions&quot; reading.</p>
<p><code>Proc R (.send Nat (fun _ =&gt; .done))</code> is <code>(n : Nat) × R</code>: a number to send, then the result.</p>
</div>


<a id="link"></a>
### `link`

def · `Session.wiz:84`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (p : Proto) → Proc A p → Proc B (Proto.dual p) → A × B
```
<div class="doc"><p>Run two processes on the two ends of one channel (cut elimination, as a program), returning both results. Total: every exchange moves both to the continuation of the same constructor, so two processes on one channel can&#39;t get stuck.</p>
</div>

<div class="doc"><p>A message of a cancellable protocol (decision CS13): a value (<code>val a</code>) or <code>cancel</code>. A protocol that may fail offers an explicit cancel branch at the points where one side sends; quantity 1 means a process can&#39;t just abandon a channel on an error path: it must say so to its peer.</p>
</div>

<a id="Chan"></a>
### `Chan`

axiom · `Session.wiz:120`

```text
Proto → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>An endpoint whose remaining protocol is <code>p</code>. Opaque: no constructor and no ω producer, so endpoints come only from <a href="#Chan.fork"><code>Chan.fork</code></a> and are used exactly once.</p>
</div>


<a id="Chan.fork"></a>
### `Chan.fork`

def · `Session.wiz:142`

```text
{B : Type} → (p : Proto) → (1 child : (1 c : Chan (Proto.dual p)) → IO Unit) → (1 parent : (1 c : Chan p) → IO B) → IO B
```
<div class="doc"><p>Make a channel following <code>p</code>: a new thread runs <code>child</code> on the dual end, and <code>parent</code> continues here with the other end. Both functions are linear, so they may capture other endpoints (that is how an endpoint moves to another thread).</p>
<pre><code>Chan.fork (.send Nat (fun _ =&gt; .done))
  (fun c =&gt; Chan.recv c (fun n c&#39; =&gt; Chan.close c&#39; (IO.println &quot;received&quot;)))
  (fun c =&gt; Chan.send c 42 (fun c&#39; =&gt; Chan.close c&#39; (IO.pure ())))</code></pre>
</div>

### `Chan.send`

def · `Session.wiz:148`

```text
{A : Type} → {k : A → Proto} → {B : Type} → (1 c : Chan (Proto.send A k)) → (a : A) → (1 next : (1 c' : Chan (k a)) → IO B) → IO B
```
<div class="doc"><p>Send <code>a</code>, then continue with the endpoint at <code>k a</code>. Sending never blocks (a channel buffers its messages).</p>
</div>

<a id="Proc.runLinked"></a>
### `Proc.runLinked`

def · `Session.wiz:180`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (p : Proto) → Proc A p → Proc B (Proto.dual p) → IO (A × B)
```
<div class="doc"><p>Run a process and a peer following the dual, and return both results. The model (what the kernel, proofs, <code>#eval</code> and <code>#run</code> see) is <a href="#link"><code>link</code></a>; compiled code runs the peer in a new thread over a real channel (<a href="#Proc.runLinkedThreads"><code>Proc.runLinkedThreads</code></a>, by <code>implemented_by</code>), so a compiled program that prints <a href="#Proc.runLinked"><code>Proc.runLinked</code></a>&#39;s result is a differential test of the native channels against the pure semantics.</p>
</div>

def · `Session.wiz:184`

```text
{A : Type} → {B : Type} → (p : Proto) → Proc A p → Proc B (Proto.dual p) → IO (A × B)
```
<div class="doc"><p>The compiled implementation of <a href="#Proc.runLinked"><code>Proc.runLinked</code></a>: the peer runs in a new thread over a real channel, and its result comes back through an <a href="#MVar"><code>MVar</code></a>, written once and read once.</p>
</div>


## Std

<a id="module-Std"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Std</h4>
<p>The standard library for systems code (stage 12a): containers and text with native representations, updated in place when they are unique.</p>
<ul><li><code>Array A</code>: a growable array (<a href="#Array.push"><code>Array.push</code></a>, <a href="#Array.getD"><code>Array.getD</code></a>, <a href="#Array.set"><code>Array.set</code></a>);</li><li><a href="#Str"><code>Str</code></a>: UTF-8 text in a native buffer (<a href="#Str.append"><code>Str.append</code></a>, <a href="#Str.slice"><code>Str.slice</code></a>, <a href="#Str.byte"><code>Str.byte</code></a>);</li><li><code>StrMap V</code>: a map from <a href="#Str"><code>Str</code></a> keys to values (<a href="#StrMap.insert"><code>StrMap.insert</code></a>, <a href="#StrMap.findD"><code>StrMap.findD</code></a>).</li></ul>
<p>They are axioms with <code>extern</code> operations, implemented by the runtime (runtime/). When a value is unique (its reference count is one), <code>push</code>, <code>set</code> and <code>insert</code> update it in place instead of copying it.</p>
<pre><code>def squares : Array Nat :=
  Array.push (Array.push (Array.push Array.empty 0) 1) 4
-- Array.getD squares 2 0 = 4, Array.size squares = 3</code></pre>
</div>

## Sys

<a id="module-Sys"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Sys</h4>
<p>System interfaces (stage 9h): the environment, files and directories, processes, clocks and file descriptors.</p>
<p>Everything here is POSIX underneath (<code>runtime/</code>, section &quot;system interfaces&quot;). An operation that can fail returns <code>IO (Except String A)</code>: the error is the C library&#39;s message for <code>errno</code>, after what was being done (<code>&quot;/x: No such file or directory&quot;</code>). <code>EIO A</code> is that type as a monad, for <code>do</code> blocks that stop at the first error, and <a href="#EIO.toIO"><code>EIO.toIO</code></a> runs one as a program (printing the error and exiting with code 1). Like every foreign function, these only run in compiled code (<code>wiz run</code>).</p>
<p>Main definitions:</p>
<ul><li>errors: <a href="#EIO"><code>EIO</code></a>, <a href="#Sys.check"><code>Sys.check</code></a>, <a href="#Sys.lift"><code>Sys.lift</code></a>;</li><li>the environment: <a href="#Env.get"><code>Env.get</code></a>, <a href="#Env.set"><code>Env.set</code></a>, <a href="#Env.list"><code>Env.list</code></a>;</li><li>files and directories: <a href="#FS.readFile"><code>FS.readFile</code></a>, <a href="#FS.writeFile"><code>FS.writeFile</code></a>, <a href="#FS.listDir"><code>FS.listDir</code></a>, <a href="#FS.stat"><code>FS.stat</code></a>, <a href="#FS.createTempDir"><code>FS.createTempDir</code></a>, <a href="#FS.removeAll"><code>FS.removeAll</code></a>, and buffered handles <a href="#File"><code>File</code></a>;</li><li>processes: <a href="#Process.output"><code>Process.output</code></a>, <a href="#Process.run"><code>Process.run</code></a>, <a href="#Process.spawn"><code>Process.spawn</code></a> (a <a href="#Child"><code>Child</code></a>), and <a href="#Process.spawnWith"><code>Process.spawnWith</code></a> with <a href="#SpawnOptions"><code>SpawnOptions</code></a>;</li><li>time: <a href="#Duration"><code>Duration</code></a>, <a href="#Clock.monotonic"><code>Clock.monotonic</code></a>, <a href="#Clock.sleep"><code>Clock.sleep</code></a>;</li><li>unbuffered descriptors with time limits: <a href="#Fd"><code>Fd</code></a>, <a href="#Fd.readWithin"><code>Fd.readWithin</code></a>, <a href="#Fd.poll"><code>Fd.poll</code></a>.</li></ul>
<pre><code>import Sys

def main : IO Unit := EIO.toIO (do
  dir ← FS.createTempDir;
  FS.writeFile (Path.join dir &quot;a.txt&quot;) &quot;hello\n&quot;;
  out ← Process.output &quot;cat&quot; (.cons (Path.join dir &quot;a.txt&quot;) .nil) &quot;&quot;;
  EIO.lift (IO.print out.stdout);
  FS.removeAll dir)</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="Fd"></a>

foreign type · `Sys.wiz:624`

```text
Type
```
<div class="doc"><p>An unbuffered POSIX file descriptor, for terminals, pipes and devices, with time limits.</p>

## Tagged

<a id="module-Tagged"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Tagged</h4>
<p>Tagged text (stage 11m; a library of its own since 11s): a pretty-printed term whose subterms are tagged, as the language server sends it (<code>infoview-protocol.md</code> §2), and what both its browser front ends do with it: flatten it, number and navigate its tags, render it as HTML with hoverable subterms, and describe a subterm (<code>wiz/subtermInfo</code>).</p>
<p>The infoview (lib/Infoview.wiz: the terminal and the web infoview, web/Web.wiz) and the documentation&#39;s pages (<code>wiz doc</code>, <a href="#DocPage.step"><code>DocPage.step</code></a>, run by the same Wasm module) share it. Pure functions; the programs do the input and output.</p>
<ul><li><a href="#TT"><code>TT</code></a>: tagged text, read from the protocol&#39;s JSON with <a href="#TT.ofJson"><code>TT.ofJson</code></a>.</li><li><a href="#TT.toString"><code>TT.toString</code></a>, <a href="#TT.toHtml"><code>TT.toHtml</code></a>, <a href="#TT.tags"><code>TT.tags</code></a>: its plain text, its HTML, its tags.</li><li><a href="#Tagged.navigate"><code>Tagged.navigate</code></a>: moving a selection between tags (<a href="#Nav"><code>Nav</code></a>).</li><li><a href="#Tagged.infoHtml"><code>Tagged.infoHtml</code></a>: the box describing a subterm.</li><li><a href="#DocSt"><code>DocSt</code></a>, <a href="#DocPage.step"><code>DocPage.step</code></a>: the model of a documentation page.</li></ul>
<pre><code>-- `Nat → Nat`, with the whole type and the first `Nat` tagged
def t : TT := .tag 0 &quot;pi&quot; &quot;&quot; (.append (.cons (.tag 1 &quot;const&quot; &quot;Nat&quot; (.text &quot;Nat&quot;))
  (.cons (.text &quot; → Nat&quot;) .nil)))
#eval TT.toString t   -- &quot;Nat → Nat&quot;
#eval TT.toHtml 2 t   -- the `Nat` span carries the class `sel`</code></pre>
</div>

## Text

<a id="module-Text"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Text</h4>
<p>Text and lists (stage 9j): the string and list functions every program needs, in one module, pure (so <code>#eval</code> runs them) and linear in the length of their input.</p>
<p><strong>Cost model.</strong> A <a href="#String"><code>String</code></a> is <a href="#String.mk"><code>String.mk</code></a> around a <code>List Char</code>, in the kernel and at runtime alike (<code>builtin string</code> only changes how values print), so:</p>
<ul><li>walking a string front to back, <a href="#String.chars"><code>String.chars</code></a>, <a href="#String.mk"><code>String.mk</code></a>, a prefix test, taking or dropping a prefix are cheap (proportional to what is walked);</li><li><code>String.append a b</code> copies <code>a</code> (not <code>b</code>): appending in a loop from the left is quadratic. Build from the right (<a href="#String.join"><code>String.join</code></a>, <a href="#String.intercalate"><code>String.intercalate</code></a> do), or keep a reversed <code>List Char</code> and reverse it once;</li><li>the end of a string is far: <a href="#String.endsWith"><code>String.endsWith</code></a>, <a href="#String.dropEnd"><code>String.dropEnd</code></a>, <a href="#String.trimRight"><code>String.trimRight</code></a> reverse it once;</li><li>every call into C converts the list to a C string and back (linear each time).</li></ul>
<p><code>Std.Str</code> is the native alternative when a program does a lot of indexing.</p>
<p>Main definitions: list functions (<a href="#List.map"><code>List.map</code></a>, <a href="#List.filter"><code>List.filter</code></a>, <a href="#List.foldr"><code>List.foldr</code></a>, <a href="#List.find"><code>List.find</code></a>, …), character tests (<a href="#Char.isSpace"><code>Char.isSpace</code></a>, <a href="#Char.isDigit"><code>Char.isDigit</code></a>), and strings: <a href="#String.splitOn"><code>String.splitOn</code></a>, <a href="#String.intercalate"><code>String.intercalate</code></a>, <a href="#String.trim"><code>String.trim</code></a>, <a href="#String.replace"><code>String.replace</code></a>, <a href="#String.parseNat"><code>String.parseNat</code></a>, <a href="#String.startsWith"><code>String.startsWith</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.repr"><code>Nat.repr</code></a>.</p>
<pre><code>import Text

#eval String.splitOn &quot;a,b,,c&quot; &quot;,&quot;                   -- [&quot;a&quot;, &quot;b&quot;, &quot;&quot;, &quot;c&quot;]
#eval String.intercalate &quot;, &quot; [&quot;x&quot;, &quot;y&quot;, &quot;z&quot;]        -- &quot;x, y, z&quot;
#eval String.parseNat (String.trim &quot;  42 &quot;)          -- some 42</code></pre>
</div>

## Trace

<a id="module-Trace"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Trace</h4>
<p>Traces and Mealy machines (<code>import Trace</code>): the common semantics of the HDL&#39;s circuits (lib/Hdl/Core.wiz, <a href="#Circuit.trace"><code>Circuit.trace</code></a>), the temporal logic over them, and anything else that runs step by step. Design: wiz-notes/cohesion-hardware.md, 2.1.</p>
<ul><li>A trace is a function <code>Nat → A</code>, not a ν-stream: equality at ν is stuck, while equality of functions is pointwise and computes (funext is a definition).</li><li>A Mealy machine is a step <code>S → I → S × O</code>; <code>stateAt</code>/<code>outAt</code> run it along an input trace. A finite simulation of <code>n</code> cycles sees <code>Trace.take n</code> of the trace.</li></ul>
</div>

<a id="Mealy.stateAt_succ"></a>
### `Mealy.stateAt_succ`

def · `Trace.wiz:61`

```text
{S : Type} → {I : Type} → {O : Type} → (m : Mealy S I O) → (s0 : S) → (xs : Trace I) → (t : Nat) → Mealy.stateAt S I O m s0 xs (Nat.succ t) = Mealy.stateAt S I O m (m s0 (xs 0)).1 (Trace.tail I xs) t
```
<div class="doc"><p>one step, then the rest: the run from <code>s0</code> at <code>t + 1</code> is the run from the next state on the rest of the inputs at <code>t</code></p>
</div>

<div class="doc"><p>One step, then the rest: the output at <code>t + 1</code> is the run from the next state on the rest of the inputs at <code>t</code>.</p>
</div>

<a id="Mealy.invariant"></a>
### `Mealy.invariant`

def · `Trace.wiz:94`

```text
{S : Type} → {I : Type} → {O : Type} → (m : Mealy S I O) → (s0 : S) → (xs : Trace I) → (env : I → Prop) → (inv : S → Prop) → inv s0 → ((s : S) → (x : I) → env x → inv s → inv (m s x).1) → ((t : Nat) → env (xs t)) → (t : Nat) → inv (Mealy.stateAt S I O m s0 xs t)
```
<div class="doc"><p>Invariance (assume-guarantee): an inductive invariant <code>inv</code> of the step, for inputs that satisfy the environment assumption <code>env</code>, holds of every state of the run.</p>
</div>


<a id="Mealy.simulates"></a>
### `Mealy.simulates`

def · `Trace.wiz:103`

```text
{S : Type} → {T : Type} → {I : Type} → {J : Type} → {O : Type} → {P : Type} → (impl : Mealy S I O) → (spec : Mealy T J P) → (embS : T → S) → (embI : J → I) → (embO : P → O) → ((s : T) → (x : J) → impl (embS s) (embI x) = (embS (spec s x).1, embO (spec s x).2)) → (s0 : T) → (xs : Trace J) → (t : Nat) → Mealy.stateAt S I O impl (embS s0) (Trace.map J I embI xs) t = embS (Mealy.stateAt T J P spec s0 xs t)
```
<div class="doc"><p>Refinement by a representation map: the implementation, started in the image of the specification&#39;s state and driven by the image of its inputs, stays in the image of its states and outputs the image of its outputs, for ever. The premise is one step.</p>
</div>


<a id="Mealy.simulatesOut"></a>
### `Mealy.simulatesOut`

def · `Trace.wiz:113`

```text
{S : Type} → {T : Type} → {I : Type} → {J : Type} → {O : Type} → {P : Type} → (impl : Mealy S I O) → (spec : Mealy T J P) → (embS : T → S) → (embI : J → I) → (embO : P → O) → ((s : T) → (x : J) → impl (embS s) (embI x) = (embS (spec s x).1, embO (spec s x).2)) → (s0 : T) → (xs : Trace J) → (t : Nat) → Mealy.outAt S I O impl (embS s0) (Trace.map J I embI xs) t = embO (Mealy.outAt T J P spec s0 xs t)
```
<div class="doc"><p>The refinement map also matches the outputs, at every time.</p>
</div>

## Vec

<a id="module-Vec"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Vec</h4>
<p>Bounded numbers and length-indexed vectors (<code>import Vec</code>).</p>
<p><code>Fin n</code> is a number below <code>n</code>; <code>Vec A n</code> is a list of exactly <code>n</code> elements of <code>A</code>, so <a href="#Vec.head"><code>Vec.head</code></a> only takes a non-empty vector and <a href="#Vec.get"><code>Vec.get</code></a> only an index in range. The length of a <a href="#Vec"><code>Vec</code></a> is an erased index (quantity 0): at runtime a vector is a list, and <a href="#Vec.length"><code>Vec.length</code></a> counts it (<a href="#Vec.length_eq"><code>Vec.length_eq</code></a> ties the count to the index); a <a href="#Fin"><code>Fin</code></a> is a <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a>, its proof erased.</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#Fin"><code>Fin</code></a> (<a href="#Fin.of"><code>Fin.of</code></a>, <a href="#Fin.zero"><code>Fin.zero</code></a>, <a href="#Fin.succ"><code>Fin.succ</code></a>, <a href="#Fin.last"><code>Fin.last</code></a>), <a href="#Vec"><code>Vec</code></a> with <a href="#Vec.get"><code>Vec.get</code></a>, <a href="#Vec.set"><code>Vec.set</code></a>, <a href="#Vec.map"><code>Vec.map</code></a>, <a href="#Vec.zipWith"><code>Vec.zipWith</code></a>, <a href="#Vec.foldr"><code>Vec.foldr</code></a>, <a href="#Vec.append"><code>Vec.append</code></a>, <a href="#Vec.reverse"><code>Vec.reverse</code></a>, <a href="#Vec.splitAt"><code>Vec.splitAt</code></a>, conversions to and from <a href="#List"><code>List</code></a>, and lemmas such as <a href="#Vec.get_set"><code>Vec.get_set</code></a> and <a href="#Vec.map_map"><code>Vec.map_map</code></a>. The <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a> lemmas the indices need are in lib/Nat.wiz.</p>
<pre><code>import Vec

def v : Vec Nat 3 := Vec.fromList [1, 2, 3]
#eval Vec.get v (Fin.of 3 1 rfl)          -- 2
#eval Vec.toList (Vec.map Nat.succ v)     -- [2, 3, 4]</code></pre>
</div>

## Word

<a id="module-Word"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>Word</h4>
<p>Machine integers (<code>import Word</code>).</p>
<p><code>UIntN w</code> is a <code>w</code>-bit unsigned integer and <code>IntN w</code> a <code>w</code>-bit two&#39;s-complement integer. Both are a number of bits, below <code>2^w</code> (normalised by construction: every operation here reduces mod <code>2^w</code>, so arithmetic wraps around). The kernel computes with these definitions (fast on numerals: <a href="#Nat.mod"><code>Nat.mod</code></a>, <a href="#Nat.pow"><code>Nat.pow</code></a>, … are native), proofs see them, and compiled code runs native implementations instead (<code>implemented_by</code>, at the end of the module).</p>
<p>One width-indexed type serves the HDL&#39;s bit vectors (<code>BitVec n := UIntN n</code>, lib/BitVec.wiz; any width: 1, 5, 65, …) and Rust&#39;s <code>u32</code> (<code>U32 := UIntN 32</code>). Division by zero follows Lean: <code>a / 0 = 0</code> and <code>a % 0 = a</code> (Rust panics; a Rust front end checks first).</p>
<p>Main definitions: <a href="#UIntN"><code>UIntN</code></a> and <a href="#IntN"><code>IntN</code></a>, built with <a href="#UIntN.ofNat"><code>UIntN.ofNat</code></a>/<a href="#IntN.ofNat"><code>IntN.ofNat</code></a>/<a href="#IntN.ofNeg"><code>IntN.ofNeg</code></a> and read with <a href="#UIntN.toNat"><code>UIntN.toNat</code></a>; wrapping arithmetic, comparisons, bitwise operations and shifts; <a href="#UIntN.resize"><code>UIntN.resize</code></a>/<a href="#IntN.resize"><code>IntN.resize</code></a> between widths; the operator instances (<code>+</code>, <code>*</code>, <code>/</code>, numerals, …); Rust&#39;s fixed widths <a href="#U8"><code>U8</code></a> … <a href="#I64"><code>I64</code></a>; and the natives compiled code uses.</p>
<pre><code>import Word

#eval UIntN.toNat (UIntN.add (U8.ofNat 250) (U8.ofNat 10))       -- 4, it wraps
#eval IntN.toNat (IntN.div (I8.ofNeg 7) (I8.ofNat 2))            -- 253, the bits of -3</code></pre>
</div>

<a id="UIntN"></a>
### `UIntN`

sealed inductive · `Word.wiz:200`

```text
Nat → Type
```
<div class="doc"><p><code>UIntN w</code>: a <code>w</code>-bit unsigned integer, a number below <code>2^w</code>.</p>
<p>No field mentions the width, but it is part of the type all the same (a phantom parameter, stage 22e): <code>UIntN 8</code> and <code>UIntN 16</code> are different types, and <code>w</code> is inferred from an argument. At runtime a word is <code>⟨0 bits⟩</code> in the model (or just its bits, compiled: see the end of the module).</p>
<p>Both <a href="#UIntN"><code>UIntN</code></a> and <a href="#IntN"><code>IntN</code></a> are sealed (22k): they have the same shape but are different types (<a href="#UIntN.toIntN"><code>UIntN.toIntN</code></a>/<a href="#IntN.toUIntN"><code>IntN.toUIntN</code></a> convert, for free), and no look-alike is either. A word carries the proof that its bits are below <code>2^w</code> (22l: an erased field, so at runtime it is still just its bits), which the natives rely on: the kernel&#39;s definitions and compiled code agree on every word there is. The constructors are private: this module keeps the invariant <code>toNat &lt; 2^w</code> (every function here returns an in-range word if its arguments are), so outside it a word is built with <a href="#UIntN.ofNat"><code>UIntN.ofNat</code></a> and read with <a href="#UIntN.toNat"><code>UIntN.toNat</code></a> (<a href="#UIntN.toNat_lt"><code>UIntN.toNat_lt</code></a> gives the range).</p>
</div>

<a id="UIntN.shiftLeft"></a>
### `UIntN.shiftLeft`

def · `Word.wiz:296`

```text
{ω w : Nat} → UIntN w → Nat → UIntN w
```
<div class="doc"><p>Shift left by <code>k</code> places, wrapping (bits shifted out at the top are lost). The exponent is capped at the width: for <code>k &gt;= w</code> the result is <code>(a * 2^w) mod 2^w = 0</code>, and the cap keeps the model from building <code>2^k</code> (which panics at large <code>k</code>) for a result that is <code>0</code>.</p>
</div>

<div class="doc"><p><a href="#UIntN.shiftLeft"><code>UIntN.shiftLeft</code></a> below the width is <code>ofNat w (a * 2^k)</code> (the capped exponent is <code>k</code>).</p>

## WordArray

<a id="module-WordArray"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>WordArray</h4>
<p>Unboxed arrays of machine words (<code>import WordArray</code>): <a href="#U8Array"><code>U8Array</code></a>, <a href="#U32Array"><code>U32Array</code></a> and <a href="#U64Array"><code>U64Array</code></a>, functional values updated in place when they are unique (as <a href="#Array"><code>Array</code></a>).</p>
<p>The model. Each is a list of words (<code>mk (toList : List U32)</code>), and every operation below is defined on that list: the kernel computes with the definitions, proofs see them (the laws at the end), and <code>#eval</code>/<code>#run</code> run them.</p>
<p>Compiled code runs natives instead (<code>runtime/</code>, <code>wiz_warray_*</code>), by <code>implemented_by</code>. An array is then a header and one C array of <code>uint8_t</code>, <code>uint32_t</code> or <code>uint64_t</code> with its length: no element is a Wiz object, so a 1M-element <a href="#U32Array"><code>U32Array</code></a> is 4 MB with nothing for reference counting to visit (an <code>Array U32</code> is 8 MB of <code>wiz_val</code>s; a <code>List U32</code> 24 MB of cells). An update copies the array when it is shared and changes it in place when it is unique. C code given an array (<code>link_c</code>, <code>glue</code>) reads it with <code>wiz_warray_data</code>/<code>wiz_warray_len</code>.</p>
<p>Trust. The natives are trusted to agree with the definitions (<code>#print axioms</code> lists them, marked <code>native</code>, 22f); the module keeps no invariant beyond the words&#39; own (each element is below 2^w). Out-of-range indices: <code>getD</code> gives the default, <code>set</code> changes nothing, as in the model. Where they part: the natives abort when memory runs out. The tests (group <code>natives</code>) run the same programs under the interpreter (the model) and compiled (the natives), C and LLVM.</p>
<p>Not here: arrays of other widths (<a href="#U16"><code>U16</code></a>, <a href="#I32"><code>I32</code></a>; add one the same way), in-place slices that share storage (a slice copies, unless it is a unique prefix), sorting.</p>
</div>

## WordBytes

<a id="module-WordBytes"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>WordBytes</h4>
<p><a href="#Bytes"><code>Bytes</code></a> as lists of <a href="#U8"><code>U8</code></a> (sys-bytes, stage 9k). A module of its own: IO and Sys count bytes as <a href="#Nat"><code>Nat</code></a>s below 256 and don&#39;t import Word, so the conversions between the byte buffer and fixed-width words live here.</p>
<ul><li><a href="#Bytes.ofU8s"><code>Bytes.ofU8s</code></a>: a list of bytes as a <a href="#Bytes"><code>Bytes</code></a> buffer;</li><li><a href="#Bytes.toU8s"><code>Bytes.toU8s</code></a>: a buffer&#39;s bytes as a list.</li></ul>
<pre><code>Bytes.toU8s (Bytes.ofU8s l) = l</code></pre>
</div>

**In this module:**

- [Bytes.ofU8sAux](#Bytes.ofU8sAux)
- [Bytes.ofU8s](#Bytes.ofU8s)
- [Bytes.toU8sAux](#Bytes.toU8sAux)
- [Bytes.toU8s](#Bytes.toU8s)


<a id="Bytes.ofU8sAux"></a>
### `Bytes.ofU8sAux`

def · `WordBytes.wiz:18`

```text
List U8 → Bytes → Bytes
```
<div class="doc"><p><a href="#Bytes.ofU8s"><code>Bytes.ofU8s</code></a>&#39;s loop: push each byte of the list onto the accumulator <code>acc</code>.</p>
</div>

```text
List U8 → Bytes
```

</div>

```text
Bytes → Nat → List U8 → List U8
```
<div class="doc"><p><a href="#Bytes.toU8s"><code>Bytes.toU8s</code></a>&#39;s loop: the first <code>k</code> bytes of <code>b</code> in front of <code>acc</code> (built from the end, so no reversing).</p>
</div>


<a id="Bytes.toU8s"></a>
### `Bytes.toU8s`

def · `WordBytes.wiz:29`


## WordMap

<a id="module-WordMap"></a>
<div class="doc"><h4>WordMap</h4>
<p>Maps from 64-bit words (<code>import WordMap</code>): <code>U64Map V</code>, a functional finite map with <a href="#U64"><code>U64</code></a> keys, updated in place when it is unique (as <a href="#StrMap"><code>StrMap</code></a>). Keys of other word types, typed ids (<code>NodeId k</code>, 22e) and interned strings (lib/Intern.wiz) go through <a href="#U64"><code>U64</code></a> (<a href="#UIntN.resize"><code>UIntN.resize</code></a>, or the id&#39;s bits).</p>
<p>The model. A map is its entries, <code>mk (entries : List (U64 × V))</code>, with the keys strictly increasing: the module keeps that invariant (the constructor is private and every operation here preserves it), so each map has exactly one model, and <code>toList</code> and <code>foldl</code> see the entries by increasing key, in the kernel, the interpreters and compiled code alike. The kernel computes with the definitions and proofs see them (the laws at the end).</p>
<p>Compiled code runs natives instead (<code>runtime/</code>, <code>wiz_wmap_*</code>): an open-addressing hash table of <code>uint64_t</code> keys and Wiz values (linear probing, deletion by backward shift, at most half full), so <code>insert</code>, <code>find</code>, <code>erase</code> and <code>contains</code> take expected constant time, and only the values are Wiz objects. An update copies the table when it is shared and changes it in place when it is unique. Reading the entries back (<code>toList</code>, <code>foldl</code>, <code>keys</code>) sorts them: O(n log n).</p>
<p>Trust. The natives are trusted to agree with the definitions (<code>#print axioms</code> lists them, marked <code>native</code>, 22f), and the natives&#39; <code>toList</code> relies on the module invariant (the model is the sorted list). They abort when memory runs out. The tests (group <code>wordmap</code>) run the same programs under the interpreter and compiled, C and LLVM.</p>
</div>
